ch14: A machine on a real plant has a screen beside it. The operator reads it at a glance, sets a temperature, starts and stops, and sees what went wrong last night. In Logix Connect that screen is the Process HMI : an operator terminal you place anywhere on the floor and point at a machine. It shows a live faceplate of a tank, the mix kitchen, a case packer, a camera, an infeed or a whole line; it is a touch screen (a mouse click is a touch) and it works in the top view and in 3D. The Operator View is the same screen as a document tab of its own, full size, with a panel of real-looking buttons beside it. Placing an HMI and connecting it In Program mode, Operator → Process HMI in the palette; click the floor to place it. In its properties, Shows : pick the machine. Left blank, it shows the nearest vessel. Heater setpoint tag : the controller tag the TEMP page writes, normally a REAL. START button tag , STOP button tag and Running indicator tag : optional; with them set, START and STOP appear on the MAIN page. Function keys : up to five more machines, by name. The keys under the screen then switch the terminal between them, so one terminal can run the whole line. Screen size and Mounting (pedestal or wall bracket) are for the 3D view. The HMI has no I/O points of its own: it reads the machine directly and writes only the tags you give it. Its properties end in a Connections section that says what it shows and which tags it writes; on a tank, the same section lists every HMI showing it and every pipe in and out. Touching the screen The screen answers in Run mode; in Program mode a click selects the part instead, so you can move it. Across the top are the page tabs: MAIN , TEMP (on a vessel with a temperature), RECIPE (on a mix tank) and ALARMS , with a red dot on ALARMS while an alarm is active. The faceplates are drawn the way plant HMIs are (ISA-101 style): a grey screen and dark text, with colour kept for what is running and what is wrong, so a lit heater or a red alarm line stands out because nothing else is bright. Theme → HMI style: classic colour switches to the older, colourful look. The mix tank’s MAIN page during a batch: the vessel at its level, the mixer, the heater, the state, the temperature, a 60-second trend, the ratio, the flows and the equipment. The TEMP page: the temperature, the heater and high-limit status, the setpoint and the thermostat cards, the trend with both as dashed lines. The RECIPE page: each inlet with its liquid and OPEN or LOCKED, the mode, the product, and the recipe’s A share, temperature and mixing time. MAIN is the overview: the vessel with its liquid, the HI and LO marks, the state (FILLING, HEAT+MIX, MIXING, DRAINING, HOLDING, EMPTY, PURGING), the temperature, the trend, the share of each ingredient in the batch, what each flowmeter reads and each pump, the heater and the mixer, grey stopped and green running. TEMP has two cards: HEATER SETPOINT , which writes the setpoint tag (what the heater does with it is up to your program), and HIGH LIMIT · THERMOSTAT , the tank’s own thermostat, which is the hardware safety and not the control. Touch a value for the keypad: digits, . , ⌫ , CLR , then ENT to write or ESC to leave it. ALARMS lists every Simulator Log line that names this machine, newest first, with anything abnormal in red. Watch for If the program writes the same tag on every scan, the operator’s value lasts one scan, and the message line says so in red: the tag has two writers and the program always writes last. Give the operator a tag of their own, and let the program read it. START and STOP on the screen Give the HMI a START and a STOP tag (BOOLs) and its MAIN page shows two pushbuttons. A touch pulses the tag: on for a quarter of a second of machine time, then off, so the program sees it for several scans, exactly like a momentary button wired to an input. Give it a Running tag too and START lights green and reads RUNNING while that tag is on. The program has to listen for them, and the plant way is in parallel with the hardwired buttons, never instead of them: the HMI tags are ordinary BOOLs (not aliases of inputs, since a real HMI cannot write an input), and the run rung takes either START and either STOP. Level 7 is set up like that. [XIC(Start_PB),XIC(HMI_Start),XIC(Run)]XIO(Stop_PB)XIO(HMI_Stop)XIC(E_Stop)OTE(Run); Try it: three ways to start On Level 7 with its reference program, start the batch from the console’s Start button, stop it with STOP on Tank_HMI, start it again from the Operator View, and stop it from the console. One seal-in rung, three operator stations. Now delete the HMI_Start branch and press START on the Operator View: the press is logged and the tag pulses (watch it in Quick Watch), and nothing happens, because no rung reads it. An HMI only asks; the program decides. The Operator View Window → Open Operator View , the Operator View under the simulator in the organizer, or HMI in the phone’s bottom bar. A row of buttons across the top switches screens in one tap; on the bottle line they are the line’s console, the mix tank, the case packer, the camera, the tanks, the totes and the feeders. Beside the screen is a control panel: a RUNNING lamp, an ALARM lamp, START and STOP (with the tag each writes under it, in red if there is no such tag) and a message line. Each screen keeps its own tags, and the first time you switch to one, the view takes them from the Process HMI on the floor that shows it. The buttons work in Run mode; in Program mode they say so and do nothing. The case packer’s faceplate: the infeed, the head, the case lane, the counts by size. The camera’s faceplate: the last image with its tools, the result and the handshake with the PLC. The packer’s screen has START, STOP, Running and its case counts; a camera has no START or STOP, because it runs when the PLC enables triggering, so its panel keeps only ON LINE and ALARM. Recipes: what goes in, what stays out A real batch tank is never trusted to the program alone to keep the wrong liquid out. The mix tank has the interlocks built in, the way a plant puts them in the pump starter circuit: a pump on a locked inlet does not run, even with its output on, and the MAIN page shows A LOCKED or B LOCKED in red. The RECIPE page is where the operator sets the batch up before START. A supply tote holds an ingredient: water, cola syrup, lemon-lime syrup, flavour concentrate, orange or apple concentrate, milk or oil. A product is made from its ingredients in the tank, to a recipe. Picking a product on the PRODUCT card loads its line of this table into the tank and the setpoint tag, and sets the mode to AUTO: Product Inlet A Inlet B A share Temperature Mix time CO2 Soda water cola syrup 83 % (5 : 1) 100 °F 8 s 3.5 volumes Lemon-lime water lemon-lime syrup 83 % (5 : 1) 100 °F 8 s — Sparkling water water flavour concentrate 95 % (19 : 1) 60 °F 4 s 3.0 volumes Juice water orange concentrate 75 % (3 : 1) 160 °F 10 s — Apple juice water apple concentrate 85 % (5.7 : 1) 160 °F 10 s — Water water — 100 % 70 °F 0 s — Milk milk — 100 % 70 °F 0 s — Oil oil — 100 % 70 °F 0 s — The MODE decides which inlets a batch uses: AUTO (whatever the recipe calls for), MIX A+B , A ONLY , B ONLY , SAME LIQUID (inlet B draws through a crossover from A’s source, so the tank fills twice as fast) and WATER RINSE . On top of the mode come three locks no mode lifts: contamination (oil and the water-based liquids never meet, and the tank remembers what is in it until it is emptied or purged), lockout / tagout (LOCK on the page, or Locked out on a tote, until someone unlocks it), and purging . Once a batch is in the tank and the process is running, the recipe is locked ( Recipe locked: a batch is in cycle ) until it is stopped, purged or finished; START, STOP, PURGE and the inlet locks stay live, because lockout is a safety function and is never locked out itself. PURGE drains the tank to the floor drain on demand, after asking, and the batch is discarded. Try it: water when water is called for On Level 7 with its reference program, open the Operator View and the RECIPE page. With the batch stopped, pick WATER: inlet B goes LOCKED. Press START: water doses as before, but when the program turns on PumpB nothing comes in, the Simulator Log says why, and the sequence waits for a HI probe that never comes. The program asked; the interlock said no. Stop, pick SAME LIQUID and start again: inlet B runs water from Supply_A and the tank fills.
ch15: The machine is the LogixPro bottle line, the exercise generations of technicians learned shift registers on, rebuilt as a plant. A main conveyor on a raised deck indexes bottles one 40 px pitch at a time past three head sensors, a fill station fed from a soda reservoir, a capper with a rotary cap magazine, a labeler, an inspection camera, a scrap gate and a divert gate. Broken bottles, and bottles the camera fails, are dropped off the deck into a shredder whose chute fills boxes on a box conveyor below, and a second labeler bands each of those boxes with hazard tape. Small bottles go down a catch incline onto a divert conveyor, which runs on under a case packer at the end of the line; large bottles run on along the deck to the same packer. The packer picks large bottles off the deck and small ones off the floor conveyor, 1.7 m below, and packs them four to a case, one size per case, on a case lane driven by a variable frequency drive. Beside the line a mix kitchen makes the soda: water and cola syrup batched in a mix tank, carbonated, and pumped to the reservoir. An operator console has Start, Stop, a Run lamp, a red fault lamp and a blue Reset, a carbonation key, a thumbwheel preset with Enter, and six displays: SMALL, LARGE, SCRAP, BOXES, IN BOX and CASES. Main_Conv: raised deck, +1.7 m, indexes one pitch per stop → Bottle_Feed LS1 LS2 LS3 Supply_Tank Filler Capper Labeler Camera Scrap_Gate Divert_Gate Grinder Scrap_Conv: Box_Feed → hazard tape → LS10 under the chute → Box_Out incline Divert_Conv (small) → lower lane Case_Packer Side elevation, not to scale. Broken and rejected bottles drop into the shredder; small ones ride the incline; large ones run to the end. The bottle line in one picture. Everything the gates do is a drop: the main conveyor is a raised deck, so a gate is a door onto the level below. The finished line running in the Side view: bottles standing at the stops, the reservoir and the filler, the capper, the labeler, the gates over the lower level. The program is fifteen routines called from the main routine, one per step, and each step is a lesson that leaves you with something that runs: Run circuit ( S1_Run ): Start / Stop seal-in, the run lamp. Dwell and feed ( S2_Dwell ): a one-second timer while the belt stands, and one bottle per stop from the feeder. Index ( S3_Index ): step exactly one pitch on the encoder when nothing holds the belt. Shift registers ( S4_Registers ): three registers take the three head sensors once per stop; a fourth takes the camera’s verdict. Fill ( S5_Fill ): a bottle under the nozzle gets its large or small charge. Supply ( S6_Supply ): the reservoir’s inlet on its floats, the head-tank protection, the tank stack light. Cap ( S7_Cap ): a cap from the chute, the cap feeder, the column lights. Sort ( S8_Sort ): the scrap and divert gates, the divert conveyor, the box conveyor and the shredder. Count and preset ( S9_Count ): the displays, the thumbwheel batch stop, Enter. Label ( S10_Label ): an FLS-style dispenser one stop past the capper: the Start / Ready / Error handshake, a latched fault, lamps. Alarms ( S11_Alarms ): the program watching the machine: overloads, an end-of-line check of the tracking, a dirty eye, the labeler, the inlet, the packer; a fault lamp and Reset. Pack ( S12_Pack ): the case packer and the VFD on its case lane: fast, a creep onto the mark, a speed reference scaled to 0–10 V with SCP, four bottles a case. Mix ( S13_Mix ): the mix kitchen: water and cola syrup batched into soda at the 5 : 1 throw, heated and mixed to the recipe, carbonated, and pumped to the reservoir whenever step 6 calls for it. Hazard tape ( S14_Hazard ): a second dispenser bands every scrap box. Inspect ( S15_Inspect ): a camera checks every bottle for its cap, its label and its fill, and the scrap gate takes the ones it fails. The steps are numbered in the order they were added to the line, and that is also the order in MainRoutine, with one exception that chapter 9 explains: step 3’s JSR is always the last, so every station’s request is seen before the belt is allowed to step. The lessons take steps 14 and 15 with the labeler (chapter 27), because they use its handshake, and step 13 last, because it changes where the soda comes from. Guided mode You can do Part IV with the book open beside the app, or let the app walk you through it. File → New Project… → Build the bottle line (or Guided → Start: Build the Bottle Line Here on an empty floor) opens a panel that follows these chapters one lesson at a time. Each lesson lists what it checks: parts placed at the book’s positions, alias tags made, the routine and its JSR in place, the routine verifying; and, for the steps that do something, what it watches for while you run the line: Line_Run coming on when you press Start, a bottle filled and capped, a label going on. A check turns green when the page sees it happen. Guided mode on a new project: the empty floor and the first lesson. The panel checks your rungs itself. A reference rung is logic verified (one tick) when a rung of yours does the same thing: the page runs both through every combination of the bits they read and write, so the order of the contacts, how you draw a branch, or writing a tag as its alias address make no difference, and a timer or a move must be there with the same operands. A rung that is close but wrong stays open with one line on what differs, and the first one still to write is marked NEXT. In Run mode a verified rung is proven (two ticks) the first time it goes true. Hints first. A reference rung you can read is a rung you will copy, so each one opens as its comment alone: the job, in words, which is how a rung arrives in real life. If you cannot write it from that, Hint lists what the rung uses, in no order; Shape shows its skeleton with every tag blanked, XIC(?)XIC(?)XIO(?)ONS(?)OTL(?) ; and only Show rung gives the text. Guided → Hints First turns this off for a project, and Predict First asks a Predict-it question before a rung is shown. Place them for me and Make them for me do a lesson’s layout or tags in one click when you would rather get to the programming. Progress saves with the project; the panel docks into the output window as a Guided tab, or folds into the Guided menu, which shows where you are. Chapter 16 lays the machine out, chapter 17 makes the tags, chapters 18 to 30 write the fifteen routines, and chapter 31 commissions the line. Every coordinate and setting below is the one the finished template uses, so your machine and the answer key are the same machine.

CASES: the case count from step 12. That is 46 parts. Their signals take 63 digital inputs, 33 digital outputs, 8 analog inputs and 1 analog output; the Scene sheet (click empty floor, Properties) counts what is in use. Switch to Side view and then 3D and walk along it: the pipe from the tank to the filler draws itself, the incline from the deck lands on the divert conveyor, the gates have their doors. Run it with no program Go to Run mode. Nothing moves, because every output is off; but the feeders set to automatic are not outputs: boxes start arriving on the box conveyor and queue at its head, because the conveyor is not running either, and cases do the same on the case lane. Back to Program mode. Watch for Positions are the centre of a conveyor’s start and the centre of every other part. A sensor must be on the conveyor’s centreline (y = 150 on the main line) to see bottles; a station must be at a stop position (x = 160 + 40n) to meet a bottle standing still. If you place by dragging, the snap does both for you.

This chapter lists the alias tags in one place, so you can see the whole shape of it and look any tag up later; you do not have to create them all now. ch18: In the app Guided mode’s lesson 3 is this chapter: it checks that this lesson’s tags are made, that S1_Run exists, is called from MainRoutine and verifies, and then watches the line while you run it and ticks each result as it happens: Press Start on the panel: Line_Run comes on and the Run lamp lights Press Stop: Line_Run drops A machine has one bit that says it is running, and everything else hangs off it. Make a routine called S1_Run ( Logic → New Routine… ) and give MainRoutine a single rung, JSR(S1_Run); . Then write these rungs in S1_Run. Tags this lesson needs Create these before you type the rungs (Verify reports any you miss as unknown). Tags from earlier lessons are not repeated. Tag Type Kind Description Start BOOL alias of Local:3:I.Data.9 LogixPro I:1/0 · Start push button, NO Line_Run BOOL base tag Seal-in run bit (LogixPro B3:0/0) Stop BOOL alias of Local:3:I.Data.10 LogixPro I:1/1 · Stop push button, NC (1 until pressed) Batch_Done BOOL base tag The large-bottle count has reached the thumbwheel preset Run BOOL alias of Local:5:O.Data.8 LogixPro O:2/10 · Run lamp Label_Req BOOL base tag Latched while the labeler is asked to apply; cleared at PadIn The rungs How it fits together Rung 0 is chapter 4’s seal-in with two extra conditions: XIC(Stop) rather than XIO, because the stop button is normally closed (pressing it makes the tag 0), and XIO(Batch_Done) , a bit step 9 will set when the batch is complete. Until then it is 0 and the XIO passes. Rung 1 drives the run lamp whenever the line runs; the main conveyor is deliberately not here, because it steps (step 3), and the divert conveyor, the box conveyor and the shredder have rules of their own (step 8). Rung 2 is housekeeping: when the line stops for any reason, drop a label request that is in progress so the labeler’s head goes home (step 10 explains the request). Notice what this routine does not do. A stopped line keeps the step in progress, the dwell’s time and every “done” bit, because the bottles have not moved: Start must carry on exactly where Stop left off, or the shift registers of step 4 and the bottles they describe drift apart. Step 11 has the check that proves it. Run it Run mode. Press Start on the panel: the Run lamp lights and Line_Run is 1 in Monitor Tags. Press Stop: it drops. Hold Stop while pressing Start: nothing, because the stop contact is open. That is the whole of step 1. S1_Run online with the finished line running: what your routine should look like once every step is in. Green is power flow. Try it Give the Run lamp a flash while the line is stopped but the controller is in Run mode: a TON that resets itself (chapter 7) and XIO(Line_Run)XIC(Flash.TT) on a branch of the lamp rung. Then take it out again: the lessons assume the lamp means running.  [XIC(Start),XIC(Line_Run)]XIC(Stop)XIO(Batch_Done)OTE(Line_Run); SEAL-IN: Start latches Line_Run through its own contact; Stop is a normally closed button (1 until pressed) so it breaks the seal; Batch_Done (step 9) also stops the line XIC(Line_Run)OTE(Run); Run lamp whenever the line runs. The main conveyor steps (step 3); the divert conveyor (step 8, it stops when the packer's lower lane is full), the box conveyor and the shredder have their own rules XIO(Line_Run)OTU(Label_Req); Line stopped: drop a label request in progress so the head goes home. Nothing else is forgotten on purpose: a step in progress (Conv_Index) and the done bits stay as they are, because the bottles have not moved, so Start carries on exactly where Stop left off and the registers stay in step with the bottles. Step 11's end-of-line check would catch it if they did not
ch19: In the app Guided mode’s lesson 4 is this chapter: it checks that this lesson’s tags are made, that S2_Dwell exists, is called from MainRoutine and verifies, and then watches the line while you run it and ticks each result as it happens: Start the line: Dwell.DN comes on after a second A bottle drops at the head of the line The line indexes: belt stops, sensors read, bottle dropped, belt steps. The dwell is the stop. Add JSR(S2_Dwell); to MainRoutine under step 1 and write the rung. Tags this lesson needs Create these before you type the rungs (Verify reports any you miss as unknown). Tags from earlier lessons are not repeated. Tag Type Kind Description Conv_Index BOOL base tag Latched while the belt steps one pitch Dwell TIMER base tag Belt stopped: sensors read, feeder drops a bottle Bottle_Feed_Emit BOOL alias of Local:4:O.Data.0 Bottle_Feed Emit: one bottle per rising edge The rungs How it fits together While the line runs and the belt is not stepping ( Conv_Index , which step 3 will latch while the belt moves), the Dwell timer counts a second, and on the same rung the feeder’s Emit is energized; the feeder is in edge mode, so one bottle appears at the head of the line on the rising edge, once per stop. When the dwell is done, step 3 steps the belt and resets the timer for the next stop. Why an RTO and not a TON? A TON resets the moment its rung goes false, and the rung goes false whenever the line stops. Press Stop half-way through a dwell, Start again, and a TON would time the whole second again; press Stop after the dwell was done and the registers (step 4, which shift when Dwell.DN comes on) would shift a second time for the same stop. The retentive timer keeps what it has: a stopped dwell resumes where it was, and a finished one stays done. An RTO only clears with RES, and that rung belongs to step 3, which moves the belt. The feeder does not drop a second bottle on Start either: an edge-mode feeder only drops when its exit is clear, and the bottle it dropped is still standing there. Run it Start the line. Exactly one bottle drops at the head of the belt and sits there, because nothing steps the belt yet; Dwell.DN comes on after a second and stays on. Watch Dwell.ACC count to 1000 and stop. That is correct for now: step 3 is next. S2_Dwell online with the finished line running: what your routine should look like once every step is in. Green is power flow. Try it Change the preset to 3000, Start, and press Stop when the accumulator reads about 1500: it holds 1500. Start again and it carries on to 3000. Set it back to 1000. In the finished line the dwell is the one number that sets the line’s speed.  XIC(Line_Run)XIO(Conv_Index)[RTO(Dwell,1000,0),OTE(Bottle_Feed_Emit)]; BELT STOPPED: a 1 s dwell runs and the feeder output is held on. Bottle_Feed is in edge mode, so it drops exactly one bottle per rising edge, that is one per stop. RTO, not TON: if the line is stopped in the middle of a dwell the time already run is kept (and a finished dwell stays done), so Start carries on and the registers do not shift twice for one stop. A new bottle is not dropped either: the feeder only drops when its exit is clear
ch20: In the app Guided mode’s lesson 5 is this chapter: it checks that this lesson’s tags are made, that S3_Index exists, is called from MainRoutine and verifies, and then watches the line while you run it and ticks each result as it happens: The belt steps one pitch (Conv_Index) Bottles walk down the line: three dropped, one at every stop This is the step that makes it a line, and it comes third because every station after it needs bottles to arrive. The belt must move exactly one pitch and stop: the encoder on Main_Conv gives one rising edge of channel A per 40 px, so the rule is latch Conv_Index , run the belt, unlatch on the next edge. Add JSR(S3_Index); to MainRoutine under step 2. From now on it stays the last JSR: each station you add in the lessons that follow goes above it (guided mode’s Add it puts it there, and says so if one ends up below). Tags this lesson needs Create these before you type the rungs (Verify reports any you miss as unknown). Tags from earlier lessons are not repeated. Tag Type Kind Description LS4 BOOL alias of Local:1:I.Data.9 LogixPro I:1/9 · Fill tube down LS7 BOOL alias of Local:1:I.Data.13 LogixPro I:1/12 · Cap ram down Fill_Req BOOL base tag A bottle stands under the filler and still needs its charge Cap_Req BOOL base tag A bottle stands under the cap ram and has not been capped Insp_Req BOOL base tag An inspection is under way: triggered, no result yet (holds the belt) Main_Conveyor BOOL alias of Local:4:O.Data.1 LogixPro O:2/0 · Main conveyor motor Main_Conv_A BOOL alias of Local:1:I.Data.2 Main_Conv encoder channel A: one rising edge per 40 px pitch A_ONS BOOL base tag One-shot storage for the encoder edge The rungs How it fits together Rung 0 starts a step: the line runs, the dwell is done, no fill, cap, label or inspection is in progress (the request bits are off), and neither the tube ( LS4 ) nor the ram ( LS7 ) is down. Those stations do not exist yet, so their bits are 0 and the rung passes; it is written complete now so it never has to be revisited. Rung 1 resets step 2’s dwell while the belt steps. Rung 2 runs the motor only while stepping and only while the line runs. Rung 3 ends the step: the next rising edge of encoder A unlatches Conv_Index , and the ONS sits right after Main_Conv_A so it tracks the encoder, not the step. A Stop in the middle of a step leaves Conv_Index latched and stops the motor; Start runs the motor again and the step ends on the same encoder edge it would have, one pitch from where it began. That is what keeps the registers and the bottles together. Why JSR(S3_Index) is the last JSR. Rung 0 looks at the fill, cap, label and inspection requests, and those are decided in their own routines, in the same scan, from Dwell.DN . If S3_Index ran first it would latch the step in the scan the dwell finished, before the filler had asked to hold the belt, and the bottle would leave the filler empty. Scanned last, it sees every request first. Run it Start the line. The belt steps, stops, a bottle drops, a second passes, the belt steps. Bottles walk down the line one pitch at a time and are removed at the end. Nothing fills, caps or sorts them yet: the lessons that follow add one station at a time, and each one works as soon as it is written because the bottles are already arriving. S3_Index online with the finished line running: what your routine should look like once every step is in. Green is power flow. Try it Change the Dwell preset to 300 ms and watch the line speed up without losing a bottle. Set it back to 1000.  XIC(Line_Run)XIC(Dwell.DN)XIO(LS4)XIO(LS7)XIO(Fill_Req)XIO(Cap_Req)XIO(Label_Req)XIO(Insp_Req)OTL(Conv_Index); START THE STEP once the dwell is done, the tube (LS4) and ram (LS7) are up, and no fill, cap or label is in progress XIC(Conv_Index)RES(Dwell); The belt is stepping: reset the dwell for the next stop. A retentive timer only clears with RES XIC(Line_Run)XIC(Conv_Index)OTE(Main_Conveyor); RUN THE BELT only while stepping and the line runs: a step cut short by Stop (or a fault) stays latched and finishes after Start XIC(Main_Conv_A)ONS(A_ONS)XIC(Conv_Index)OTU(Conv_Index); END THE STEP on the next rising edge of encoder A, which is exactly one 40 px pitch. The ONS sits right after Main_Conv_A so it tracks the encoder, not the step. Try it: change Dwell to 300 ms and watch the line speed up without losing a bottle
ch21: In the app Guided mode’s lesson 6 is this chapter: it checks that this lesson’s tags are made, that S4_Registers exists, is called from MainRoutine and verifies, and then watches the line while you run it and ticks each result as it happens: Exist[0] bit 0 is set: LS1 saw the bottle at the head of the line The bit walks with the bottle: Exist[0] bit 3 is set Chapter 10 is the theory; this is the rung. Add JSR(S4_Registers); to MainRoutine above JSR(S3_Index) , and write it in S4_Registers. Tags this lesson needs Create these before you type the rungs (Verify reports any you miss as unknown). Tags from earlier lessons are not repeated. Tag Type Kind Description Exist DINT base tag Bottle present, one bit per stop (LogixPro B3:10). During the dwell: filler 6, capper 9, scrap gate 13, divert gate 20; after the shift (Dwell.DN) one bit higher Exist_Ctl CONTROL base tag LogixPro R6:1 LS1 BOOL alias of Local:1:I.Data.4 LogixPro I:1/6 · Exist sensor: a bottle at the start of the line Large DINT base tag Large bottle (LogixPro B3:20). During the dwell: filler 5, capper 8, scrap gate 12, divert gate 19; after the shift one bit higher Large_Ctl CONTROL base tag LogixPro R6:2 LS2 BOOL alias of Local:1:I.Data.5 LogixPro I:1/7 · Size check: beam set so only a large bottle breaks it Broken DINT base tag Broken bottle (LogixPro B3:30). During the dwell: filler 4, capper 7, scrap gate 11, divert gate 18; after the shift one bit higher Broken_Ctl CONTROL base tag LogixPro R6:3 LS3 BOOL alias of Local:1:I.Data.6 LogixPro I:1/8 · Broken check: sees broken bottles only Reject DINT base tag Bad bottle (the camera found no cap, no label or a short fill), one bit per stop from the stop past the camera. During the dwell: scrap gate 0, divert gate 7; after the shift one bit higher Reject_Ctl CONTROL base tag BSL control for Reject Cam_Bad BOOL base tag The verdict for the bottle at the camera, shifted into Reject at the next stop The rungs How it fits together At the end of every dwell the registers shift once, the three head registers each taking their head sensor into bit 0, and a fourth, Reject , taking Cam_Bad , the camera’s verdict from step 15. Cam_Bad is 0 until step 15 is written, so the fourth BSL shifts zeros and changes nothing: write it now and the register is in step with the bottles from the first run. The CONTROL tags ( Exist_Ctl and the others) belong to the BSLs; 48 is the length, more than the stops on the belt, so a bottle is tracked all the way to the end and off. Make the four registers DINT arrays with Dim 2 and Style Binary. Run it Start the line and open Monitor Tags with Exist , Large and Broken expanded. After the first dwell, bit 0 of Exist is 1: a bottle is at the head. At every stop the registers shift and the 1 walks one bit, in step with the bottle on the belt. A large bottle leaves a 1 in Large, a broken one in Broken, and those walk with it too. S4_Registers online with the finished line running: what your routine should look like once every step is in. Green is power flow. Try it Stop the line, then toggle Conv_Index on and off by hand ( Ctrl+T , twice): the dwell runs again, the registers shift, and every bit moves on although no bottle did. That is a register out of step with the world, and why only step 3 may end a dwell. Reset Sim afterwards. Then set Bottle_Feed’s Broken bottles to 50 % for a run and watch the Broken register fill; then back to 15.  XIC(Dwell.DN)[BSL(Exist[0],Exist_Ctl,LS1,48),BSL(Large[0],Large_Ctl,LS2,48),BSL(Broken[0],Broken_Ctl,LS3,48),BSL(Reject[0],Reject_Ctl,Cam_Bad,48)]; SHIFT ONCE PER STOP, while the bottles stand still: LS1 (bottle present) into Exist, LS2 (large) into Large, LS3 (broken) into Broken. Watch Exist[0] in Binary style in Controller Tags and see the bits walk down the line one place per stop The fourth register, Reject, takes Cam_Bad: the camera's verdict on the bottle that stood under it during the last stop, so Reject bit n is that verdict n stops on
ch22: In the app Guided mode’s lesson 7 is this chapter: it checks that this lesson’s tags are made, that S5_Fill exists, is called from MainRoutine and verifies, and then watches the line while you run it and ticks each result as it happens: A bottle is filled at the filler The fill station needs five rungs: a request, the tube, the valves, a done latch and a clear. The request is written in the after-the-shift frame (it waits on Dwell.DN , which means the registers have just shifted and the belt is about to step), so it reads Exist bit 7 and Large bit 6 (chapter 10’s table). Add the JSR above JSR(S3_Index) and write: Tags this lesson needs Create these before you type the rungs (Verify reports any you miss as unknown). Tags from earlier lessons are not repeated. Tag Type Kind Description Fill_Done BOOL base tag Latched when the charge is in; cleared when the belt steps Fill_Tube BOOL alias of Local:4:O.Data.6 LogixPro O:2/6 · Lower the fill tube LS5 BOOL alias of Local:1:I.Data.10 LogixPro I:1/10 · Large charge delivered Large_Fill BOOL alias of Local:4:O.Data.7 LogixPro O:2/7 · Large fill valve LS6 BOOL alias of Local:1:I.Data.11 LogixPro I:1/11 · Small charge delivered Small_Fill BOOL alias of Local:4:O.Data.8 LogixPro O:2/8 · Small fill valve The rungs How it fits together Rung 0: a bottle under the nozzle, not broken, not yet filled, the registers shifted, the belt not stepping, the line running → Fill_Req . The request is an OTE, so it drops the moment Fill_Done latches. Rung 1 lowers the tube while requested; the filler reports LS4 (tube down). Rung 2 opens a valve once the tube is down: a branch with the large valve on one leg and the small valve on the other, chosen by the Large register, each held until the filler’s own sensor ( LS5 large charge, LS6 small) says the charge is in. One rung for both sizes means it works on whichever bottle reaches the filler first. Rung 3 latches Fill_Done at that moment, which drops the request and lifts the tube, and rung 4 unlatches it when the belt steps so the next bottle is treated as new. Step 3 will not let the belt step while the tube is down or the request is on. Run it Start the line. At stop 7 the tube comes down and the bottle fills (a large charge for a large bottle, a small one for a small; watch the lamps on the filler’s post), then the tube lifts and the belt steps. The Simulator Log lists every fill. The filler tops its head tank up from the reservoir, and the reservoir is going down: step 6 keeps it supplied. S5_Fill online with the finished line running: what your routine should look like once every step is in. Green is power flow. Try it Why is the bottle Exist 7 but Large 6? Count the sensors: LS2 is one stop past LS1, so the same bottle is one bit further along in Exist than in Large. Then move JSR(S3_Index) above JSR(S5_Fill) in MainRoutine and run: the belt steps in the same scan the fill is asked for, and bottles leave the filler empty. Put it back. That is the scan-order lesson in one move. The shift happens at the END of the dwell, so a rung that runs after it reads one bit higher than a rung that runs during the dwell. ch23: In the app Guided mode’s lesson 8 is this chapter: it checks that this lesson’s tags are made, that S6_Supply exists, is called from MainRoutine and verifies, and then watches the line while you run it and ticks each result as it happens: The reservoir inlet opens at the low float The filler draws every charge from its head tank, and the head tank tops itself up from the reservoir, Supply_Tank , which nothing refills yet: run step 5 long enough and the line stalls with the tube down, waiting for a charge that never comes. This step keeps the filler fed, so it comes straight after it. Add the JSR above JSR(S3_Index) and write: Tags this lesson needs Create these before you type the rungs (Verify reports any you miss as unknown). Tags from earlier lessons are not repeated. Tag Type Kind Description Supply_Low BOOL alias of Local:1:I.Data.8 Supply_Tank low float Supply_Inlet BOOL alias of Local:4:O.Data.2 Supply_Tank inlet valve Supply_High BOOL alias of Local:1:I.Data.7 Supply_Tank high float Tank_Low BOOL alias of Local:1:I.Data.12 Filler head tank below 15 % Tank_Red BOOL alias of Local:4:O.Data.3 Tank_Light red: reservoir at the low float (flashes) Tank_Amber BOOL alias of Local:4:O.Data.4 Tank_Light amber: inlet open, refilling Tank_Green BOOL alias of Local:4:O.Data.5 Tank_Light green: level healthy The rungs How it fits together Rung 0 is a seal-in on the floats: the low float opens the inlet valve, and the valve stays open until the high float. Rung 1 protects the fill: if the filler’s head tank runs low (the reservoir empty, the inlet too slow) the line is stopped rather than pouring short charges. Rungs 2–4 drive the stack light on the tank: red flashing at the low float (the light is set to flash its red segment), amber while refilling, green when healthy and not refilling. Run it The tank starts at 35 %: watch it fall a little with every charge (a trend of Supply_Level , chapter 11), reach 20 %, the red flash, the inlet valve open and the level climb to 90 %. Set the reservoir’s Inlet flow to 10 and the line will eventually stop on rung 1; the Simulator Log says why. S6_Supply online with the finished line running: what your routine should look like once every step is in. Green is power flow. Try it Make amber mean head-tank low instead of refilling. Then fit the reservoir’s flow meter (a setting; it adds an analog input) and trend Supply_Flow against the charges. ch24: In the app Guided mode’s lesson 9 is this chapter: it checks that this lesson’s tags are made, that S7_Cap exists, is called from MainRoutine and verifies, and then watches the line while you run it and ticks each result as it happens: Start the line: the green column lamp on the capper lights A bottle is capped Same shape as the fill, plus the cap supply. Add the JSR above JSR(S3_Index) and write: Tags this lesson needs Create these before you type the rungs (Verify reports any you miss as unknown). Tags from earlier lessons are not repeated. Tag Type Kind Description Cap_Done BOOL base tag Latched when the ram has been down; cleared when the belt steps Cap_Present BOOL alias of Local:1:I.Data.15 Capper CapPresent: a cap is waiting at the chuck Cap_Ram BOOL alias of Local:4:O.Data.9 LogixPro O:2/9 · Cap ram Cap_Low BOOL alias of Local:1:I.Data.14 Capper CapLow: the chute is down to its low count Cap_Feeder BOOL alias of Local:4:O.Data.10 Capper Feeder: runs the vibratory cap bowl, refilling the chute Cap_Fill_T TIMER base tag Cap feeder run-on after CapLow clears Cap_Green BOOL alias of Local:4:O.Data.11 Capper green indicator (column) Cap_Amber BOOL alias of Local:4:O.Data.12 Capper amber indicator (column) The rungs How it fits together Rungs 0–3 mirror the fill station: a whole bottle under the head (Exist 10, not Broken 8), a cap waiting ( Cap_Present ), not yet capped → Cap_Req ; the head comes down; LS7 at the bottom of the stroke latches Cap_Done ; the belt stepping clears it. The Broken bit matters here: a head that comes down on a broken bottle crushes it (try it, below). Rungs 4–5 are the cap feeder: when the chute runs low, Cap_Feeder starts the magazine and seals in; once Cap_Low clears, the run-on timer gives it eight more seconds (about 24 caps) and then the seal-in breaks. Rungs 6–7 drive the two lights on the column: green while running with caps in the chute, amber while cycling or low. Run it Start the line. At stop 10 the head comes down on each filled bottle and presses a cap on, and the magazine turns one pocket per cap; the green column lamp is on. Tag Type Kind Description Scrap_Gate BOOL alias of Local:5:O.Data.0 LogixPro O:2/4 · Scrap gate: swings a bottle into the grinder Divert_Gate BOOL alias of Local:5:O.Data.2 LogixPro O:2/5 · Divert gate: swings a bottle onto the divert conveyor Lower_Full BOOL alias of Local:10:I.Data.5 Packer lower lane full: small bottles arriving now wait at the stop LS12 BOOL alias of Local:2:I.Data.13 Stop eye at the end of the divert conveyor, just before the packer lower lane Divert_Conveyor BOOL alias of Local:5:O.Data.3 LogixPro O:2/2 · Divert conveyor for large bottles LS10 BOOL alias of Local:3:I.Data.0 LogixPro I:1/15 · Scrap box under the grinder chute Box_Full BOOL alias of Local:2:I.Data.9 Grinder BoxFull: the box under the scrap drop holds its share Scrap_Conveyor BOOL alias of Local:5:O.Data.4 LogixPro O:2/1 · Box conveyor under the grinder Scrap_Waiting BOOL alias of Local:2:I.Data.8 Grinder Detect: a broken bottle is waiting in the hopper Grinder BOOL alias of Local:5:O.Data.1 LogixPro O:2/3 · Grinder motor The rungs How it fits together Rung 0: a broken bottle at the scrap gate, or one the camera failed ( Reject bit 0, step 15) → the arm swings it off the deck and it drops into the shredder hopper. Rung 1: a small, unbroken bottle the camera passed at the divert gate → down the catch incline to the divert conveyor; large bottles carry on to the end. The Exist bit stops the gate firing at empty slots at start-up; the Broken bit stops it firing at the empty slot a scrapped bottle left behind, because its Exist bit is still set. Rung 2 is the divert conveyor. It carries the small bottles on under the case packer to its lower lane, a stop and a buffer of eight at the end of the conveyor, where the packer’s head comes down for them (step 12). While there is room the bottles roll straight into the lane. When the lane is full ( Lower_Full ) the next bottle waits at the stop and the conveyor should not go on running under it: the rung keeps the conveyor running until a bottle reaches the stop eye LS12 , then stops it, so the bottles close up nose to tail behind the stop. It is the accumulation pattern of every conveyor that feeds a machine: [XIO(Lower_Full),XIO(LS12)] reads room in the lane, or nothing at the eye yet. Rung 3 runs the box conveyor until a box reaches LS10 under the chute, and again once the box is full to carry it out and bring the next one. Rung 4 runs the shredder only with an empty box in position and a bottle waiting in the hopper. Why the dwell frame? A gate arm acts on whatever is standing at the gate. The registers shift at the end of the dwell, before the belt moves; a rung that fired on the shifted bit would swing the arm while the previous bottle still stands there and push the wrong one. Qualifying with Dwell.TT fires the arm only while the belt is still and the bits describe the bottles in front of it. Run it Start the line with the Side view on the grinder. A broken bottle reaches the scrap gate; the arm swings, the bottle drops into the hopper; the shredder waits until a box is under the chute, then runs, glass falls into the box and the IN BOX count rises; when the box is full the box conveyor carries it out and brings the next. Small bottles go down the incline and ride the divert conveyor to the packer’s lower lane; large ones run on to the packer’s deck infeed. Until step 12 is written nothing packs them, so both fill up: watch the lower lane fill, the next small bottle stop at LS12 and the divert conveyor stop with it. ch27: One stop past the capper stands an Inline Labeler, a pressure-sensitive dispenser in the mould of a Novexx FLS 204: a web of labels on a liner runs from the unwind reel over the dispensing edge to the rewind, and an applicator presses the peeled label onto the bottle. Its handshake is the one every dispenser has (Start, here Apply ; Ready; Error; Label low), and the rules are the same as on a real panel: start only when Ready, treat Error as a fault that needs a person, never step the belt mid-cycle. This chapter writes that handshake for the bottle labeler (step 10), then uses it again for a second dispenser that bands the scrap boxes with hazard tape (step 14), and ends with a camera that checks every bottle (step 15). Step 10: the labeler In the app Guided mode’s lesson 12 is this section: it checks that the lesson’s tags are made, that S10_Label exists, is called from MainRoutine and verifies, and then watches the line while you run it and ticks each result as it happens: A bottle leaves the labeler with a label Add the JSR above JSR(S3_Index) and write: Tags this lesson needs Tag Type Kind Description Label_Applied BOOL base tag Latched when the label is pressed on; cleared when the belt steps Label_Ready BOOL alias of Local:2:I.Data.1 Labeler ready: web loaded, head home, no fault Label_Fault BOOL base tag Latched on the labeler Error input (end of roll or a missed label); Enter clears it Label_Apply BOOL alias of Local:4:O.Data.13 Labeler Start: the applicator comes in and presses a label on Label_PadIn BOOL alias of Local:2:I.Data.0 Labeler applicator at the end of its stroke (label pressed on) Label_Error BOOL alias of Local:2:I.Data.2 Labeler fault: end of roll, or the last cycle found no label Label_Low BOOL alias of Local:2:I.Data.3 Labeler roll low Label_Green BOOL alias of Local:4:O.Data.14 Labeler green indicator Label_Amber BOOL alias of Local:4:O.Data.15 Labeler amber indicator The rungs How it fits together Rung 0 asks for a label in the after-the-shift frame, one bit past the capper (Exist 11, Broken 9), only when the dispenser says Ready, and it is a latch, because Ready drops the moment the head leaves home: an OTE here would start the cycle and cancel it in the next scan. Rung 1 drives Apply while the request stands; rung 2 takes the end-of-stroke switch ( Label_PadIn ) as “pressed on”, remembers it for this bottle and drops the request so the head returns; rung 3 forgets it when the belt steps. Rung 4 latches a fault on the dispenser’s Error (end of roll, or a cycle that found no label); rung 5 lets Enter acknowledge it. Rungs 6–7 are the frame lights. Step 3’s start rung has checked XIO(Label_Req) since you wrote it, so the belt never steps with the applicator in, and step 1’s housekeeping rung drops the request when the line stops. Run it Every capped bottle leaves with a label (Side or 3D view: the band on the body; the unwind reel shrinks as the roll goes down). Set the Labeler’s labels on the roll at start to 3 and run: three labels, then the Error input, the amber lamp and Label_Fault latched, and the line keeps running, bottles leaving bare, because a labeler fault is not a reason to stop a filler. Click the labeler in Run mode to load a new roll (Ready comes back), press Enter, and labeling resumes. S10_Label online with the finished line running. Green is power flow. Try it Make the fault stop the line instead (add XIO(Label_Fault) to step 1’s seal-in) and decide which you would want on a real line. Then switch the Labeler’s Hand to LH and Applicator to Tamp pad in Properties and watch the machine rebuild on the other side of the lane; the program does not change. How the label goes on. The applicator works the way the machine does, so what you see in 3D is what the handshake means. Wrap-around: the roller arm slides in until it touches the bottle, the bottle turns against the roller and the label wraps on as a band that grows with the stroke, finishing just before PadIn ; then the arm comes home. Tamp: the label rides down on the pad and is pressed on in one touch. Blow-on: the label flies the gap on a puff of air. Wipe-on: the dispensing edge feeds the label out as the bottle moves and a brush lays it down. Watch for A band that stops part-way round is a cycle that was cut short: Apply dropped before PadIn, which on the bottle line means the belt stepped with the applicator in, or the line was stopped mid-cycle. The bottle leaves with half a label, and the labeler’s own Labeled input stays off for it. On a real dispenser that is a label on the floor and a stop to rethread. Step 14: hazard tape on the scrap boxes In the app Guided mode’s lesson 15 is this section: it checks that the lesson’s tags are made, that S14_Hazard exists, is called from MainRoutine and verifies, and then watches the line while you run it and ticks each result as it happens: A box leaves the dispenser with its hazard band (Haz_Labeler has cycled) A taped box takes glass at the grinder with none logged untaped The scrap boxes come off Box_Feed blank, and a second dispenser on the box conveyor, Haz_Labeler , bands each one with yellow and black hazard tape on its way to the grinder’s chute: a box of broken glass must say so before anyone picks it up. It is the same Inline Labeler part with What it applies set to hazard tape and a wipe-on applicator: the band is wiped on as the box rolls under the head, so the cycle is started from an eye ten pixels ahead of the head, LS13 . The handshake is step 10’s, in a routine of its own, S14_Hazard , called from MainRoutine under step 12 and, like every station, above JSR(S3_Index) . Its Labeled input means the box under the head carries tape, so no done bit is kept in the program: the box carries its own. A box that takes glass with no band on it is logged at the grinder, and again if it leaves at Box_Out . S14_Hazard online with the finished line running. Green is power flow. Try it Set Haz_Labeler’s labels on the roll at start to 2 and run. Two boxes leave banded, then the Error input, the amber lamp and Haz_Fault ; the third box reaches the chute blank and the log says so. Load a new roll (click the dispenser in Run mode), press Enter. Then move LS13 to x 480 and watch the band miss: the cycle completes before the box is under the head. An on-the-fly applicator is a timing problem; the eye’s place is part of the program. Step 15: inspect every bottle In the app Guided mode’s lesson 16 is this section: it checks that the lesson’s tags are made, that S15_Inspect exists, is called from MainRoutine and verifies, and then watches the line while you run it and ticks each result as it happens: A bottle is inspected (Insp_Count moves) A passed bottle goes on past the scrap gate (a whole bottle stands there with Reject bit 0 clear and Scrap_Gate stays down) A bottle the camera failed is scrapped (Insp_Reject_Count moves and Scrap_Gate turns for Reject bit 0). Inject a fault to see one: Tools → Inject Machine Fault → labeler web break Steps 1 to 14 trust the stations: a bottle that stood under the capper is capped, one that stood under the labeler is labeled. A real line checks. A camera stands over the belt one stop past the labeler, the In-Sight of Level 8 with its job set to bottle inspection: cap on, label on, filled to the line. It is Cam1 in I/O Configuration, and a screen of its own, Cam_HMI , stands beside the line showing each result with its picture. The step is S15_Inspect , called from MainRoutine after the hazard tape; the guided lesson’s fix button adds the camera module for you. The register frame does the work. After the shift, Exist bit 12 is the bottle under the camera, and Broken bit 10 says whether it is whole (a broken one is for the scrap gate already). The step triggers the camera once per stop, keeps the result code for that bottle (0 = pass; bit 0 no cap, bit 1 no label, bit 2 short fill), and latches a verdict, Cam_Bad . Step 4 shifts the verdict into the fourth register, Reject , at the next shift: in the dwell frame, bit 0 is the bottle at the scrap gate and bit 7 the bottle at the divert gate, which is why step 8’s scrap rung has XIC(Reject[0].0) beside Broken[0].11 and its divert rung has XIO(Reject[0].7) . A rejected bottle goes to the shredder exactly as a broken one does. Tags this lesson needs Tag Type Kind Description Insp_Done BOOL base tag This stop's bottle has been inspected Insp_Code DINT base tag The camera's result code for this stop's bottle: 0 pass; bit 0 no cap, bit 1 no label, bit 2 short fill Shift_ONS BOOL base tag One-shot storage: clear the verdict after the shift has taken it IC_ONS BOOL base tag One-shot storage for the inspected count Insp_Count DINT base tag Bottles inspected RC_ONS BOOL base tag One-shot storage for the rejected count Insp_Reject_Count DINT base tag Bottles the camera rejected Cam_Off_T TIMER base tag The camera has been off line for 2 s with the line running CAM_ONS BOOL base tag One-shot storage for the camera alarm Alarm_Word DINT base tag Latched alarms, one bit each: 0 main conveyor overload, 1 divert conveyor overload, 2 end-of-line check failed (a jam, a lost bottle, tracking out of step), 3 LS1 dark too long (dirty lens or feeder empty), 4 labeler fault, 5 reservoir inlet open but level not rising, 6 case lane drive tripped, 7 packer infeed full Alarm_Unack BOOL base tag New alarm, not yet acknowledged (Reset) Reset_PB BOOL alias of Local:3:I.Data.12 Blue Reset button: acknowledge alarms and clear the ones whose cause is gone The rungs How it fits together Rung 0 enables triggering and the results buffer while the line runs. Rung 1 is the trigger: a whole bottle under the camera, the shift just done, not inspected yet this stop, the belt not stepping, the line running and the camera ready; a latch, because Trigger_Ready drops the moment the camera takes the trigger. It also latches Insp_Req , which step 3’s start rung holds the belt on, the same hold the fill, cap and label requests have. Rung 2 drops Trigger at Trigger_Ack and remembers this stop’s bottle is done. Rung 3 takes the result when Results_Valid rises: the code into Insp_Code , the acknowledge up, and the belt released. One bottle a stop means the result always belongs to the bottle under the camera, so there is no FIFO to keep; rung 4 drops the acknowledge once the camera has dropped Results_Valid. Rung 5 is the verdict: any defect bit latches Cam_Bad . Rung 6 clears the verdict and the code after the shift has taken them, so a stop with no bottle under the camera shifts a 0; rung 7 forgets the inspection when the belt steps. Rungs 8–9 count inspections and rejects for the screen. Rungs 10–12 are the camera’s own alarm, bit 8 of the alarm word: off line for two seconds with the line running, a result lost to a full buffer, or a trigger the camera missed. The line runs on, because an uninspected bottle is not a rejected one; the console shows the fault and you stop and look. Reset clears it once the camera is back. S15_Inspect online with the finished line running. Green is power flow. Try it Run the line and put Insp_Code , Cam_Bad , Reject[0] and Insp_Reject_Count in Quick Watch: the code is 0 for every whole bottle and the register stays empty. Then Tools → Inject Machine Fault → labeler web break . The labeler’s Ready drops, step 10 stops asking for labels, and the bottles leave it bare: under the camera Insp_Code reads 2 (no label), Cam_Bad latches, and a 1 walks down Reject until the scrap gate swings for a whole, capped, filled bottle with no label. Watch Cam_HMI as it goes: the picture, the code, the verdict. Clear Machine Faults, load a roll and press Enter: the next bottles pass again. Watch for A camera triggered while the belt is stepping sees a smear and fails good bottles: that is what the XIO(Conv_Index) in rung 1 and the XIO(Insp_Req) hold in step 3 are for. Without the hold, a result that arrives after the shift belongs to a bottle that has moved on, and the verdict lands on the wrong one. Alarm bit 8 with the line running is the other thing to look for: the camera is not inspecting, every bottle passes, and the only tell is the fault on the console. ch28: In the app Guided mode’s lesson 13 is this chapter: it checks that the lesson’s tags are made, that S11_Alarms exists, is called from MainRoutine and verifies, and then watches the line while you run it and ticks each result as it happens: Inject an overload on Main_Conv: bit 0 latches, the fault lamp flashes, the line stops Inject a jam on Main_Conv: the end-of-line check (LS11) latches bit 2 Clear Machine Faults, press Reset, press Start: the alarms clear and the line runs again Everything so far assumes the machine does what it is told. Real machines do not. A bottle jams; a lens gets dirty and the eye stays dark, or stays made; a motor overload trips and the conveyor stops although the output is still on; a label web breaks; a valve sticks shut. The controller is fine through all of this (the scan goes on, no instruction faults), so nothing tells you unless your program checks. This step is the checks. The template has three parts for it (chapter 16): LS11 , an eye one stop before the end of the line, a red Fault_Lamp and a blue Reset_PB on the console. Each belt also reports Running (the auxiliary contact on its motor contactor, made when the motor really turns), which the template aliases as Main_Conv_Running and Divert_Conv_Running . The alarms are the bits of one DINT, Alarm_Word , shown in Binary: Bit Alarm Raised when Stops the line 0 Main conveyor overload Main_Conveyor commanded, Main_Conv_Running missing for 0.5 s yes 1 Divert conveyor overload Divert_Conveyor commanded, Divert_Conv_Running missing for 0.5 s yes 2 End-of-line check once per stop, LS11 disagrees with the tracking for that stop: a bottle missing or one extra yes 3 LS1 dark too long the line running and LS1 dark for 8 s yes 4 Labeler fault Label_Fault (step 10) latched no 5 Inlet not filling Supply_Inlet open with Supply_Low still made for 10 s yes 6 Case lane drive tripped Case_VFD_Fault (the drive of step 12) no 7 Packer infeed full Infeed_Full: eight bottles waiting to be packed yes 8 Camera fault (latched in step 15) a result lost to a full buffer, a missed trigger, or the camera off line for 2 s with the line running no Bits 6 and 7 watch the case packer and its drive, which step 12 programs; their alias tags are in your list from chapter 17, so type the rungs now and they will make sense in the next chapter. Add the JSR under step 10 and write: Tags this lesson needs Tag Type Kind Description Main_Conv_Running BOOL alias of Local:1:I.Data.1 Main conveyor running feedback (motor contactor) Main_OL_T TIMER base tag Main conveyor overload timer (no running feedback) OL_ONS BOOL base tag Divert_Conv_Running BOOL alias of Local:2:I.Data.12 Divert conveyor running feedback Div_OL_T TIMER base tag Divert conveyor overload timer (no running feedback) DOL_ONS BOOL base tag EOL_Inhibit BOOL base tag Tracking cleared by Reset: the end-of-line check waits until the first bottle tracked since then reaches LS11 EOL_ONS BOOL base tag LS11 BOOL alias of Local:3:I.Data.11 End-of-line eye at 1240: verifies the tracking (only large, whole bottles reach it) EOL_Missing BOOL base tag LS11 dark when the registers said a large, whole bottle was there EOL_Extra BOOL base tag LS11 saw a bottle the registers did not expect BLK_ONS BOOL base tag LS1_Dark_T TIMER base tag LS1 dark too long timer DRK_ONS BOOL base tag LBL_ONS BOOL base tag Inlet_T TIMER base tag Inlet not filling timer INL_ONS BOOL base tag Case_VFD_Fault BOOL alias of Local:10:I.Data.14 Case lane drive tripped VFD_ONS BOOL base tag Infeed_Full BOOL alias of Local:10:I.Data.1 Packer infeed buffer full: bottles arriving now wait on the belt INF_ONS BOOL base tag RST_ONS BOOL base tag Flash_T TIMER base tag Fault lamp flasher Fault_Lamp BOOL alias of Local:5:O.Data.9 Red fault lamp on the console: flashing = unacknowledged alarm, steady = alarm still active The rungs How it fits together Rungs 0–3, overloads. The output says run; the feedback says not running. Half a second allows for the contactor to pull in. When the timer is done, latch the bit and Alarm_Unack . The one-shot matters: without it an alarm the operator has acknowledged would be raised again every scan while the cause is still there. Rungs 4–6, the end-of-line check. This is the shift register’s own proof. Once per stop (halfway through the dwell, so the belt is standing still and LS11 has settled, and once only), compare LS11 with what the registers say stands in front of it. LS11 at x 1240 is 27 stops after LS1, so in the dwell frame that is Exist[0].26 , Large[0].25 , Broken[0].24 , and a bottle should be there only if it exists, is large (small ones were diverted), is whole and was not rejected. Expected and dark is EOL_Missing ; not expected and made is EOL_Extra . Either is bit 2. A jammed bottle shows up here a few stops after it jams: the bottles behind it pile up, the stops they should be at stay empty, the registers walk on regardless. Rungs 7–8, LS1 dark too long. The feeder drops a bottle every stop, so LS1 sees one every couple of seconds. Eight seconds dark with the line running means the eye is dirty and stuck off, or nothing is coming. Rung 9 turns the labeler’s fault into bit 4, and rungs 10–11 watch the reservoir: the inlet clears the low float in a second or two, so ten seconds commanded open with the float still made means the valve did not open. Rungs 12–13 are the packer: a drive trip is bit 6, a full infeed bit 7. Rung 14 stops the line on bits 0, 1, 2, 3, 5 and 7, an OTU of Line_Run after step 1’s seal-in, so Start cannot hold while one of them is set. Rung 15, Reset. One press does two things. It acknowledges ( Alarm_Unack off), and it clears every alarm whose cause has gone. An end-of-line alarm is different: its cause is that the registers no longer describe the belt, so Reset clears the register words and sets EOL_Inhibit , and the check stays off until the first bottle tracked since the reset reaches LS11 (rung 6). That is how a real line recovers after a jam: clear the jam, reset the tracking, purge the line. Rung 16 lets a drive trip clear itself from the alarm word once the drive reports healthy. Rungs 17–18 , the lamp: it flashes while an alarm is unacknowledged and is steady while an acknowledged alarm is still set. Off means healthy. A machine fault is not a controller fault Chapter 9’s major fault is the controller stopping itself: an instruction it cannot execute. The scan stops and Communications → Clear Faults clears it. A machine fault is everything in this chapter: the controller is healthy, the scan runs, and the only way anyone finds out is a rung like these. The first kind is the PLC protecting itself; the second is your program protecting the machine, the product and the people near it. Inject a fault The simulator can break the machine on purpose. Tools → Inject Machine Fault… lists, for the parts on your floor, a bottle jammed on a conveyor, a sensor with a dirty lens stuck on or stuck off, a conveyor overload, a labeler web break, a reservoir inlet stuck shut, a drive trip, and more. Each is logged and drawn with a red dashed outline. Tools → Clear Machine Faults or Reset Sim takes them away; click a jammed bottle in Run mode to free it. Tools → Fault Drill… injects a random one as a timed exercise, which is how you practise finding a fault you did not choose. Tools → Inject Machine Fault: the kinds of fault, and the parts on this floor each one can be injected into. Run it Start the line and leave it three minutes: Alarm_Word stays 0 and the lamp stays dark. Press Stop and Start at any moment you like, mid-step, mid-dwell, mid-fill: still 0. Now break things, one at a time, with Clear Machine Faults, Reset and Start between each. Overload on Main_Conv: at the next step bit 0 latches, the line stops, the lamp flashes. Jam on Main_Conv: a few stops later LS11 disagrees with the registers, bit 2; free the bottle, Reset (the registers clear and the check waits), Start. Dirty LS1, stuck off: eight seconds later, bit 3; after the reset, bit 2 follows, because the bottles that passed LS1 while it was blind were never entered in the registers. Labeler web break: bit 4 at once, the line keeps running. Inlet stuck shut: nothing until the reservoir falls to the low float; ten seconds after that, bit 5. S11_Alarms online with the finished line running. Green is power flow. Try it Add an alarm for the head tank ( Tank_Low ): step 6 already stops the line on it, but nothing tells the operator why. Give it a free bit, latch it like the others, and make Reset clear it once the tank has recovered. Then run the fault drill for ten minutes and keep a log of what you found and how long each took. ch29: In the app Guided mode’s lesson 14 is this chapter: it checks that the lesson’s tags are made, that S12_Pack exists, is called from MainRoutine and verifies, and then watches the line while you run it and ticks each result as it happens: A case stops under the packer head (Case_In_Place) The drive runs at the creep speed (Case_Speed_Ref 2500 = 15 Hz) A case is packed (Case_Full) A case of small bottles is packed from the lower lane (Case_Small_Count) A case of large bottles is packed from the deck (Case_Large_Count) STOP on Pack_HMI stops the packer and START runs it again (Pack_Run) A packed case leaves at Case_Out The last station packs the finished bottles. A top-load case packer stands at the end of the main line with two lanes to pick from. The large bottles that reach the end of the deck go into its deck infeed (it holds eight). The small bottles come down the divert conveyor on the floor to its lower lane. On a rising edge of Pack_Drop the pick head takes four from one lane, lifts them across to the case lane beside the line and lowers them into the case standing under the head; from the lower lane the head first runs out over the floor conveyor and drops the full 1.7 m to the bottle tops. One size per case: the program chooses the lane, and every case is either four large or four small. The case lane is the other new thing in this lesson. Its motor is not switched by a contactor like every other conveyor on the line: it runs on a variable frequency drive, and the program tells the drive how fast through an analog output. How the drive is wired This is how most drives are wired to a CompactLogix. Digital outputs: Case_Run (two-wire: the drive runs while it is 1) and Case_VFD_Reset . One analog output, the speed reference: a 0–10 V signal from channel 0 of the 1769-OF4 to the drive’s analog input, which the drive reads as 0–60 Hz. Digital inputs back: Case_VFD_Ready , Case_VFD_Running (output frequency above zero, also while it slows down), Case_At_Speed and Case_VFD_Fault ; and one analog input, the drive’s output frequency, 0–10 V for 0–60 Hz. The analog channels are in engineering units: the number in the tag is millivolts, 0–10000 for 0–10.000 V. So the program cannot write “15 Hz” to the drive; it writes the voltage that the drive will read as 15 Hz: 15 ÷ 60 × 10000 = 2500. That conversion is the whole of analog output, and SCP (chapter 8) does it. Case_VFD in the Properties drawer: the frequency at 10 V, the accel and decel times, the at-speed band, and its signals with their points. Why a creep speed A drive does not stop when Run drops: it ramps down on its decel time, 0.5 s from 60 Hz to 0 on this one. The case lane runs at 150 px/s at 60 Hz, so a case told to stop at full speed travels on for about 37 px, and the packer’s case-in-place window is ±6 px. The cure every packaging line uses: a slow-down eye a little before the mark ( Case_Slow , 100 px before the head), a creep speed from there (15 Hz), and the stop on the mark. From 15 Hz the drive is down in an eighth of a second and the case stops within about 2 px. BOOL alias of Local:6:O.Data.0 Case lane drive: fault reset (rising edge) The rungs How it fits together Rungs 0–1 give the packer a run seal-in of its own: a one-scan Pack_Auto_Start when the line starts, so the console’s Start starts the packer too, and a seal-in on Pack_Run that START and STOP on Pack_HMI also work. Stop the packer while the line runs and its lanes fill; when the deck infeed is full, step 11’s bit 7 stops the line. Stop the line and the packer keeps packing what is waiting. Rungs 2–4 come first, because without them nothing on the case lane moves: the drive runs at whatever its speed reference says, and that is 0 until the program writes one. Rung 2 sets the fast speed, 60 Hz, whenever the case is not creeping. Rung 3 is the analog output: SCP maps 0–60 Hz onto 0–10000. Rung 4 is the same instruction the other way round: the drive’s output frequency back to Hz in a REAL, so you can watch the ramps in Monitor Tags. Rung 5 runs the lane whenever no empty case stands under the head: either nothing is in place (bring the next case in) or the case in place is full (carry it out). Rungs 6–7 are the creep, latched: the slow-down eye only sees the case going past it, and the case still has 60 px to go when the eye clears. An empty case under the head ends the creep. Rung 8 is the creep speed, 15 Hz, while the latch is on. Rung 9 chooses the lane. The packer reads its Pick_Lower output on the rising edge of Drop: 1 picks from the lower lane, 0 from the deck. If only the lower lane is ready, it is chosen; if both are, GEQ(Lower_Count,Infeed_Count) takes the fuller lane, so neither lane backs up while the other is served. Rung 10 packs: the packer running, a case worth in a lane, an empty case on the mark, the head home, and the lane stopped. XIO(Case_VFD_Running) , not XIO(Case_Run) : Run drops the moment the case is in place, but the drive is still ramping down for a few scans, and a head that comes down on a moving case misses it. Rung 11 counts the case by size for Pack_HMI, rung 12 lets Enter clear the counts with the others, and rung 13 sends Reset to the drive’s fault reset: a drive clears a trip only on that rising edge, and only once the cause has gone. Run it Start the line and put Case_Hz , Case_Speed_Ref , Case_Hz_Actual , Case_In_Place and Infeed_Count in Quick Watch. The first carton comes in at 60 Hz ( Case_Speed_Ref 10000), reaches the slow-down eye, drops to 2500 and creeps, and stops under the head. Bottles collect in both lanes; when one lane holds four, the head picks them and lowers them into the case, goes home empty, and the case leaves with four bottle tops showing. CASES counts 1, and CASES LARGE or CASES SMALL on Pack_HMI. S12_Pack online with the finished line running. Green is power flow. Watch for: the stop that is not a stop Take the creep out (or set it to 60 Hz) and run: the case reaches the mark, Run drops, and the case sails on 30-odd px on the decel ramp, out of the window; case-in-place goes back to 0, the lane runs again, and the case leaves empty. Nothing in the program is wrong except the physics. Every positioning problem with a drive is this one: the stopping distance is speed × decel time ÷ 2. Try it Press STOP on Pack_HMI while the line runs: the head finishes its cycle and stops, the lower lane fills and the divert conveyor stops at LS12, the deck infeed fills and bit 7 stops the line. Press START, Reset, Start, and watch both lanes drain. Set the creep to 30 Hz (5000) and count how often the case still lands in the window. Then inject a drive trip on Case_VFD: bit 6 latches, the lane coasts to a stop, the infeed fills, and at eight bit 7 stops the line. Clear Machine Faults, Reset, and watch the drive come back. From 60 Hz the drive's 0.5 s decel ramp would carry it about 37 px past the head; from 15 Hz, about 2. The SCALE rung above picks it up on the next scan XIC(Lower_Ready)[XIO(Group_Ready),GEQ(Lower_Count,Infeed_Count)]OTE(Pick_Lower); WHICH LANE: one size per case, so the head picks from whichever lane holds four. With both ready it takes the fuller one (small bottles on a tie), so neither lane backs up. The packer reads Pick_Lower on the rising edge of Drop XIC(Pack_Run)[XIC(Group_Ready),XIC(Lower_Ready)]XIC(Case_In_Place)XIO(Case_Full)XIO(Case_VFD_Running)XIC(Packer_Ready)ONS(Drop_ONS)OTE(Pack_Drop); PACK: four bottles in either lane, an empty case centred under the head and the lane stopped (Running is still 1 while the drive decelerates), head home: one rising edge on Drop. The head drops back to its home position empty: the four stay in the case XIC(Case_Full)ONS(Case_ONS)[ADD(Case_Count,1,Case_Count),XIC(Case_Small)ADD(Case_Small_Count,1,Case_Small_Count),XIO(Case_Small)ADD(Case_Large_Count,1,Case_Large_Count)]; CASES: one count each time a case is packed, on the CASES display, and split by size for CASES LARGE and CASES SMALL on Pack_HMI. Case_Small says which lane filled the case under the head XIC(Enter)[CLR(Case_Count),CLR(Case_Large_Count),CLR(Case_Small_Count)]; Enter on the thumbwheel clears the case counts with the others (step 9) XIC(Reset_PB)OTE(Case_VFD_Reset); DRIVE RESET: Reset on the console also pulses the drive's FaultReset. A drive only clears a trip once its cause has gone
ch30: In the app Guided mode’s lesson 17 is this chapter: it checks that the lesson’s tags are made, that S13_Mix exists, is called from MainRoutine and verifies, and then watches the line while you run it and ticks each result as it happens: The kitchen makes a batch: Mix_Step goes through 3 (heat and mix) to 4 (ready) A ready batch transfers to Supply_Tank while its inlet is open (Mix_PumpOut) The carbonator holds its CO2: Carb_Press between 19 and 22 psi with soda going through START on Tank_HMI after a STOP runs the kitchen again (Mix_Run) Until now Supply_Tank has been filled from the plant supply header: open the inlet and soda arrives, as much as you like. A real filling line rarely works like that. The product is made a batch at a time in a mix kitchen beside the line and pumped across to a surge tank in front of the filler, which is what Supply_Tank becomes in this lesson. The kitchen is the Mix Tank of Level 7 with two supply totes, water on inlet A and cola syrup on inlet B, a carbonator after it, and a Process HMI to run it (chapter 14). Soda is made here, not bought: water and syrup at the 5 : 1 throw, then chilled and carbonated on the way to the filler. Steps 1 to 12 do not change. Step 6 still opens the Supply_Tank inlet at the low float and closes it at the high float. What changes is where that inlet draws from: it is piped from the kitchen, and liquid only moves while the mix tank’s outlet pump runs. So step 13 has to have a batch ready whenever step 6 asks, and pump it across while the inlet is open. If it is late, step 11’s alarm bit 5 is the first to tell you, and step 6’s head-tank protection the second. Place the kitchen The kitchen stands to the right of the console. Place: The mix kitchen Supply Tote at x 1720, y 130, named Supply_A : Holds (units) = 20000 . Water, a big tote: it lasts a long shift. Supply Tote at x 1720, y 380, named Supply_B : Ingredient = Cola syrup ; Holds (units) = 20000 . Cola syrup: five parts of water go with each part of it, so it lasts five times as long as the water. Mix Tank at x 2020, y 300, named Mix_Tank : Product (picked on the RECIPE page of its HMI) = Soda ; Starts at (%) = 90 ; Pump A flow (units/s) = 150 ; Pump B flow (units/s) = 150 ; LO level probe (%) = 15 ; Panel and HMI: heater setpoint tag (a REAL the operator sets on the TEMP page) = Mix_Target_T ; Recipe: A share the HMI aims for (%) = 83 ; Recipe: mixing time (s) = 8 ; Starts holding a finished batch: the start level made to the recipe A share and already mixed = ticked ; Inlet A fed from = Supply_A ; Inlet B fed from = Supply_B . Inlet A from Supply_A, inlet B from Supply_B; the heater setpoint tag is the one Tank_HMI writes; it starts at 90 % holding a finished batch, so the first transfer does not wait for a batch to be made. Carbonator at x 2300, y 330, named Carbonator : Fed from = Mix_Tank ; Starts at (psi) = 20 . To the right of the tank, fed from Mix_Tank. It chills what goes through to 38 °F and dissolves CO2 in it; it starts at 20 psi, pressurised from the last shift. Process HMI at x 2050, y 490, named Tank_HMI : Shows = Mix_Tank ; Function keys F2–F6: other machines this terminal can switch to (names, comma-separated; F1 is Shows) = Supply_Tank, Case_Packer, Camera, Bottle_Feed ; Heater setpoint tag (REAL; blank = the tank's own) = Mix_Target_T ; START button tag (BOOL, pulsed while touched) = Mix_Start ; STOP button tag (BOOL, pulsed while touched) = Mix_Stop ; Running indicator tag (BOOL: lights START) = Mix_Run ; Recipe A share tag (REAL, %) = Mix_Ratio ; Recipe mixing time tag (REAL, s) = Mix_Time ; Recipe carbonates tag (BOOL: 1 when the recipe takes CO2; the kitchen's CO2 rung reads it) = Mix_Carb ; Carbonation key tag (BOOL: the key switch on the console; the MAIN page shows CARBONATION ON / OFF) = Carb_Key . In front of the tank, where the operator stands. Its START, STOP and Running tags are the kitchen’s own; its ratio, mixing time and carbonation tags take the RECIPE page’s values. Then select Supply_Tank and set its Inlet fed from to Carbonator . The transfer line runs from the mix tank’s outlet pump through the carbonator and along a pipe rack at the back of the floor to the reservoir’s inlet. Guided mode’s Place the kitchen for me does all of this in one click. The mix kitchen in 3D: the water and cola syrup totes, the mix tank with its pumps and meters, the carbonator and the line on to Supply_Tank, and Tank_HMI in front. The batch One percent of Mix_Tank’s level is 20 units, and one pulse of a flowmeter is 20 units, so the room left to the HI probe (90 %) is 90 − Mix_Level pulses. A batch tops the tank up to HI: the water dose is the recipe’s water share of that room, counted on flowmeter A, and the syrup runs until HI. From an empty tank at the soda recipe’s 83 % water that is 75 pulses of water, 1500 units, and 300 of syrup: five to one. Then the batch is heated with a 2 °F band and mixed for the mixing time once it is up to temperature, and it is ready. Why top up, and not wait for the tank to empty the way Level 7 does? Because the transfer is not up to the kitchen. Step 6 closes the inlet at the high float, whatever is left in the mix tank, and opens it again at the low float, ready or not. A kitchen that waits for an empty tank before it makes the next batch will sooner or later be half-way through one when the reservoir calls. Topping up the moment a transfer ends means a full, mixed batch is standing in the tank every time Supply_Tank asks, and what was left from the last batch is already at the recipe.
