high-limit thermostat (180 °F) Mix_Heater BOOL alias of Local:6:O.Data.4 Mix_Tank heater Mix_Timer TIMER base tag Mixing time at temperature Mix_Empty_T TIMER base tag LO uncovered this long: the tank is empty Carb_Press INT alias of Local:11:I.Ch2Data Carbonator tank pressure, psi Carb_CO2 BOOL alias of Local:6:O.Data.6 Carbonator CO2 inlet valve Carb_Key BOOL alias of Local:3:I.Data.13 The carbonation key on the console, 1 turned to ON: the kitchen may carbonate Carb_Lamp BOOL alias of Local:5:O.Data.10 The amber CO2 lamp beside the key: carbonation enabled The rungs How it fits together Rung 0 gives the recipe tags their defaults the first time: a REAL that nobody has set is 0, so 0 means “not set yet”: 100 °F, 83 % water, 8 s, and Mix_Carb latched, because soda takes CO2. Picking a product on Tank_HMI’s RECIPE page loads its recipe into the same tags. Rungs 1–2 are the kitchen’s own run circuit. It is separate from Line_Run because a kitchen often runs when the line does not (the first batch is made before the shift starts), and the operator at Tank_HMI must be able to stop it without stopping the line. The console’s Start starts both: rung 1 turns the rising edge of Line_Run into a one-scan start. Rungs 3–4 turn the screen’s units into the program’s: seconds into milliseconds for the mixing timer, the setpoint into the bottom of the heater band. Rung 5 is power-up: a tank standing at HI holds a finished batch, so step 0 goes straight to 4. Rung 6 is the transfer: a ready batch, the kitchen running, and step 6’s inlet open. That one rung is the whole interface between the kitchen and the line. Rung 7 starts a batch, either from empty (step 0) or as a top-up (step 4, the inlet closed, the tank below 80 %), and only while both totes are above their low switches. CPT works out the water dose from the room and the recipe in one expression; RES clears the counter; MOV goes to step 1. From here each output comes straight after the step that runs it: rung 8 runs pump A in step 1; rungs 9–10 dose the water, a CTU on flowmeter A whose preset is the tag Dose_Pre ; rung 11 runs pump B in step 2, never past HI, and rung 12 ends the syrup at HI. Rung 13 runs the mixer in steps 3 and 4, only with the impeller covered; rungs 14–16 are the heater band and the heater, never past the high-limit thermostat; rungs 17–18 time the mix once the batch is up to temperature and make it ready. Rungs 19–20: if a transfer empties the tank, the sequence returns to 0 and starts again. Rung 21 is the carbonator. Everything the transfer pumps across goes through it, chilled to 38 °F, and takes up CO2 according to the tank pressure, so 19 to 22 psi gives the 3.5 volumes of the soda recipe. The rung is an on-off band with a seal-in: under 19 psi the CO2 valve opens, and XIC(Carb_CO2) keeps it open until 22, where LES(Carb_Press,22) goes false and the valve shuts until the pressure falls under 19 again. XIC(Mix_Carb) in front of it is the recipe (only a product that takes CO2 is carbonated) and XIC(Carb_Key) beside it is the operator’s key on the console; rung 22 lights the amber CO2 lamp beside the key. Run it Run mode, Start. Put Mix_Step , Dose_A.ACC , Mix_Level , Mix_Temp , Carb_Press and Supply_Level in Quick Watch. Within a few seconds Supply_Tank falls under its low float, step 6 opens the inlet, and with the batch ready the outlet pump runs: the transfer line fills, Supply_Level climbs to 90 % and the inlet closes. Then Mix_Step goes to 1, the water doses, pump B tops up to HI, the heater and mixer run to 100 °F and eight seconds, and Mix_Step is 4 again long before Supply_Tank is back down at its low float. During a transfer Carb_Press saws between 19 and 22. On Tank_HMI, STOP stops the kitchen while the line keeps running, and START runs it again. S13_Mix online with the finished line running. Green is power flow. Try it: make the kitchen late Press STOP on Tank_HMI, set MIX TIME to 60 s on the RECIPE page, press START and run for five minutes. Find the moment Supply_Tank reaches its low float while Mix_Step is still 3, and watch alarm bit 5 latch ten seconds later. Then put MIX TIME back to 8 s, and in rung 7 delete the top-up branch so the kitchen waits for an empty tank before it makes the next batch. Run again: how long before the same alarm? That is the reason for the top-up. Try it: flat soda Delete rung 21 and run. The carbonator starts at 20 psi, so the first transfers are fine, but each one takes some of the pressure and nothing puts it back. Watch Carb_Press fall and the Simulator Log start to report flat soda at the filler. Put the rung back. Then take LES(Carb_Press,22) out of it: the valve opens and seals itself in for good, the pressure climbs until the relief valve lifts. That is what the relief valve is for, and why every real band has its top as well as its bottom. Step 6 is unchanged: it still opens the inlet at the low float and closes it at the high float; the kitchen just answers it XIC(Mix_Run)[EQU(Mix_Step,0),EQU(Mix_Step,4)XIO(Supply_Inlet)LES(Mix_Level,80)]XIO(Water_Low)XIO(Conc_Low)[CPT(Dose_Pre,(90-Mix_Level)*Mix_Ratio/100),RES(Dose_A),MOV(1,Mix_Step)]; START A BATCH: the tank is empty (step 0), or a transfer has just ended with room left (step 4, inlet closed, below 80 %), and both totes have product. The batch tops the tank up to HI. One percent of level is 20 units, one pulse of the flowmeter, so the room to HI is 90 − Mix_Level pulses; the water dose is the recipe share of that room, and the syrup fills the rest. At 38 °F that dissolves 3.5 to 3.8 volumes of CO2 in the soda going through. Under 19 psi the valve opens and seals itself in; at 22 it drops out and stays shut until the pressure falls back under 19. Every 100 units of soda going through takes about 3 psi of CO2 with it XIC(Carb_Key)OTE(Carb_Lamp); The amber CO2 lamp beside the key: carbonation is enabled. Off, and a soda batch goes to Supply_Tank still; the kitchen's screen says so in yellow
ch31: In the app Guided mode’s last lesson is this chapter, and File → Load Reference Solution: Complete Bottle Line (15 steps) in another project is the answer key to compare against. With all fifteen routines in place, MainRoutine is fifteen JSRs, S3_Index last. Logic → Verify Controller : 0 errors. Reset Sim. Then run this checklist, the one the program’s own test runs on every release: Run mode. Press Start. Run lamp on; Pack_HMI shows RUNNING; the belt steps and a bottle drops every stop. Within a minute bottles are filling at stop 7 (a large charge for large bottles, a small one for small) and capping at stop 10 (the magazine turns a pocket per cap). Every capped bottle leaves the labeler with a label, and the camera passes it; Label_Fault stays off and the inspection count climbs. Broken bottles are dropped into the shredder; the box conveyor brings a box, banded with hazard tape, under the chute; IN BOX counts up; the full box leaves and the next arrives; BOXES counts 1. Small bottles ride the incline to the divert conveyor and are counted on SMALL; large bottles run to the end and are counted on LARGE; SCRAP counts the broken ones. Both sizes are packed, four to a case and one size per case: CASES LARGE and CASES SMALL on Pack_HMI both climb, and no empty case is sent out. Nothing is lost (the simulator’s counters show no red lost ) and the Simulator Log has no line about a bottle with nothing under it or nothing to land on. Supply_Tank falls to its low float, the red light flashes, the inlet opens, the level climbs. Every time it does, Mix_Tank has a batch ready and pumps it across; when the inlet closes, the kitchen tops itself up. Supply_Tank never stays below its low float. Dial 0010 on the thumbwheel; the line stops at ten large bottles; Enter clears; Start runs again. Alarm_Word stays 0 and the fault lamp dark for the whole run, including when you press Stop and Start at random moments. Each fault of chapter 28’s Run it, and a drive trip on Case_VFD, injected with Tools → Inject Machine Fault, is caught by the bit the table says, stops the line if it should, and clears with Clear Machine Faults, Reset and Start. The whole line running in Top-down view: the simulator’s counters read the program’s own tags. The regression runs that list on every release. If any line fails for you, the Simulator Log names the device, Monitor Tags shows the bit, and the matching lesson’s Run it says what should have happened. The finished template ( File → New Project… → LogixPro-style Bottle Line ) is the answer key; File → Export / Copy as Text… on both and compare. Appendix B is the complete listing and Appendix C the bit map. Save the project. You have built a bottling line from an empty floor and written every rung that runs it.
ch32: Part IV built one machine and one program. Part V is twenty-two puzzles, each on a machine built from the same palette parts as everything else in this book, each with a score and a par time: the graded levels. Every program printed in the chapters that follow has run to completion, every part in the right bin, before it was printed, and the program’s own regression runs them again on every release. Opening a level File → New Project… : the graded levels are the first section of the catalogue, as tiles in order of difficulty, each with its picture, its difficulty, its par and your best score; the Start Page’s plant floor opens them too (chapter 3). A level you have not touched opens with an empty program and its machine; one you have worked on opens where you left it, because each level keeps its own floor and program. Finishing a level records your best score and time, and My Progress keeps them all. The bottle-sort machine Levels 1 to 5 share one machine: Hopper : an Emitter in edge mode, limited to the level’s number of bottles. Infeed_Release drops one bottle on each rising edge; Infeed_Ready is 1 while the exit is clear. Main_Belt : one belt the length of the floor; Conveyor_Run runs it. The inspection gantry : PE_Inspect (a bottle is here), three retro beams at 30, 44 and 52 px ( PE_Low , PE_Mid , PE_High : a small bottle is 40 px tall and breaks only the low one, a medium is 48 and breaks two, a large is 56 and breaks all three), the colour sensor’s three banks ( Color_Red , Color_Blue , Color_Green ) and the crack eye ( Crack_Sensor , broken bottles only). The filler : a dispenser over the belt ( Fill_Valve ), the fill-level sensor beside the nozzle with its analog percent ( Fill_Level , 0–100 % of the bottle’s own label) and the presence eye under the nozzle ( PE_Fill ). One pusher and one bin per lane : Div1 … Div6 extend the pushers; each pusher has its own eye, PE_Div1 …, just ahead of the arm. The end of the line : PE_LineEnd and a remover that takes anything nobody pushed. The console : Start_PB , Stop_PB (a plain button on this machine), E_Stop (1 while healthy), Lamp_Run , Lamp_Fault . Every name in the list is an alias tag the level makes for you, pointing at the part’s I/O point: Tag Alias for Description Start_PB Local:3:I.Data.1 Start push button, momentary Stop_PB Local:3:I.Data.2 Stop push button, momentary E_Stop Local:3:I.Data.3 E-stop, NC: 1 = healthy Infeed_Ready Local:1:I.Data.0 Hopper exit clear: a bottle can be released Infeed_Release Local:4:O.Data.0 Release one bottle onto the belt (rising edge) Conveyor_Run Local:4:O.Data.1 Belt motor PE_Inspect Local:1:I.Data.2 Presence eye at the inspection gantry PE_Low Local:1:I.Data.3 Height beam at 30 px: blocked by every size PE_Mid Local:1:I.Data.4 Height beam at 44 px: blocked by M and L PE_High Local:1:I.Data.5 Height beam at 52 px: blocked by L only Color_Red Local:1:I.Data.6 Colour sensor bank 1: red Color_Blue Local:1:I.Data.7 Colour sensor bank 2: blue Color_Green Local:1:I.Data.8 Colour sensor bank 3: green Crack_Sensor Local:1:I.Data.10 Crack eye: the bottle in front of it is broken PE_Fill Local:1:I.Data.14 Presence eye under the fill nozzle Fill_Valve Local:4:O.Data.2 Fill valve Fill_Level Local:7:I.Ch1Data Fill of the bottle under the nozzle, 0-100 % of its label Fill_Done Local:1:I.Data.13 Liquid at the fill line of the bottle under the nozzle PE_Div1 Local:2:I.Data.1 Presence eye ahead of diverter 1 Div1 Local:4:O.Data.4 Diverter 1 cylinder PE_Div2 Local:2:I.Data.5 Presence eye ahead of diverter 2 Div2 Local:4:O.Data.5 Diverter 2 cylinder PE_Div3 Local:2:I.Data.9 Presence eye ahead of diverter 3 Div3 Local:4:O.Data.6 Diverter 3 cylinder PE_Div4 Local:2:I.Data.13 Presence eye ahead of diverter 4 Div4 Local:4:O.Data.7 Diverter 4 cylinder PE_LineEnd Local:2:I.Data.15 Presence eye at the end of the belt Lamp_Run Local:4:O.Data.8 Run lamp Lamp_Fault Local:4:O.Data.9 Fault lamp The later levels bring their own machines: Level 6 ends the belt in the case packer and VFD lane of the bottle line’s step 12; Level 7 and Level 12 are the mix tank and its kitchen; Levels 8, 9, 11, 13, 15 and 16 are a finished-bottle line with a camera, a laser marker, a labeler or a reject station; Level 10 is the servo axis; Level 14 is a paint line and Level 22 its bulk filler; Level 17 a checkweigher; Levels 18 and 19 a line of machine blocks; Levels 20 and 21 no machine at all, only a camera on a socket. Each chapter describes its machine and lists its tags. Graded bins and the score Each bin carries a Grading rule (whole or broken bottles, a size, a colour, must be filled) set in its Properties, and it scores what lands in it: +100 for the right part, −50 for the wrong one, −40 for the right bin with a wrong fill. A part that falls off the line is −50. The later levels add their own rules, each in its brief. When the hopper is empty and the belt is clear, the level completes: +200 if you are under par, and a card with your score and stars: three for no mistakes under par, two for no mistakes, one for 70 % right. Specs on the simulator toolbar shows each bin’s rule. The level’s brief sits under the simulator, and Help → Level Brief and Scoring has it in full. Level 1, Height sort, running its reference program. Ten bottles — small, medium and large, in three colours, some of them broken — come out of the hopper one per release. Sort them by height into four bins: broken bottles to bin 1, small to 2, medium to 3, large to 4. The filler is there but not scored on this level; leave it alone. Par is 150 s. The plan is the simplest one that works: release a bottle, let it run past the gantry, remember what the gantry saw, fire the right pusher when the bottle reaches it, wait for it to land, release the next. One bottle on the belt at a time means one set of memory bits, and that is the whole idea of this level: a sensor tells you something for a fraction of a second, and the program has to keep it until it is needed further down the belt. On this machine Stop is a plain normally-open button, so it is XIO(Stop_PB) , not the XIC(Stop) of the bottle line, whose stop button is normally closed — read the device’s settings, not your habits. E_Stop is 1 while the E-stop is healthy. Rung 1 runs the belt and lights the run lamp whenever the line runs; on this level the belt never stops. Releasing one bottle The release rung fires once — the one-shot — when the line runs, no bottle is in progress ( XIO(Busy) ) and the hopper’s exit is clear. On the same scan it latches Busy , so nothing else is released until this bottle is dealt with, and unlatches the four memory bits, so this bottle starts with a clean slate. The hopper is in edge mode: one rising edge of Infeed_Release , one bottle. A way out of Busy: the watchdog Busy is latched, so the next thing to write is a way to free it. Rungs 3–4 are the watchdog: while a bottle is in progress a 16 s timer runs, and when it is done the line is freed anyway — a bottle nobody wanted, or a bug, runs to the end of the belt and the next one is released. Written straight after the latch, it also keeps the line feeding while you write the rest: every bottle runs to the end and 16 s later the next one drops, so each rung below can be tested in Run the moment it is written. A latch with no way out written next to it is how lines stall. Remembering what the gantry saw Four latches. Each beam is broken only while the bottle passes it — about half a second — but the pushers are metres downstream, so the program latches what it saw. A small bottle sets only Is_Low ; a medium sets Is_Low and Is_Mid ; a large sets all three; the crack eye sets Is_Broken . Nothing clears them except the next release. Firing the right pusher Each pusher has its own eye just ahead of the arm; the rung pushes while that eye sees the bottle and the memory says the bottle belongs in this bin. The size tests are written as this beam and not the next one up : small is low-not-mid, medium is mid-not-high, large is high. Every whole-bottle bin tests XIO(Is_Broken) first: a broken bottle is broken whatever its size, and bin 1 is upstream, so it has already gone by the time a broken bottle could reach bin 2 — but the test costs nothing and saves you when the bins are reordered. Freeing the line Rung 13 latches Done when any pusher fires, because the pusher’s eye — and so the pusher rung — goes false the moment the bottle is pushed off the belt. A timer fed straight from Div2 would see half a second, never 1.5. Rungs 14-15 give the bottle a second and a half to land, then free the line and reset the watchdog: that bottle was dealt with, so the next one gets its own 16 s. The RES(Trip) matters because of where the watchdog sits. Its timer is above the release, and Busy is freed at the bottom of one scan and latched again by the release near the top of the next, so the timer never sees Busy off and never resets by itself; without the RES it would time across bottles and free the line early. Watch for: the res The first draft of this program had XIC(After.DN)OTU(Busy); with no RES , and released bottles in pairs. Walk the scan: the timer finishes and rung 15 unlatches Busy. Next scan, rung 2 sees Busy off, releases a bottle and latches Busy again — so rung 14’s timer sees its rung true , as it was last scan. It never saw the rung go false, so it never reset: it is still done, and rung 15 unlatches Busy again, and the next bottle is released right behind the first. A timer resets only when its rung is false for a whole scan. When the thing that ends a cycle also starts the next one, reset the timer yourself. Run it Run mode, press Start on the console. A bottle drops, runs past the gantry (watch the four Is_ bits in Monitor Tags latch), reaches its pusher and goes into its bin; a moment later the next one drops. The header counts Correct and Wrong; the Simulator Log names every bottle and the bin it landed in. A run of this program on 10 of 10 bottles in the right bin, nothing lost, in about 100 s against a par of 150 s: 1200 points and three stars. Try It Take XIO(Is_Broken) out of the small-bin rung and set the hopper’s Broken bottles to 60 % — then move bin 1 to the far end of the line (swap the pushers’ names). A broken small bottle now reaches bin 2 first. Put the test back. Then shorten After to 300 ms and see what the next bottle does to a bottle still sliding into its bin. Level 2, Fill by label, running its reference program. The same bins and the same ten bottles, but every whole bottle must be filled before it is binned: a bin graded must be filled gives −40 for a bottle that arrives short or overfilled, and a broken bottle that is filled leaks and costs −40 too. Par 170 s. Everything from Level 1 stays; the new problem is stopping the belt in the right place, filling to a measured level, and going again . Three things on the machine do the work: PE_Fill , an eye with a short range placed 20 px past the nozzle, so a bottle that stops the belt on it is standing under the nozzle; Fill_Valve , the dispenser’s valve; and Fill_Level , the fill-level sensor’s analog input, the bottle’s fill as a percent of its own label — 60 units for a small bottle, 80 for a medium, 100 for a large all read 100 when full, so one number fills all three sizes. The lamp gets a rung of its own, because it should stay lit while the belt is held for a fill — the line is still running. Release, the watchdog and the gantry As in Level 1, with one addition to the release rung: OTU(Filled) , so the new bottle starts unfilled. The fill The fill comes next because that is where it is on the belt: a bottle reaches the nozzle before the pushers. Rung 10 holds the belt when PE_Fill sees a bottle that is whole and not yet filled. It is an OTE, so the hold lasts exactly as long as those three things are true. Rung 11 opens the valve while held and the percent is under 97 — an LES compare on an analog input, chapter 8. Rung 12 latches Filled once it reaches 97, which drops the hold (rung 10’s XIO(Filled) ), which restarts the belt. A broken bottle is never held: XIO(Is_Broken) lets it ride through to bin 1 dry. Pushers and freeing the line As in Level 1. Why 97 and not 100? The valve closes on the scan after the compare goes true, and liquid is still in the air. Stop a fraction short and the last of it brings the bottle to its label; aim at 100 and you overfill. Every real filler has this in-flight allowance. Watch for: where the eye is The first draft of this program used an eye 8 px before the nozzle with a long range. The belt stopped with the bottle short of the nozzle, the valve opened, and the dispenser’s tank emptied onto the floor while Fill_Level sat at 0 — the sensor reads the bottle under it , and there was none. The level’s PE_Fill sits past the nozzle with a 6 px range for that reason. Before you trust any stop position, watch it once in the Side view. Run it Each whole bottle stops under the nozzle, the liquid rises in the Side view (watch Fill_Level climb in Monitor Tags), the belt goes again, and the bottle is sorted as in Level 1. Broken bottles pass the filler without stopping. A run on 10 of 10 bottles in the right bin, nothing lost, in about 111 s against a par of 170 s: 1200 points and three stars. Try It Change 97 to 100 and run: the score card shows −40s for overfilled bottles. Then try 90 and see the short fills. Level 3, Color sort, running its reference program. Twelve bottles, bins by colour now — broken, red, blue, green — and every whole bottle filled. Par 190 s. The machine is the same; only the question the gantry answers changes, and this lesson is about how little of a good program has to change when the question does. The colour sensor has three banks, one per colour, each on its own input: Color_Red , Color_Blue , Color_Green . Like the height beams, a bank is on only while the bottle is in front of the sensor, so the pattern is the same: latch it, test the latch at the pusher. ch36: In the app A level project opens with guided mode on this chapter: the panel lists the tags the program needs ( Make them ), shows every rung below under its fold with Copy and Add , checks that MainRoutine verifies, and while you run the level ticks three results — the level completes, every bottle in the right bin, under par. Level 4, Two on the line, running its reference program. Height sort with fill again — Level 2’s bins — but fourteen bottles and a par of 110 seconds. Level 2’s program takes about 10 s a bottle; fourteen bottles is over two minutes. No setting fixes that. The trap is the program’s shape : as long as the next bottle waits for the last one to reach its bin, the belt runs mostly empty. The next bottle has to leave the hopper while the last one is still on the belt, and as soon as there are two bottles on the belt, one set of Is_ bits is not enough memory: by the time the first bottle reaches its pusher, the gantry has overwritten what it saw. The idea: a queue per stretch of belt On the indexing line of Part IV, the memory that moved with the bottles was a shift register, one bit per stop, shifted once per index. This belt does not index — bottles arrive at the pushers whenever they arrive — but it keeps them in order : nothing on a belt overtakes anything else. Memory that keeps things in order is a FIFO , first in, first out. So: latch → Class FFL → Q1 FFU Q1 the belt → bottles stay in order FFU Q2 FFU Q3 gantry latch → Class filler FFL → Q1 Q1: zone 1 FFU Q1 the belt → bottles stay in order Div1 Q2: zone 2 no fit: pass on Div2 FFU Q2 Q3: zone 3 no fit: pass on Div3 FFU Q3 Each diverter unloads the head of its own zone’s queue when a bottle reaches its eye: fit → push; no fit → load the class into the next zone’s queue FFL(source,array,control,length) — FIFO Load — copies source to the tail of the queue in array on a rising edge of its rung; FFU(array,dest,control,length) — FIFO Unload — copies the head into dest and moves everything up. The CONTROL tag’s .POS says how many are in the queue (chapter 5). Eight entries per zone is far more than this belt holds. BOOL alias of Local:4:O.Data.7 Diverter 4 cylinder D4_ONS3 BOOL base tag The run circuit and the release As in Level 2, with one change in meaning: Busy now means a bottle is between the hopper and the filler , not a bottle is somewhere on the line . Leaving the filler: the way out of Busy Rung 4 latches AtFill when the eye under the nozzle sees the bottle. Rung 5 fires once when that eye then loses it — the bottle has left — and does four things in one scan: loads Class into zone 1’s queue, frees the front of the line ( OTU(Busy) , so rung 3 releases the next bottle), clears AtFill , and forgets the gantry’s latches. They come straight after the release because they are its way out: Busy is latched in rung 3 and freed in rung 5, so from here on the line feeds one bottle at a time and every rung you write below can be tested in Run as you write it. The order inside the branch does not matter: the FFL copies Class as it was at the end of the last scan, and the latches feed Class through rungs 13-19, which run after it. Until the diverters are in, nothing unloads the queue and it fills up; use Tools → Clear Tag Values before you run with the diverters, so they start on an empty queue. The gantry and the class word The seven latches are Level 1’s and Level 3’s together (the colour bits are not needed on this level; they are there because this is the one program for all five, and they cost nothing). Rungs 13-19 fold them into the bits of the DINT Class with OTEs — a tag used a bit at a time, chapter 5. Class is Binary style, so Monitor Tags shows the bits. The fill Level 2’s fill, unchanged. Diverter 1 Five rungs per diverter, and the same five for every lane. Rung 23 : a bottle arrives at the eye — unload the head of zone 1’s queue into Cur . Rung 24 : if Cur fits this bin (here: bit 3, broken), arm the pusher. Rung 25 : push while the bottle is at the eye and the pusher is armed. Rung 26 : the bottle has gone, disarm. Rung 27 : if it did not fit, pass the class on to zone 2’s queue. The three one-shots on the same eye ( D1_ONS , D1_ONS2 , D1_ONS3 ) all fire on the same scan, in rung order — that is the scan of chapter 4 doing the work. Rung 23 unloads, so Cur is fresh when rung 24 tests it; rung 24 arms, so when rung 27 asks XIO(Fire_1) it already knows the answer (rung 26 cannot disarm in between: it waits for the eye to clear, and the eye is still made). The pass-on rung comes last so that it works the moment it is written: written before the push and the disarm, a broken bottle would leave Fire_1 armed for good and the pass-on rung would never see it off. That is how otherwise is written without repeating the match in reverse. Each needs its own storage bit: a one-shot remembers last scan’s rung state, and three rungs sharing one bit would see each other’s. Diverters 2, 3 and 4 The same five rungs, with the match changed: small is XIO(Cur.3)XIC(Cur.0) , medium XIO(Cur.3)XIC(Cur.1) , large XIO(Cur.3)XIC(Cur.2) . The last diverter’s pass-on rung ends in NOP() : a bottle no bin wanted rides to the remover at the end of the belt, and there is no queue after the last zone. Watch for: a slipped queue Everything depends on every bottle that enters a zone being loaded into its queue exactly once, and unloaded exactly once. Miss one load — a pass-on rung with the wrong condition — and every class in the next zone is one bottle late: the next diverter sorts the wrong bottle, and so does every diverter after it, until the line is emptied. That is the same failure as a shift register that misses a pulse in Part IV, and the same check finds it: Monitor Tags, Q1_Ctl.POS and Q2_Ctl.POS , against the bottles you can see in each stretch of belt. Run it Bottles leave the hopper every few seconds; several are on the belt at once, and each still goes to the right bin. Expand Q1 and Q2 in Monitor Tags and watch the classes move through the queues as the bottles move down the belt. A run on 14 of 14 bottles in the right bin, nothing lost, in about 90 s against a par of 110 s: 1600 points and three stars. Try It Delete diverter 1’s pass-on rung (rung 27) and run: from the first non-broken bottle on, diverter 2 unloads nothing (its queue is empty) and nothing is sorted. Put it back and delete rung 26 instead: Fire_1 stays armed and diverter 1 pushes the next bottle too, whatever it is.  [XIC(Start_PB),XIC(Run)]XIO(Stop_PB)XIC(E_Stop)OTE(Run); RUN: the seal-in. ch38: In the app File → New Project… → A graded level → 6 . The level opens with guided mode on this chapter: the tags to make, every rung below under its fold, a Verify check, and five results it ticks while you run — a case stops on the mark, a case is packed, the level completes, every bottle right, under par. Level 6, Pack it, running its reference program. Sixteen bottles. The broken ones go into the scrap bin as before; every other bottle is filled and then packed : the belt ends in the case packer of step 12 (chapter 29), and a case lane on a VFD runs beside it. Four bottles to a case, and when the hopper is empty whatever is left in the infeed goes out as a part case. Par 140 s. How the level is scored What happens Points A good, filled bottle packed into a case +100 A broken bottle in the scrap bin +100 A broken or short-filled bottle packed into a case −50 A whole bottle in the scrap bin −50 Bottles dropped by the packer with no case under the head (each) −50 An empty case shipped at Case_Out −25 What happens Points Complete under par (140 s) +200 The level is complete when the hopper is empty, no bottle is left on the belt or in the packer’s infeed, and every packed case has reached Case_Out. Three stars: no mistakes and under par. How to pass it, step by step 1. Start from Level 5. Run circuit, release one bottle at a time to the filler, latch the gantry into a class 2. One diverter only. Diverter 1 takes broken bottles into the scrap bin. A whole bottle is not pushed: it 3. Run the case lane. Case_Run while no empty case is under the head: 4. Two speeds and a latch. 60 Hz normally; 15 Hz from the slow-down eye until an empty case is on the 5. Scale to the analog output. SCP(Case_Hz,0,60,0,10000,Case_Speed_Ref) . Writing 60 or 15 6. Drop only on a stopped, empty case. Group ready, case in place, case not full, 7. Finish the batch. Diverter 1: broken bottles to the scrap bin The last diverter’s "otherwise" rung passes nothing on: a whole bottle simply runs to the end of the belt. The case lane: run, creep, speed and scaling The same seven rungs as the bottle line’s step 12, with Run in place of Line_Run . The speed comes first, or the case cannot move: 60 Hz while not creeping, SCP out to the 0-10 V reference and back from the drive’s output frequency. Then the lane runs while no empty case is on the mark, a latched creep from the slow-down eye, and 15 Hz while creeping. Counting the batch and packing The CTU counts rising edges of Infeed_Release ; at 16 the hopper is empty. The TON starts when the last bottle has left the filler ( Busy off) and gives it 15 s to run down the belt — the belt is 780 px long at 80 px/s, so about 5 s is needed; 15 s is generous and costs nothing, because the timer only starts at the very end. The PACK rung drops on a full group as usual, or, once the tail timer is done, on whatever is left in the infeed ( GRT(Infeed_Count,0) ): the packer takes up to four, so the part case gets the last one, two or three. Watch for: the level that never ends Sixteen bottles minus the broken ones is rarely a multiple of four. Pack only on Group_Ready and the last bottles wait in the infeed for a group that never comes: the hopper is empty, the belt is clear, and the level does not complete. A real line has the same problem at the end of every batch — the last case is a part case, and someone has to decide to send it. Run it Load your program, Run mode, Start. Watch the first case come in fast, slow at the eye, stop on the mark; bottles collect in the infeed (the count on the packer’s table), and the fourth starts the head. The Simulator Log shows every pack and every scrap-bin push, with points. A run on 16 of 16 bottles in the right bin, nothing lost, in about 112 s against a par of 140 s: 1800 points and three stars. Try It Go for a faster time: the line stops at the filler for every fill, so the packer is never the bottleneck — or is it? Set the case feeder’s interval to 8 s and find out. ch39: In the app File → New Project… → A graded level → 7 . Guided mode opens on this chapter: the tags, every rung below under its fold, a Verify check, and five results — pump A stops on its count and B tops up to HI, the batch heats with the mixer running, all three batches made, every batch on spec, under par. Level 7, Batch Mix, running its reference program. No belt, no bottles. One Mix Tank (built after the LogixPro Batch Mix) and a console. Make three batches, one of each recipe, in the order the recipe selector shows: the level turns the selector to the next recipe each time a batch drains. Par 240 s. The tank Where the ingredients come from Each inlet is piped to a Supply Tote : Supply_A holds water, Supply_B orange concentrate, 10,000 units each. The pipes are part of the scene. The Mix Tank’s Inlet A fed from and Inlet B fed from settings name the totes, and the pumps take what they move out of them. An empty tote runs its pump dry: no flow, no flowmeter pulses, and a line in the Simulator Log. An inlet fed from nothing is on the plant supply header , drawn in 3D as a riser out of the floor with a ball valve. The outlet, with nothing piped to it, runs to a floor drain. The flowmeters are inline digital meters. The LCD shows the rate in units a second and the running total; the green lamp is on while liquid moves and the amber one blinks with each pulse the meter sends the controller. Tick Flowmeters also report their rate and each meter adds an analog input, FlowA_Rate and so on. Bind that signal to a REAL tag in its properties and the program reads 87.5, not 87. While the ingredients go in, the tank’s contents look clear and pale; mixing, faster when warm, turns them cloudy, and the next batch starts clear again. The tank has a local panel on its shell, and the console side of the floor has a Process HMI on a pedestal, Tank_HMI . Both show the same live faceplate: the vessel with its level and probes, the temperature against the high limit, the mixing time, a one-minute trend, the ratio, the flows, which pumps and heater are on, the state and an alarm line. It is drawn the way plant HMIs are, grey with colour only for what is running or wrong, so a lit heater or an alarm stands out at a glance. The HMI reads the tank directly; it is a window for you, not an input to the program. How each batch is scored Recipe Ingredient A Temperature Mix at least A 50 % 150 °F 10 s B 75 % 130 °F 15 s C 25 % 170 °F 8 s Graded when the batch drains Points A share within ±5 % of the recipe +100 (−50 if not) Temperature when the outlet pump started: recipe −3 to +8 °F +100 (−50 if not) Mixed at least the recipe time +100 (−50 if not) Less than 80 % of the tank (a short batch) −50 Overflowed past the top −100 Scorched (heater on with the element uncovered) −100 Outlet pump ran dry more than 3 s −25 All three batches under par (240 s) +200 How to pass it, step by step 1. Think in steps, not in rungs. One DINT, Step , says what the tank is doing: 0 waiting for an empty 2. Read the recipe into tags. Three rungs: the selector position sets Target_A (pulses of A), Target_T 3. Dose A by counting. Pump A runs in step 1; a CTU counts Flow_A; at Target_A move to step 2. 4. Top up with B to HI. Pump B runs in step 2 until Hi_Level, and the HI probe ends it — B is "whatever 5. Heat with hysteresis. Latch Heat_On below the target minus 2 °F, unlatch it at the target. Gate the 6. Mix on a timer with a preset tag. TON(Mix_T,Mix_Pre,0) in step 3 — the preset operand can be a 7. Drain to empty. Pump_Out in step 4. The level reads 0 % with a few units still in the tank, so run the Tags this lesson needs The alias tags of the machine are made for you; create these before you type the rungs. Verify reports any you miss. neither = B Lamp_Run BOOL alias of Local:4:O.Data.5 Run lamp Lamp_Idle BOOL alias of Local:4:O.Data.6 Idle lamp: waiting for an empty tank or a Start Lamp_Full BOOL alias of Local:4:O.Data.7 Full lamp Lamp_Fault BOOL alias of Local:4:O.Data.8 Fault lamp Run, recipe A and the start of a batch The recipe rungs run every scan; the level only turns the selector when a batch has drained, so the values never change in the middle of one. Only recipe A is here: the first batch is always A, and the rungs for B and C come after the batch-out rung, where they can be seen working the moment they are written. SUB(Target_T,2,Target_Lo) is the bottom of the heater’s band. A batch starts only on an empty tank: XIO(Lo_Level) and LEQ(Tank_Level,0) . Dosing: A by count, B to HI The CTU counts every rising edge of Flow_A, whatever step it is in — fine, because only step 1 runs pump A, and the batch start resets it. Heating and mixing Rung 12 unlatches Heat_On at the target, outside step 3, or at the high limit; rung 13 is the only rung that drives the heater, and it refuses an uncovered element. Rung 14 leaves step 3 when the mixing timer is done and the batch is at least at the bottom of its band. Draining and counting Recipes B and C Written after batch A has drained, these go true as soon as the level turns the selector to B, and to C after the next batch. Lamps Run it Load your program, Run mode, Start. Watch the display: FILLING with the A share climbing, then B pulling it down to the recipe; HEAT+MIX with the temperature climbing at a little over 2 °F a second; DRAINING; EMPTY; and the selector turns. The Simulator Log grades each batch as it drains. A run on 3 of 3 bottles in the right bin, nothing lost, in about 181 s against a par of 240 s: 1100 points and three stars. Try It The reference program wastes most of its time heating after the tank is full. Start the heater as soon as Lo_Level is covered — in step 1 — and watch two things happen: the batch is ready much sooner, and every slug of cold ingredient pulls the temperature down (the tank mixes it in), so the heater works against the fill. Beat 150 s. Then take XIC(Lo_Level) out of the heater rung and start a batch: the element comes on before the liquid covers it, and the batch is scorched. Last, give the heater no band at all — LES(Tank_Temp,Target_T)OTE(Heater) — and watch it chatter on and off at the setpoint in Monitor Tags. Try it: run a tote dry Set Supply_B’s Starts at to 15 % (1,500 units) and run the reference program. Batches 1 and 2 take about 1,350 units of B between them, so in batch 3 the tote empties while pump B is topping up. Pump B runs dry, the HI probe never makes, and the program sits in step 2 forever with the Run lamp on. A real line would be exactly as stuck. Make two fixes. First, a watchdog: XIC(Run)EQU(Step,2)TON(B_Fill_T,20000,0) , and when it is done, light Lamp_Fault and stop. Second, use the tote’s own LowLevel switch, a digital input like any other (alias it as Tote_B_Low ): do not start a batch while it is on. The watchdog catches the failure; the low switch stops you walking into it. In Run mode, clicking an empty tote swaps in a full one, the way a forklift would. A mix tank on the bottle line The Mix Tank pipes to a filler the way the Reservoir does: put one in place of Supply_Tank and pick it in the Filler’s Fed from , which lists every tote, tank, reservoir and mix tank in the scene. A Tank can also be fed from the Mix Tank (its Inlet fed from ); it then fills only while the mix tank’s outlet pump runs and its own inlet valve is open. The filler then only gets product while the tank’s outlet pump runs, so the program has to make a batch first and then hold Pump_Out on while the filler draws — a batch-to-line handoff that a supply tank never asked for. ch40: In the app File → New Project… → A graded level → 8 . Guided mode opens on this chapter: the tags, every rung below under its fold, a Verify check, and six results: the camera inspects a bottle, a result is acknowledged, a defective bottle is rejected, the level completes, every bottle in the right bin, under par. Level 8, Vision check, running its reference program. This level is the one most plants would recognise first: a camera on the line. Finished bottles arrive from an upstream line, filled, capped and labeled, but about a third of them have one defect: no cap, no label, or a short fill. An In-Sight smart camera on a stand over the belt looks at each bottle as it passes. Your program triggers it, takes each result, carries it down the belt to the reject pusher, and pushes every defective bottle into Reject_Bin . The good ones run on into Good_Bin at the end of the belt. Twenty bottles, par 45 s. The camera is not a made-up part. It is a camera module in I/O Configuration, Cam1 , built from Cognex’s own device file for the In-Sight 5700 series, at 192.168.1.18. Every tag is named the way the real camera names it, so the rungs in this chapter are the rungs you would write for a real 5705 on a CompactLogix. The camera’s job here is Bottle inspection : three tools, one for the cap, one for the label, one for the fill level. The machine The camera’s tags The module’s tags are Cam1:O.… (the PLC writes them) and Cam1:I.… (the camera writes them). The ones this level uses: Tag Meaning Cam1:O.Trigger_Enable Allows triggers at all. Off, the camera ignores Trigger and Trigger_Ready stays off. Cam1:O.Trigger Rising edge: acquire an image now. Tag Meaning Cam1:O.Buffer_Results_Enable Queue results until each one is acknowledged (below). Cam1:O.Inspection_Results_Ack The PLC has read the result. Cam1:I.Trigger_Ready The camera can take a trigger: on line, enabled, not acquiring or inspecting. Cam1:I.Trigger_Ack The trigger was taken; stays on until Trigger goes off. Cam1:I.Missed_Acq A trigger arrived while the camera was busy: that bottle has no image. Cam1:I.System_Busy Acquiring or inspecting. Cam1:I.Inspection_Completed Changes state at the end of every inspection: it toggles, so look for a change, not for a 1. Cam1:I.Results_Valid A result is presented in the tags below. Cam1:I.Results_Buffer_Overrun A result was thrown away because the buffer was full. Cam1:I.Job_Pass The presented result passed. Cam1:I.Inspection_ID The number of the inspection the presented result belongs to. Cam1:I.Inspection_Result_Code Bit 0 no cap, bit 1 no label, bit 2 short fill, bit 3 no part in view; 0 is a good bottle. Cam1:I.Inspection_Results[…] The result data: bytes 0-3 the part’s serial number, 4-5 the result code, 6 the size (1 S, 2 M, 3 L), 7 metal, 8 pass, 9 the fill in % of the label. The two handshakes The trigger. Wait for Trigger_Ready , raise Trigger , wait for Trigger_Ack , drop Trigger ; the camera drops Trigger_Ack . System_Busy covers the 30 ms exposure and the 150 ms inspection, and Trigger_Ready comes back when both are over. Trigger while it is busy and nothing is acquired: Missed_Acq comes on and that bottle goes by with no image. The result. When an inspection ends, the camera presents its result and raises Results_Valid . Read the result, then raise Inspection_Results_Ack . The camera drops Results_Valid , and then the PLC drops the ack. That makes four edges, always in that order: Valid up, Ack up, Valid down, Ack down. Buffered results. With Buffer_Results_Enable on, a result that finishes while the last one is still unacknowledged is not thrown away. It waits in a queue, up to the camera’s buffer depth (4 here), and the camera presents it once the PLC has finished the handshake for the one before. With buffering off, each new result simply overwrites the last, whether the PLC has read it or not. Buffering is what lets the program look away for a scan or two without losing a bottle. It has a limit, though: a result that finds the queue full is lost, and Results_Buffer_Overrun comes on. Lose one result and every bottle after it gets the wrong verdict, because the FIFO is one short. How the level is scored What happens Points A defective bottle in Reject_Bin +100 A good bottle in Good_Bin +100 A defective bottle in Good_Bin (shipped) −100 A good bottle in Reject_Bin −50 A bottle that passes the camera without being inspected −25 Complete under par +200 How to pass it, step by step 1. Set the camera up once. Trigger_Enable and Buffer_Results_Enable on whenever the 2. Space the bottles. A timer that restarts itself releases one every 0.9 s. At 80 px/s that puts four or five 3. Trigger once per bottle. An ONS on PE_Trigger latches a request; the trigger goes out only when the 4. Take each result into a FIFO. Results_Valid and not yet acknowledged: FFL the result code into 5. Unload at the pusher. When a bottle reaches PE_Reject, FFU the oldest code. Bottles on a belt stay in 6. Verify reports any you miss. Rung 3 is the self-restarting timer of chapter 7: XIO(Rel_T.DN) resets it the scan after it is done, so Rel_T.DN is on for exactly one scan, which rung 4 turns into one rising edge on Infeed_Release . The trigger handshake The request is latched because the eye’s edge and the camera being ready do not have to happen in the same scan. With 0.9 s between bottles and 180 ms of camera time they always do here, but the program does not rely on it. Rung 7 drops Trigger the moment the camera acknowledges it; a Trigger held on is not a second trigger, and the camera waits for it to drop before it can be acknowledged again. The results handshake FFL loads on the rung going true. Latching the ack on the same rung makes the rung go false on the next scan, so each result is loaded exactly once, even though Results_Valid stays on until the camera sees the ack. Rung 9 is the other half: the ack comes off when Valid has gone, and only then does the camera present the next queued result. The reject pusher and the counts The pattern is Level 4’s diverter, with one FIFO instead of one per zone: unload on the eye’s rising edge, arm, push while the bottle is at the eye, disarm when it has gone. The counts are for the toolbar; the score card keeps the official ones. The fault lamp Run it Load your program, Run mode, Start. Camera_HMI shows each image as it is taken, with the three tools drawn on it in green or red. In a run on v2.02, 20 of 20 bottles in the right bin, nothing lost, in about 38 s against a par of 45 s: 2200 points and three stars. Watch for: the toggle and the level Inspection_Completed toggles. A rung with XIC(Cam1:I.Inspection_Completed) on it is true for every other inspection, not every one. If you want to use it, remember its last state in a BOOL and compare. Results_Valid with the ack handshake is simpler, and it is the signal that means the result is ready to read. Watch for: acking without dropping Raise the ack and never drop it (leave out rung 9) and you get exactly one result. With buffering on, the camera queues the next four and throws the fifth away, and from then on every verdict belongs to a different bottle. The fault lamp lights on the overrun, but by then the FIFO is already wrong. Try it: see an overrun Take rung 9 out and run. Watch the RESULT BUFFER bar on Camera_HMI climb to 4 / 4 and the overrun count start. Then put rung 9 back, take out Cam1:O.Buffer_Results_Enable in rung 2, and slow the ack by putting TON(Ack_T,500,0) before it: the results overwrite each other instead, and nothing tells you, which is why plants buffer. Try it: a missed acquisition Set Rel_T to 300 ms and take XIC(Cam1:I.Trigger_Ready) out of rung 6. Some bottles now arrive while the camera is still inspecting the last: Missed_Acq, the fault lamp, and −25 for every bottle that passes uninspected. On a real camera The module’s Mode in I/O Configuration is Simulated , and the Vision Sensor then plays the camera. In the desktop app, switch Cam1 to implicit I/O at the camera’s address and the same program drives a real In-Sight. The real camera takes the trigger, runs its own job on whatever is under its lens, and sends back its own Job_Pass, result code and Results_Valid. The sim only mirrors its bits: the ring light flashes when the real camera acquires. That mode is for working the handshake on real hardware and is not scored, because the score is kept against the sim’s bottles. For the program to work unchanged, the job on the camera has to report the same result layout: the defect bits in the result code and the fill in the result data. Which spreadsheet cells feed those is set in In-Sight Explorer’s EtherNet/IP settings. Card mode: the card decides On a live camera the verdict comes from whatever is under the lens, and the sim’s bottles have their own defects, so the two do not match and the run is not scored. Card mode fixes that. Tick Card mode in the Camera’s properties and the hopper sends only good bottles; each bottle waits at the camera until its result is presented, then takes that verdict and moves on. The verdict comes from a bottle card under the camera: Card Bottle Result code Fill (byte 9) Card ID (byte 10) SN-4801 good 0 100 1 SN-4802 no cap 1 100 2 SN-4803 no label 2 100 3 SN-4804 short fill 4 70 4 no card no part in view: a reject 8 0 0 Level 8’s rungs do not change: they trigger, read the code, carry it in the FIFO and reject on it, exactly as before. What changes is the belt. A bottle that waits at the camera holds the bottles behind it, so the line runs at the pace of the camera’s answers, and with a real camera that is the pace at which you swap cards. With the simulated camera , choose the card in Card under the lens , or on Camera_HMI’s CARDS page touch the card you want under the lens. The page draws the four cards as the camera sees them through the red filter and keeps a tally per card: what it should read, how many times it was seen, how many it read right and its last code. MAIN names the card on the image, reads HOLDING while a bottle waits for its result, and turns the card line red when a card reads the wrong verdict. With a real camera (Cam1 on implicit I/O in the desktop app), the 5705 decides. The sim reads three things from it when Results_Valid rises: Inspection_Result_Code for the verdict, byte 9 of Inspection_Results for the fill and byte 10 for the card ID. The job on the camera writes those, so the card ID is something the job reads off the card, not something typed in. A result whose code does not match its card ID shows up on the CARDS page and in the event log. Try it: swap cards mid-run Tick Card mode, start with SN-4801 under the lens and run. After five bottles touch SN-4804 on the CARDS page, then the empty card, then SN-4803. Watch each bottle stop under the camera, take the card, and go to the bin its verdict sends it to. The score card at the end lists every card you used, and if the rungs are right every count in the Right column matches Seen. Try it: break the ack In card mode, take rung 9 out (the ack never drops). The first bottle gets its verdict, the second waits at the camera and never moves: its result is in the buffer but never presented, and the line stays held. Put the rung back and the line runs again. That is the same fault as the overrun Try it, made visible on the belt. The bottle cards The cards are printed on the bench printer from STEP files in the repository’s cards folder: 100 × 70 × 4 mm, a chamfered corner so a card only sits one way in its nest, and two bodies in each file, a dark base and red features inlaid 0.8 mm and standing 0.6 mm proud. Through the red band-pass filter the red reads bright and the base dark. Everything on a card is something the job uses: the bottle’s outline (to locate it), the cap, the liquid (its top edge is the fill line), a label window with the product name for OCR, and a DataMatrix that encodes the card’s number. There is no text for people on a card. The number is SN-48RK : R is the product (0 SODA, 1 WATER, 2 MILK, 3 JUICE, 4 OIL) and K the defect (1 good, 2 no cap, 3 no label, 4 short fill at 70 %). The job puts R × 10 + K in byte 10, so the SODA set reads 1 to 4, the IDs in the table above. Level 8 uses the SODA set; Level 9 uses the whole set (see its chapter, Card mode on Level 9 ). On Camera_HMI’s CARDS page a tab per product picks the row of four cards. The camera’s own image With Cam1 live, the camera screen shows the picture the 5705 actually took. Every time Inspection_Complete toggles, the page asks the bridge for it; the bridge logs in to the camera’s FTP server, reads image.bmp (an In-Sight always keeps its last acquired image there), scales it down to the width set in the Camera’s properties and hands it back. The screen fits it into the image pane and writes under it what came back from the camera: the result code, the fill (byte 9) and the card (byte 10). The camera’s own graphics are not in image.bmp ; it is the raw image. Nothing is added to the camera job for this. The bridge pulls the file, so there are no spreadsheet cells, no Event and no FTP server on the PC. The login is admin with a blank password unless you set another user (one with FTP Read under Sensor → User Access Settings) in the Camera’s properties: Live image , FTP user , FTP password and width to fetch . One fetch runs at a time; inspections that finish while an image is on its way ask for one more when it lands, so at a fast trigger rate the screen shows the latest image, not every one. A refused login or a camera that does not answer is written in the pane. Touch the image and it fills the screen: the IMAGE view shows it as large as Camera_HMI allows, with the inspection ID, the image size and how long the fetch took above it, and the code, fill and card below. Touch it again to go back. Live image: width to fetch sets the size the bridge sends: 800 is plenty for the screen; set it to the camera’s own width (1600 on a 5603) to get every pixel on the screen. FULL SIZE on the IMAGE view goes further: it fetches the last image unscaled and opens it over the whole window, with Fit, 100, 200 and 400 %, scrolling to pan, and the pixel under the pointer with its grey value, which is handy for checking a threshold or a DataMatrix module against what the job sees. Esc closes it. The screen keeps its smaller copy, so the full image is only fetched when you ask for it. Each image is work for the camera, on top of inspecting and keeping the I/O connection going, so Live image: at most one image every (1 s by default) keeps a fast trigger from queueing one fetch after another. If a busy camera goes quiet for a moment, the I/O connection is held, not dropped: the module log says stalled and then resumed after the stall , and only ten seconds of silence closes and reopens it. On an older camera such as the 5603, an RPI of 50–100 ms and In-Sight Explorer offline (no live video) keep the stalls away. A real In-Sight 4.x job On In-Sight 4.x firmware (a 5603, say) a spreadsheet job sends its results to the PLC with two cells: FormatOutputBuffer , which packs values into bytes, and WriteEIPBuffer(A0, …) , which puts them in Inspection_Results after each inspection. Lay them out the way the simulated camera does, and Logix Connect reads them where it expects them: Bytes Value Format 0–3 inspection count 32-bit 4–5 result code (bit 0 no cap, 1 no label, 2 short fill, 3 no card, 4 wrong product) 16-bit 6, 7 0 8-bit 8 pass (1/0) 8-bit 9 fill % 8-bit 10 card ID, R × 10 + K 8-bit Then set the Camera’s Live camera: where the inspection ID and result code are read to Results buffer : the screen, the RESULTS page and card mode take the ID from bytes 0–3 and the code from bytes 4–5. On 4.x the module’s own Inspection_Result_Code field is not set by the job, so Level 8’s results rung has to read the code from the buffer too: FFL(Cam1:I.Inspection_Results[4],Res_Q[0],Res_Q_Ctl,8) in place of the code field, the change you would make on a real line with that camera. Two more things a 4.x camera does its own way. With Buffer_Results_Enable on, it raises Results_Valid only when the job writes a results buffer; a job without WriteEIPBuffer never raises it, Level 8’s results rung never runs, and nothing is rejected. (The screen still counts such a camera’s inspections on Inspection_Complete until it has seen Results_Valid once.) And PASS / FAIL on the screen is the camera’s Job_Pass , which follows the job’s pass/fail cell (Sensor → Job Pass/Fail Cell Setup): a cell such as And($F$6==1,$F$13==1) that is 1 when the label read and the code decoded. Try it: sn-4801 to sn-4804 on a real camera With the two buffer cells in the job and Results buffer selected, put each SODA card under the lens in turn and trigger. SN-4801 should read code 0, fill 100 and card 1; SN-4802 code 1 (no cap); SN-4803 code 2 (no label: the OCR fails); SN-4804 code 4 with fill 70 and card 4. The CARDS page tallies every one, and any card whose code does not match what it should read shows red: that is the job to fix, not the program. Without card mode, a live camera’s inspections count too. Each time Inspection_Complete toggles (or Results_Valid rises, with the results buffer on) the screen takes the camera’s Inspection_ID , its result code, Job_Pass and, on a bottle job, bytes 9 and 10, and shows them as the simulated camera’s would: PASS or FAIL, the counts, the RESULTS page and the banner. Those results do not move the sim’s bottles; that is what card mode is for. Try it: see what the camera saw With Cam1 live in the desktop app, tick Card mode and run Level 8 with SN-4804 under the lens. Each bottle that stops at the camera brings the card’s picture to Camera_HMI with code 4 · fill 70 % under it. Now cover half the card with your hand and trigger again: the picture shows your hand and the code shows what the job made of it. Then set FTP password to anything and watch the pane report the camera’s refusal.  [XIC(Start_PB),XIC(Run)]XIO(Stop_PB)XIC(E_Stop)OTE(Run); RUN: the seal-in. ch41: In the app File → New Project… → A graded level → 9 . Guided mode opens on this chapter: the tags, every rung below under its fold, a Verify check, and the run results: the camera changes job to WATER and then JUICE, the stray bottle of the old product is rejected, the first trace record reads SODA,01,000001 , the level completes, every bottle in the right bin, under par. Level 9, Changeover, running its reference program. Level 8 had one product. This line runs three, one batch after another: eight SODA, eight WATER, eight JUICE. Each product has its own camera job, because each has its own bottle, label and fill line: SODA passes at 95 % of the label, WATER at 90 %, JUICE at 97 %. Between batches the program has to do what an operator does at a real changeover: hold the infeed, let the last bottle of the old product clear the camera, load the next job and wait for the camera to confirm it, then start feeding again. Two more things come with it. Every changeover leaves a bottle of the old product behind somewhere upstream, and in this level it turns up as the third bottle of the next batch: a SODA bottle among the WATER, a WATER bottle among the JUICE. The camera has to catch it, and it does, because the job it is running knows what product it expects. And every bottle gets a trace record : the PLC tells the camera which bottle is coming (its position in the batch and its number on the line), the camera puts that into its answer, and the PLC files the answer in a STRING array. Twenty-four bottles, par 65 s. The machine The camera’s new tags Everything from Level 8 still applies. These are the tags this level adds. They are the In-Sight 5700 series’ own names. Tag Meaning Cam1:I.Current_Job_ID The job the camera is running now (1, 2 or 3). Cam1:O.Command_ID The job to load when Execute_Command rises. Cam1:O.Execute_Command Rising edge: run the command (here, load job Command_ID). Hold it until Command_Complete. Tag Meaning Cam1:I.Command_Complete The command has finished; stays on until Execute_Command drops. Cam1:I.Command_Failed The command could not run, for example a job number the camera does not have. Cam1:O.User_Data[…] Bytes the PLC sends with an inspection. The job reads bytes 0-1 as the bottle’s position in its batch and bytes 4-7 as its number on the line. Cam1:O.Set_User_Data Rising edge: the camera latches User_Data for the next trigger. Cam1:I.Set_User_Data_Ack The camera has the data; stays on until Set_User_Data drops. Cam1:I.Inspection_Results[12… 27] The trace: 16 ASCII characters, PRODUCT,PP,NNNNNN . PRODUCT is the job’s product, PP the position and NNNNNN the number the PLC sent. Result code bit 4 Wrong product: the bottle is not the product the running job expects. Any job, any bottle. Three handshakes, in order The job change. Put the job number in Command_ID and raise Execute_Command . The camera loads the job (about half a second, with Trigger_Ready off while it does), sets Current_Job_ID and raises Command_Complete . Drop Execute_Command and the camera drops Command_Complete . A trigger during the change is a missed acquisition. A bottle inspected under the wrong job gets the wrong verdict: a SODA bottle inspected under the WATER job is a wrong-product reject. The user data. Before each trigger, write User_Data and raise Set_User_Data . Wait for Set_User_Data_Ack , then trigger. The camera ties the data it latched to the next image it takes. Trigger before the ack and the inspection carries the last bottle’s data. The trigger and the result are Level 8’s, unchanged. How the level is scored What happens Points A defective or wrong-product bottle in Reject_Bin +100 A good bottle in Good_Bin +100 A defective bottle in Good_Bin (shipped) −100 A good bottle in Reject_Bin −50 A bottle that passes the camera without being inspected −25 Each Trace[n] that holds bottle n+1’s record exactly, checked at the end +25 Complete under par +200 The trace check compares Trace[0] to SODA,01,000001 , Trace[1] to SODA,02,000002 and so on to Trace[23] , JUICE,08,000024 . The stray bottle’s record names the batch it was in, not the product it was: the 11th bottle is a SODA bottle in the WATER batch, and its record is WATER,03,000011 . That is what the camera knows: the job it ran and the data it was sent. How to pass it, step by step 1. Start from Level 8. Run, belt, camera setup, trigger, results FIFO, reject: all of it stays. 2. Work out the wanted job from the selector, every scan. 3. Gate the release on the job. A bottle leaves the hopper only while the camera is running the wanted 4. Wait for the line to clear once the hopper is held: 5 s is enough for the last bottle of the old batch to 5. Change the job , and drop Execute_Command on Command_Complete. 6. Send the user data with each trigger, and trigger only on the ack. 7. File the trace when each result is read. Exactly one leg is true at a time. With neither Prod_SODA nor Prod_JUICE on, the middle leg writes 2. Rung 4 is the gate for everything below it: Job_OK is on only when the camera’s job matches and no change is in progress. Because rung 3 is written before rung 4, the job is worked out and then tested in the same scan. Release, only on the right job Rung 5 is Level 8’s release timer with Job_OK in it. When the last SODA bottle leaves the hopper, the selector moves to WATER, Want_Job becomes 2, Job_OK drops and the timer stops: nothing more is released until the camera has job 2. The changeover Rung 7 counts the line-clear time from the moment the hopper is held. The last SODA bottle is somewhere between the hopper and the camera. At 80 px/s it needs about 4 s to reach the camera and pass it, and its result comes back 180 ms after that. Five seconds covers it. Rung 8 is the command: it fires once, because XIO(Cam1:O.Execute_Command) is in it and it latches Execute_Command. Rung 9 drops the command when the camera answers. On the next scan Current_Job_ID equals Want_Job and Execute_Command is off, so rung 4 sets Job_OK, rung 7 resets Clear_T and rung 5 starts releasing the WATER batch. Watch for: changing job too soon Take the 5 s out (Clear_T at 0) and the camera loads the WATER job while the last SODA bottle is still on its way. The last SODA bottles are inspected under WATER and rejected as the wrong product, −50 each for good bottles in Reject_Bin, and their trace records name the wrong batch. In the reference program with Clear_T at 0, six bottles go wrong and the score drops from 3200 to 2150. A bottle that reaches the camera during the half-second load is worse off still: its trigger is missed and it goes by with no image at all. User data and the trigger Rung 10 counts the bottle as it reaches the camera, so Bottle_No is its number on the line: 1 for the first SODA bottle, 24 for the last JUICE bottle. Rung 11 works out its position in the batch, ((Bottle_No-1) MOD 8)+1 , and copies both numbers into User_Data. Pos is a DINT, so COP with a length of 4 copies its four bytes into User_Data[0] to [3]. Bottle_No goes into [4] to [7]. Rung 12 triggers only after the camera has acknowledged the data, and rung 13 drops both requests when the trigger is acknowledged. The next bottle gets fresh data. The result and the trace Rung 14 is Level 8’s result rung with one more branch. While Trace_Idx is under 24, COP copies the 16 trace bytes into Trace[Trace_Idx] , then ADD moves the index on. The index addresses the array at run time, so one rung fills all 24 records in the order the results arrive, which is the order of the bottles. The LES stops it at the end of the array: Trace[24] does not exist, and writing to it would be a major fault. The reject pusher, the counts and the fault lamp These are Level 8’s, with one more fault on the lamp: Command_Failed . Ask for job 4, which this camera does not have, and the camera keeps job 1, raises Command_Failed instead of Command_Complete, and the line stays held. The lamp tells the operator why. Run it Load your program, Run mode, Start. Watch Product_Sel jump to WATER as the eighth SODA bottle leaves, the hopper hold, Camera_HMI’s JOB box change to Job 2: WATER (min fill 90 %) , and the WATER batch start. The third WATER bottle has a red label: the camera fails it with code 16, WRONG, and the pusher takes it. In a run on v2.02, 24 of 24 bottles in the right bin, nothing lost, in about 54 s against a par of 65 s: 3200 points and three stars, and all 24 trace records right. Try it: the wrong job In rung 3, swap the 1 and the 3. The camera now runs JUICE on the SODA batch and SODA on the JUICE batch, and bit 4 fails every bottle in both, because none of them is the product the job expects. The reject bin fills with good bottles: 19 of the 24 end up there, and the score falls to about 1150. That is the changeover mistake a plant fears most, and the reason a camera job carries the product it expects. Try it: trigger without the data Take XIC(Cam1:I.Set_User_Data_Ack) out of rung 12. Rungs 11 and 12 now go true in the same scan, so Set_User_Data and Trigger reach the camera in the same I/O update, and the camera takes the image before it has latched the data. Every record carries the previous bottle’s data: Trace[0] reads SODA,00,000000 and Trace[1] reads SODA,01,000001 . The trace score falls to 0 while every bottle still lands in the right bin. A trace can be wrong while the product is right, so check the records as well as the bins. Card mode on Level 9 Card mode works on Level 9 the same way it does on Level 8 (tick Card mode in the Camera’s properties): the hopper’s bottles wait at the camera and each takes the verdict of the card under the lens. What Level 9 adds is the product. A card is SN-48RK , R the product and K the defect, and the camera answers WRONG (bit 4) when the card’s product is not the loaded job’s. The bottle becomes what the card shows: under the SODA job a WATER card is a WATER bottle in the SODA batch, and it is rejected as a stray. So the cards are swapped at the changeover, as an operator would swap product: when the camera loads WATER, put a WATER card under the lens. To give the camera its stray, show it the old product’s card for a bottle or two after the change; the level’s stray check is met when one of those is rejected. The CARDS page opens on the loaded job’s product, marks it on its tab (JOB: at the top right) and lists what each card of the row should read under that job. With the camera live, the real job decides. The page reads the card from byte 10 (R × 10 + K) and the loaded job from Current_Job_ID , and counts a result right when the code matches the card’s defect plus WRONG for a card of another product. Your In-Sight job does the same: decode the DataMatrix for R and K, read the label with OCR, and set bit 4 when the text is not the job’s product. Try it: run level 9 on cards Tick Card mode with SN-4801 under the lens and run your Level 9 program. When Product_Sel turns to WATER and the camera loads job 2, leave SN-4801 there for two more bottles: both read WRONG and go to the reject bin. Then touch the WATER tab and SN-4811, and at the JUICE change SN-4831. The level completes, and the score card lists SN-4801 with its WRONG reads counted as right. ch42: In the app File → New Project… → A graded level → 10 . Guided mode opens on this chapter: the tags, every rung below under its fold, a Verify check, and the run results: the axis is homed, a bottle is picked up, a bottle is set down in a bin, then complete, every bottle right and under par. File → Load Reference Solution loads the program printed here. Level 10, Servo pick, running its reference program. The axis chapter in Part VI (chapter 55) taught the FHPP handshake on a panel. This level puts it to work. Twelve bottles, small, medium and large, come down a short infeed one at a time. The belt ends under a servo axis standing across it: a Size 120 toothed-belt axis with a 4.5 m stroke and a vacuum gripper on its carriage. Three bins sit under the axis at 1500, 3000 and 4500 mm, one per size. Pick each bottle off the end of the belt, carry it to its bin, set it down, come back. The drive’s own rules are the level’s traps: no move before the axis is homed, no second Start while a move is running, and a bottle set down anywhere but over a bin is on the floor. The machine How the level is scored What happens Points A bottle set down in its own bin +100 A bottle in the wrong bin −50 A bottle set down off the bins, or run off the end of the belt −50 Every drive fault at the end (a Start before Referenced, a record that is not set, a target past the stroke) −50 each Every double start at the end (a Start while a move was running: the drive ignores it and raises Warning) −25 each What happens Points All twelve bottles done under par (80 s) +200 The drive keeps the count: the axis properties show faults and double starts as you run, and the simulator log prints the Drive record line when the level completes. The gripper Grip is the vacuum. On its rising edge the gripper takes whatever bottle is under the carriage ( Part_Below says there is one) and Gripped comes on; the bottle rides with the carriage and no eye, belt or bin sees it on the way. Drop Grip and the bottle is set down where the carriage is: into the bin under it, or onto the floor. Grip with nothing under the carriage does nothing but a line in the log. There is no Z axis here: the pick and the set-down are the vacuum alone, which is how a short-stroke vacuum pick on a gantry often is. How to pass it, step by step 1. Power the drive with Run: Enable, Stop and Halt high, as in the axis chapter. 2. Home it before anything else, and only release bottles once Axis1:I.Referenced is on. 3. Run the belt until PE_Pick sees a bottle, then stop it, or the bottle runs off the end. 4. Latch the gantry beams as the bottle passes, as Level 1 did. 5. Grip when a bottle is at the pick point and the carriage is at rest at 0 mm. Pick the record from the 6. Over the bin, at rest: Grip off. Then record 1 and Start again, back to the pick point. 7. Drop Start when Start_Ack answers, every time. Tags this lesson needs The alias tags of the machine are made for you; create these before you type the rungs. Verify reports any you miss. Now Start is latched every scan the rung is true, and the drive sees a second Start the moment Motion_Complete comes back over the bin, before rung 10 has let go of the bottle. The log says Start while moving: ignored (a double start) , Warning comes on, and the drive record at the end costs 25 for each one. ch43: In the app File → New Project… → A graded level → 11 . Guided mode opens on this chapter: the tags, every rung below under its fold, a Verify check, and the run results: the marker carries its message, a bottle is marked, a bottle of the second lot carries L0102, then complete, every bottle right and under par. File → Load Reference Solution loads the program printed here. Level 11, Date code, running its reference program. Every bottle that leaves a plant carries a code: the lot it came from, so a complaint can be traced back to a tank and a day. Printing it is one machine’s job and reading it back is another’s, because a printer that has stopped printing does not know it has. Level 11 is Level 8’s line with a laser marker in front of the camera. The marker writes the lot code on each bottle as it passes; the camera, on a code-verify job, reads it back and tells you whether it is there and whether it is the right lot. Three lots of six bottles go through, and the lot changes while bottles are still on the belt. The traps are all in the handshakes: the marker’s message, the camera’s expectation, and keeping each bottle’s lot with the bottle. The marker The Date Coder part under Bottling is a CO2 laser marker by default (an inkjet is the other option; its I/O differs only in the service signal). It marks the bottle under its head when Print rises, and only while Laser_On arms it: that is the marker’s interlock, and a Mark with the laser disarmed does nothing but a line in the log. Its message is L , the four-digit lot, a dash and a running count: L0101-001 . The lot comes from Lot_No , but writing Lot_No changes nothing by itself: the message is loaded on the rising edge of Load_Msg , the load takes half a second with Ready off, and Msg_Ready comes on when the message carries the lot Lot_No holds. A mark is missed now and then (the bottle rocked), and after ten marks the protective window has fumed up: Window_Dirty comes on and every other mark comes out faint until the window is cleaned. The head’s own eye, Detect , says a bottle is under it. The camera’s code-verify job The camera runs Bottle code verify : cap, label and fill as before, and the code read back by OCR. Two result bits are new: 32 , wrong lot code: the camera read a code, but not the lot it was told to expect; 64 , no code: nothing readable, a missed mark, a faint one or a bottle that was never marked. The lot the camera should expect comes from the PLC in User_Data bytes 0-1, latched with Set_User_Data ahead of each trigger, the way Level 9 passed its batch data. Tell it nothing and it checks nothing: every code reads as right, and a bottle with the wrong lot ships. The string it read comes back in Inspection_Results bytes 12-27 ( NOREAD when there was nothing), and Camera_HMI shows it. How the level is scored What happens Points A bottle in Good_Bin that is good and carries its own lot code +100 What happens Points A defective bottle in Reject_Bin (cap, label, fill, no code, wrong lot code) +100 A bottle shipped with a defect, no code or the wrong lot code −100 A good bottle rejected −50 All eighteen bottles done under par (45 s) +200 The lot a bottle should carry is the lot the selector showed when it left the hopper. A bottle marked with the lot of the batch before or after it is wrong even if the camera, told the wrong thing, let it through. The Coder record line in the simulator log at the end counts marks, misses, faint marks, marks with no bottle and marks with the laser disarmed. Three handshakes and two FIFOs The selector tells you the lot of the next bottle out of the hopper. The bottle under the marker left the hopper 2.5 s ago, and the bottle under the camera a second before that: at a lot change there are bottles of the old lot on the belt when the selector already shows the new one. So the lot has to travel with the bottle, and the program does that the way Level 8 carried result codes: a FIFO from the hopper to the marker ( Lot_Q ), loaded with the selector’s lot at each release and unloaded as each bottle reaches the marker’s eye, and a second FIFO from the marker to the camera ( Cam_Q ). Then three handshakes: the marker’s message load, the camera’s user data, and the camera’s trigger and results, which are Level 8’s. One more thing the FIFO gives you: its head, Lot_Q[0] , is the lot of the next bottle to reach the marker. The program hands the marker that lot as soon as it changes, while the bottle is still on its way, so the half-second load is over before the bottle arrives. Load it on arrival instead and the bottle is past the head before Msg_Ready returns. Tags this lesson needs The alias tags of the machine are made for you; create these before you type the rungs.
