ch44: In the app File → New Project… → A graded level → 12 . Guided mode opens on this chapter: the tags, every rung below under its fold, a Verify check, and the run results. File → Load Reference Solution loads the program printed here. Level 12, Kitchen changeover, running its reference program. Level 7 made three batches of one family of recipes in one tank. A real kitchen changes product, and the change is where the trouble is. Level 12 is Level 7’s kitchen making two batches of Soda (water and cola syrup, 5:1) and then two of Juice (water and orange concentrate, 3:1). Between them comes the changeover, and three things about it are new. The tank’s outlet sits above the bottom, so the outlet pump leaves a heel , five per cent of the tank, that carries the last batch into the next one unless it is rinsed out. The syrup tote has to be swapped for the concentrate tote, by an operator, and only when the tank is down to its heel. And the recipe changes: not just the amounts, but how you dose them, because a heel in the tank means topping up to the HI probe no longer gives you the ratio. The machine How the level is scored What happens Points Each batch: the ratio within 5 % of the recipe +100 / −50 Each batch: the temperature at drain within −3 / +8 °F +100 / −50 Each batch: mixed at least the recipe time +100 / −50 A batch with more than 0.5 % of the other product in it −200 A short batch (under 80 % of the tank), an overflow, a scorched batch −50, −100, −100 Four batches out under par (270 s) +200 The recipes are the plant’s: Soda 83 % water at 100 °F, mixed 8 s; Juice 75 % water at 160 °F, mixed 10 s. Without a rinse the Juice carries about 1 % cola out of the heel, twice the limit. Why the heel changes the dosing Level 7 dosed A by counting its flowmeter and topped up with B to the HI probe: the ratio came out of the probe’s height. With 100 units of the last batch already in the tank, the probe is reached 100 units sooner, and whatever B is short, the ratio is off. So Level 12 doses both ingredients by their flowmeters, to counts the recipe rungs set, and the HI probe is left to the Full lamp. That is also the honest way: a recipe is amounts, not levels. ch45: In the app File → New Project… → A graded level → 13 . Guided mode opens on this chapter: the tags, every rung below under its fold, a Verify check, and the run results: the roller comes in and PadIn answers, a bottle leaves with a label, the roll runs out and a new one is loaded, then complete, every bottle right and under par. File → Load Reference Solution loads the program printed here. Level 13, Label it, running its reference program. On the bottle line (chapter 27) the labeler is one station among many, and its handshake is written in two rungs between the capper and the scrap gate. This level is the labeler alone, so you can see the whole of it: what the dispenser tells you, what it wants from you, and what goes wrong when the roll runs out. Twenty-four bottles come down a short belt, filled and capped but with no label, and about a fifth of them with no cap at all. Every capped bottle has to leave with a label; the uncapped ones get none and go to the reject bin. The roll holds sixteen labels, which is not enough: somewhere past bottle twenty the dispenser runs dry, and the program has to stop feeding bottles into it until the operator loads a new roll. The hopper is a timing-screw infeed with its own screen, the pusher a guided cylinder squared up with its eye (both in the Real models section of the simulator chapter). A level you saved in an older version keeps its scene in your browser; when a level’s layout changes between versions the app rebuilds the scene the next time you open it, keeping your program, your view and the guide’s progress, so the reference solution always does what the level says it does. The machine What the dispenser says and wants Signal Direction Meaning Ready in Web loaded, no fault, roller home. The only time an Apply is any use Apply out Drive the roller in. Hold it until PadIn; on a real FLS the stroke aborts if Apply drops early PadIn in The roller is at the end of its stroke: the label has been pressed on. Drop Apply now Labeled in The bottle under the roller carries a label Label_Present in A label is peeled and waiting at the dispensing edge Label_Low in Five labels or fewer on the roll Error in The roll is out, or the last cycle found no label. Stays on until a new roll is loaded (click the labeler) Two things are easy to miss. Labeled is about the bottle under the roller , not the one at the pusher two metres on, so a verdict has to be carried down the belt in a bit of your own. And an uncapped bottle is not an error: with Only label capped bottles on the dispenser cycles, finds no cap, logs a skip and leaves the bottle alone, so after PadIn the bottle still reads Labeled = 0, and that is how the program knows it has to go to the reject bin. How the level is scored What happens Points A labeled, capped bottle in Good_Bin +100 An uncapped bottle in Reject_Bin +100 A bottle in Good_Bin with no label or no cap −100 A labeled bottle in Reject_Bin −50 Every Apply with no bottle under the roller, at the end −25 each Every cycle on an empty roll, at the end −25 each Under par (75 s) +200 How to pass it, step by step 1. Release one bottle at a time, and none while Error is on: a bottle sent into a dry dispenser is a cycle 2. Stop the belt when PE_Label sees a bottle that has no label yet. Let it settle. 3. Wait for Ready , then latch Apply . Unlatch it on PadIn (or on Error ). 4. After PadIn, if the bottle still has no label, remember it: that one is for the pusher. 5. With the roller home, let the bottle go. Release the next one as soon as this one has left the eye: the trips 6. At PE_Reject, push the remembered bottle while the eye sees it; let the rest run on. 7. Amber on Label_Low , red on Error . Run and release Rung 2 is the one that keeps the level honest: XIO(Error) in the release. Leave it out and the hopper keeps feeding bottles into a dispenser that cannot label them; each one costs 25 at the end and goes to Good_Bin bare for another 100. Rung 3 runs the belt unless a bottle is being held. Hold, dwell and the Apply handshake Rung 4 latches Hold for a bottle at the eye with no label, and XIO(Done) keeps it from re-latching for the same bottle once the dispenser has had its turn. Rung 5 is a 0.3 s dwell so the bottle has stopped moving before the roller touches it. Rung 6 is the request: held, settled, Ready , and not already done: latch Apply . Rung 7 is the answer: PadIn unlatches it, and so does Error , which is what the dispenser does with a cycle that finds no label. Watch for: apply as an ote Write rung 6 with an OTE instead of a latch and the roller never gets there. The moment it leaves home Ready drops (the dispenser is cycling), the rung goes false, Apply drops, the roller comes back, Ready returns, and it starts again: a roller twitching at the bottle. A latch set on Ready and cleared on PadIn is the shape of every start/acknowledge handshake in this book, the servo axis’s Start included. The verdict, and letting the bottle go Rung 8 runs on PadIn: it marks the bottle Done , and if Labeled is still off it latches No_Label , the verdict that rides down to the pusher. Rung 9 releases the hold once the roller is home. Rung 10 clears Done and Busy when the bottle has left the eye, so the next release goes out while this bottle is still on its way to the pusher. Rung 11 counts labels. Try it: what the skip looks like Run the level and watch the Simulator Log for Labeler skipped an open bottle . Find that bottle in Monitor Tags: at PadIn, Labeled stays 0 and No_Label comes on; two seconds later Reject fires at the pusher and the log says → Reject_Bin (no cap, no label) 100 . Now set the labeler’s Only label capped bottles off and run again: the roller puts a label on the open bottle, the pusher lets it through, and Good_Bin charges 100 for a bottle shipped with no cap. The property is there because a real line rejects an open bottle before it wastes a label on it. The pusher and the lamps Rung 12 is Level 8’s pattern: on the eye’s rising edge, arm Fire from the verdict and forget the verdict; rung 13 pushes while the eye sees the bottle; rung 14 disarms when it is clear. The one-shot matters: without it rung 12 would clear No_Label in the same scan it read it, and the push would last one scan. Try it: run the roll out Run with the reference. Around bottle 19 LOW lights (five left). At the twentieth capped bottle the roller comes in and nothing goes on: Error comes on, Apply is unlatched by rung 7, the red lamp lights, and rung 2 stops the hopper. The bottle under the roller waits. Click the labeler: a new roll of 16 labels loaded , Error drops, Ready returns, rung 6 fires again and that bottle gets its label; the hopper carries on. Now take XIO(Error) out of rung 2 and watch what the hopper does while the roll is out. Run it Load the program, Run mode, Start. The first bottle stops at the eye, the roller comes in and back, the bottle runs on to Good_Bin and the next one is already on its way. The fourth or fifth is an open one: the roller comes in, nothing goes on, and the pusher takes it two metres later. ch46: In the app A level project opens with guided mode on this chapter: the panel lists the tags the program needs ( Make them ), shows every rung below under its fold, checks that MainRoutine verifies, and ticks these results while you run the level: A pail is filled to 24.0 kg net and leaves the fill A lid is seated (Lid_Seated) The magazine runs out (Lids_Out), it is reloaded and the line carries on The reader reads a label (Reader1:I.Result_Code bit 0) A bad pail is pushed into Reject_Bin Run mode, Start: the level completes (hopper empty, belt clear) Every bottle in the right bin, none lost Under par (200 s) Expert · par 200 s Level 14, Paint line, running its reference program. The job A paint line, start to finish, one pail per station. Empty 5-gallon pails come out of the hopper one at a time. THE FILL : stop each one under the lance (PE_Fill), let the scale settle, tare it, fill white latex paint by net weight to 24.0 kg on the tank's two valves (Weight is in tenths of a kg), hold the lance in until both valves are proved shut, and keep the tank topped up from the tote. THE LID : stop the pail under the lid press (PE_Lid) and run its sequence on its own switches — cup down with the vacuum on until Vac_OK, cup up, arm out to Arm_At_Pail, cup down, vacuum off, cup up, arm home, press down and hold, then, with the platen still down, close the four fingers on the lid's tabs (Clamp, until Clamp_Closed) and open them again (Clamp_Open) before the press goes up — then read Lid_Seated and Lid_Locked: a lid that went on cocked will not seat, and a seated lid whose tabs are not locked is a reject. Lifting with the fingers closed pulls the lid off; coming down with them closed bends the tabs. The magazine holds 8 lids: when Lids_Out comes on, flash the red lamp and wait; click the lid press to reload it. THE LABEL : Level 13's handshake on a pail (only a pail with its lid seated gets a label). THE CODE : the DataMan (Reader1, on EtherNet/IP) reads the code on the label as the pail passes PE_Code. The code is the paint's colour and the pail's number in it — WH0001, WH0002 … for white (RD for red, BL blue, YL yellow, GR green, BK black) — and this line runs white: the roll has a red label spliced in (RD…) and a smudged code, and both are rejects. Push off at PE_Reject anything that is not right; the good pails run off the end into Good_Bin. The program The program runs each station on its own flags, one pail per station. The fill: the release on Fill_Busy ; the stop on the eye, the tare after 0.6 s for the scale to settle, the net weight, the two-stage fill (fast, then the dribble valve to the target), and the lance held in until Valve_Closed proves both valves shut; then the hand-on to the lid conveyor once the press is free. The lid is a step register: 0 waiting, 10 pick, 20 lift, 30 carry, 40 place, 50 let go, 60 cup up, 70 arm home, 80 press and dwell, then the fingers closed on the tabs and opened again, and 90 the check. Every output comes from the step numbers, so each one is written in one place. The label is Level 13’s handshake, only for a pail with its lid seated. The code is the DataMan’s trigger and results handshakes, the string’s first two letters taken with MID and compared with WH . One reject flag per pail, which the lid, the label and the code can each set, fires the pusher at PE_Reject ; and the lamps. ch47: In the app A level project opens with guided mode on this chapter: the panel lists the tags the program needs ( Make them ), shows every rung below under its fold, checks that MainRoutine verifies, and ticks these results while you run the level: The marker carries the message (Coder_Msg_Ready) A bottle is marked (the marker's count moves) The camera inspects a bottle (Cam1:I.Inspection_ID counts up) A result is acknowledged (Cam1:O.Inspection_Results_Ack) A defective bottle is pushed into Reject_Bin Run mode, Start: the level completes (hopper empty, belt clear) Every bottle in the right bin, none lost Under par (55 s) Hard · par 55 s Level 15, Code and verify, running its reference program. The job Level 11’s line with one lot and a serial on every bottle. The PLC gives the laser marker each bottle’s serial before the bottle reaches it (Serial_No with Lot_No 151, then Load_Msg and wait for Msg_Ready): the marker marks L0151-001, L0151-002 … one serial per bottle, never twice. The camera’s code-verify job reads the mark back and sends the string it read in Inspection_Results bytes 12-27 (L at 12, the lot at 13-16, the serial at 18-20; NOREAD when it read nothing). Compare it with the serial you sent for that bottle (it rides in a FIFO from the marker to the camera): a mismatch is a reject, and Mismatch_Count counts every one (it is on the console). The marker misprints a digit now and then, misses a mark, and its window fumes up after so many marks (faint marks the camera cannot read: Lamp_Lens on Window_Dirty and the operator cleans it three seconds later). Three mismatches in a row are not three bad bottles: stop the line (Lamp_Fault) until START. +100 per right bin, −100 for a bottle shipped with a misprinted, missing or repeated code, −50 for a good bottle rejected. The program The marker needs each bottle’s serial before the bottle reaches it: the program moves the next serial into Serial_No with the lot, pulses Load_Msg and waits for Msg_Ready before it releases the bottle. The serial rides a FIFO from the marker to the camera. When the camera’s result comes in, the program turns the characters it read (bytes 12 to 27 of Inspection_Results ) back into numbers, each digit’s character code minus 48, and compares the serial with the one unloaded from the FIFO. A mismatch, a NOREAD or a defect bit marks the bottle for the reject pusher and counts in Mismatch_Count ; three in a row stop the line on Lamp_Fault until START, because three bad codes in a row are a marker problem, not three bad bottles. The job Level 8’s line with the reject station proved. The pusher’s air is weak now and then: it strokes and the bottle stays on the belt. Reject every bottle with a defect bit as before, then make sure it went: the reject bin has a photo-eye in its chute (Reject_Confirm), on for a moment as a bottle drops in. Give each push a reject-verify window (0.6 s, shorter than the time between bottles): confirmed, the bottle has left the belt; not confirmed, it is still on the belt. Track the bottles from the pusher to the end of the line (a FIFO: 0 good, 1 a reject that did not drop) and stop the line when a 1 reaches PE_End, before it can fall into the good bin. Light Lamp_Fault: the operator takes the bottle off three seconds later, and START carries on. Count the unconfirmed rejects in Reject_Fail. +100 per right bin, −100 for a defective bottle in the good bin, −50 for a good bottle rejected. The program The vision line’s trigger, results and reject are Level 8’s. Then each push is proved: a reject-verify window of 0.6 s on a timer from the push, shorter than the time between bottles so the order of the bottles is kept. Reject_Confirm , the eye in the bin’s chute, inside the window means the bottle has gone; no confirmation means it is still on the belt. Each bottle that passes the pusher is loaded into a pusher-to-end FIFO, 0 for a good bottle and 1 for a reject that did not drop, and unloaded at PE_End : a 1 there stops the line and lights Lamp_Fault before the bottle can fall into the good bin. Reject_Fail counts the unconfirmed ones; START carries on once the operator has taken the bottle off. ch49: In the app A level project opens with guided mode on this chapter: the panel lists the tags the program needs ( Make them ), shows every rung below under its fold, checks that MainRoutine verifies, and ticks these results while you run the level: Run mode, Start: the level completes (hopper empty, belt clear) Every bottle in the right bin, none lost Under par (220 s) Hard · par 220 s Level 17, Checkweigher, running its reference program. The job A gravity filler fills each bottle by time: the valve is open for Fill_Time, and what goes in is the flow times the time. The flow does not hold still. The product warms through the run and flows faster; then a fresh, cold tank comes on and it flows slower; and every fill scatters a little. A checkweigher after the filler weighs each bottle on the move and gives the program its net weight in grams (CW_Net), a strobe as each new weight comes in (CW_New) and its verdict (CW_Under, CW_OK, CW_Over). The target is 960 g; the band is 950 to 985 g. Push off every bottle out of the band. Then close the loop: average the last few weights and trim Fill_Time so the average comes back to the target, a little at a time, inside the trim's limits (1460 to 1780 ms, about ±10 % of the nominal 1620 ms); at a limit, light Lamp_Fault. The HMI shows the checkweigher, the weights against the band and your fill time on its trend. +100 per bottle in the band in the good bin, +40 per bottle out of the band caught in the reject bin (product made and thrown away), −100 for one out of the band shipped, −50 for one in the band rejected. The program The fill is by time: a TON whose preset is Fill_Time . Each new weight ( CW_New ) goes into a three-deep FIFO, and when the FIFO is full AVE averages it. Outside a ±2 g dead band round the 960 g target, the fill time is scaled by target over average, clamped to the trim’s limits (1460 to 1780 ms), and the averaging starts again on fresh weights, so one correction is judged before the next is made; at a limit Lamp_Fault lights. A bottle out of the band is marked for the pusher. The scoring rewards the trim: a bottle caught out of band is worth less than one filled right. ch50: In the app A level project opens with guided mode on this chapter: the panel lists the tags the program needs ( Make them ), shows every rung below under its fold, checks that MainRoutine verifies, and ticks these results while you run the level: Run mode, Start: the level completes (hopper empty, belt clear) Every bottle in the right bin, none lost Under par (145 s) Hard · par 145 s Level 18, Line balance, running its reference program. The job Three machines on one line: the unscrambler, the filler and the capper, with an accumulation table between each pair. The filler is the key machine: fixed at 60 bottles a minute, and the line is judged by it; it fills each bottle from Product_Tank and the capper caps it; Good_Bin takes filled and capped bottles. Every second it stands starved (nothing at its infeed) or blocked (its discharge backed up) is output the line never gets back; each time it stops costs 20 points. The unscrambler's supply runs thin now and then, and the capper's cap chute jams now and then. Each table has three eyes, Full, High and Low: a bottle standing in front of one for half a second says the table has backed up to it (a bottle flowing past only covers it for a moment). At Start the tables are empty: let the filler's table fill before the filler starts. Step the unscrambler's and the capper's speeds (Speed_Ref, bottles a minute, up to 90) so the filler stays fed and clear: faster either side of it, the V-curve. Hold a machine before it runs blocked: three seconds blocked and line pressure tips bottles over (a fault, −50, Reset to clear). The HMI shows the line: each machine's speed as a share of the filler's, its state, the tables, and the filler's efficiency. +100 a bottle into Good_Bin. The program Each table eye is debounced with a half-second timer, so it reads a table backed up to it and not a bottle flowing past. The unscrambler runs fast short of the low eye, at the V-curve speed between the eyes and at the filler’s speed past the high eye, and is held when its table is full until it drains below the high eye. The filler is held when the capper’s table backs up to it. The capper runs fast past its high eye, at the V-curve speed between the eyes and at the filler’s speed short of the low eye. Start resets the machines’ faults. Tags this lesson needs The alias tags of the machine are made for you; create these before you type the rungs. Verify reports any you miss. The job One unit, a filler fed by an unscrambler, run by the PackML state model: seventeen states, nine commands. The program is the transitions. StateCurrent holds the state; CntrlCmd brings one command at a time (1 Reset, 2 Start, 3 Stop, 4 Hold, 5 Unhold, 6 Suspend, 7 Unsuspend, 8 Abort, 9 Clear), from the console's buttons, from the HMI's, or from the program itself. A command moves the unit only from a state it is valid in: Reset from Stopped or Complete, Start from Idle, Hold from Execute, and so on; Stop from almost anywhere, Abort from anywhere. The acting states (Resetting, Starting, Holding, Stopping, Aborting, Clearing and the rest) do their work and go on by themselves when it is done. The filler makes bottles only in Execute. Power-up is Stopped: press Reset, then Start. During the batch the unscrambler's supply runs out for a while (a unit waiting on its supply suspends itself), the operator holds the unit from the HMI and lets it go again, and someone hits the E-stop: Abort, then Reset to clear, Reset and Start. The batch is 48 bottles, and it is over when the unit reaches Complete. Each transition outside the state model costs 50, a bottle made outside Execute 20, an E-stop that does not abort the unit within half a second 100, a Hold that does not hold 50, four seconds starved in Execute 50. +100 a bottle into Good_Bin. The program The console’s buttons and the E-stop are turned into commands first, the E-stop last so nothing overrides its Abort (Reset is a Clear while Aborted). The unit suspends and unsuspends itself from the infeed eye. A state-complete timer for each acting state comes ahead of the transitions; then one rung for each transition of the state model, each moving StateCurrent only from a state the command is valid in; then the outputs and the lamps from the state; and the command is cleared at the end of the scan. Tags this lesson needs The alias tags of the machine are made for you; create these before you type the rungs. Verify reports any you miss. ch52: In the app A level project opens with guided mode on this chapter: the panel lists the tags the program needs ( Make them ), shows every rung below under its fold, checks that MainRoutine verifies, and ticks these results while you run the level: A socket is connected to Cam1 at 192.168.1.18:3000 Cam1 gets a TRIG while Inspect_Req is on The answer is read back (ReadSocket brings it into Read_Resp) All 8 requests answered Medium · par 18 s Level 20, Socket to the camera, running its reference program. The job No machine this time: the controller talks to Cam1, an In-Sight camera at 192.168.1.18, over a TCP socket of its own. The camera listens on port 3000: send it TRIG and it inspects and answers PASS,98 or FAIL,62 (the verdict, a comma, the score; no line ending). The line raises Inspect_Req 8 times; for each one, write TRIG and read the answer back. The socket is the controller's socket object, reached with MSG instructions: CIP Generic, class 342, path THIS. Socket Create (service 4B, instance 0) makes a socket and returns its instance: MOV it into the .Instance of the other messages. OpenConnection (4C) connects to the address in a STRING, 192.168.1.18?port=3000; WriteSocket (4E) sends BufLen bytes of Buf; ReadSocket (4D) waits up to its Timeout for the answer. Each request and reply is a data type laid out the way the socket object reads it: make SocketCreate, OpenConnection, WriteSocket, ReadRequest and ReadResponse first (with SockAddr inside two of them), and give the requests their starting values in Monitor Tags. +100 for each request answered; −50 for a TRIG with no request on, or a second one for the same request; −50 for a request with no answer read back within 8 s. The program The program is a step sequence in one DINT, Step : delete any sockets left open, create a socket and move its instance into the other messages, connect, then for each request write TRIG and read the answer, and wait for the request to drop. A message that fails waits two seconds and starts over. Tags this lesson needs The alias tags of the machine are made for you; create these before you type the rungs. Verify reports any you miss. The level sets it and clears it Trig_Cmd STRING base tag The command Cam1 inspects on Write_Req WriteSocket base tag WriteSocket's request: Timeout 5000 ms, BufLen and Buf from Trig_Cmd Retry_T TIMER base tag Two seconds before trying again after an error The rungs Watch for A socket left open from the last run blocks the next connect. ch54: In the app A level project opens with guided mode on this chapter: the panel lists the tags the program needs ( Make them ), shows every rung below under its fold, checks that MainRoutine verifies, and ticks these results while you run the level: Run mode, Start: the level completes (hopper empty, belt clear) Every bottle in the right bin, none lost Under par (230 s) Hard · par 230 s Level 22, Bulk fill, running its reference program. The job The bulk filling line on its own, before Level 14 puts a lid press, a labeler and a code check after it: the silo of white paint, its two-stage outlet and fill lance, and the weighing conveyor under it, the infeed, the scale and the outfeed all on one VFD. Containers come down the feed in batches: 4 pails, 3 bag-in-boxes, 3 jugs, then 2 drums. Between batches the operator holds the feed until the line is clear and turns the FORMAT thumbwheel: 1 pail, 2 drum, 3 bag-in-box, 4 jug. Register each container on the encoder from Reg_PE (creep the last few pulses), stop it centred under the lance, tare it once it settles, put the lance in, fill fast then dribble, and lift the lance only once both valves are proved shut. Off centre the lance misses the opening and the paint goes over the side. Net targets, in tenths of a kg as the scale reads: pail and bag-in-box 240 (± 3), jug 48 (± 1), drum 2600 (± 20). Keep the silo topped up from Bulk_Supply. +100 for each container into Filled_Out at its weight, −100 for one shipped off weight or empty, −50 for each spill. The program The program is the classic silo’s, its routines one after another in MainRoutine: the first scan, the recipe from the thumbwheel, Start and Stop, the registration on the encoder with the creep, the tare and the two-stage fill with the lance held in until the valves are proved shut, the refill band, the count and the alarms. ch55: File → Share Link…: the project packed into the address itself. Three things outlive a run: the project file, a link that carries the project to someone else, and the recording of the last two minutes of the machine. This chapter is about all three, and about using the recording to debug. Being able to wind a machine back and watch the scan where it went wrong is something no real line gives you. The project file File → Save (Ctrl+S) writes one .json file holding everything: the scene and every device’s settings, the tags, the routines, the I/O configuration and, if you tick it, the network settings. File → Open reads it back. The page also keeps your work by itself between visits, so the file is for versions and for moving a project to another PC. A share link File → Share Link… packs the same project into the address itself. The JSON is deflated and written after #lc= , so nothing is uploaded anywhere: whoever has the link has the project. Opening a link asks first, with a summary of what is in it, because it replaces the project you have open. The project you have open is put aside first (a level keeps its program, the sandbox project comes back as My sandbox project), and your other levels are kept. In the desktop app, File → Open Link… takes a pasted link, or the whole message it came in. Watch For Some mail and chat apps cut very long links short. A link cut short is refused with a clear message rather than opening half a project. For a big scene (over about 60 KB of link, which the dialog warns about) send the file instead. The scene recorder While a sandbox scene runs, the recorder keeps a frame every 0.25 s of machine time for the last two minutes (one minute on a phone). A frame holds every part on the floor, every device’s state (a timer half run, a cylinder half out, a tank’s level and temperature, a case on the packer’s lane), the simulator’s counters and log, the machine faults you injected, the random generator that picks the part mix, and every tag in the controller. The bar under the simulator toolbar shows the span recorded, REC 0:00.05 – 0:40.38 . Drag the slider back, or press ◀, and the scene goes into REPLAY : Because the random generator is rewound with everything else, running on from a frame with the same program gives the same run, bottle for bottle. Change a rung and run on from the same frame, and the only difference between the two runs is your change. That is the most useful thing the recorder does. Try it: catch a jam and read the scan Run the bottle line. After a few bottles, use Tools → Inject Machine Fault… → Jam . The jammed bottle stops, LS11 does not see it where the registers say it should be, Alarm_Word bit 2 sets and the line stops. Switch to Program mode, open S11_Alarms and drag the slider back a second at a time to the frame where EOL_Missing first goes true. The rung above it shows why: LS11 dark while the Exist and Large bits said a bottle was due. Now drag back to before you injected the jam and press Run from here . The jam is gone, because the fault was injected after that moment and the recorder rewinds faults with the rest. The line runs as if it had never happened. Try it: prove a change on the same run On Level 6, run until the first case creeps onto the mark under the packer head, then scrub back to the frame where Case_Slow makes. Note where the case stops: on the mark. Change the creep rung from MOV(15,Case_Hz) to MOV(30,Case_Hz) , accept the edit and press Run from here . The same case, on the same frame, now runs past the head before Case_In_Place can stop it, because at 30 Hz the drive’s 0.5 s decel ramp carries it beyond the ±6 px window. With no case under the head nothing is packed, and the case goes out empty for −25. Put 15 back, scrub to the same frame, run from here again, and it lands. Two runs that differ only in one number. What is and is not rewound Rewound: the parts, the devices, the controller’s tags (timers, counters, ONS bits, arrays, UDTs), its periodic task schedule, the machine faults and the random part mix. Not rewound: your program and the scene layout (they are what you are testing), the trend charts, and anything outside the page: a real device on the bridge, or an EtherNet/IP module. Reset Sim, New Order or opening another project starts a new recording.
ch56: The servo axis sandbox: the axis with its gripper, the panel and the drive’s status lamps. Everything so far moved on a contactor or a VFD: a belt runs or it does not, faster or slower. A servo axis is the other kind of motion. The PLC names a position and the drive puts the carriage there, to a hundredth of a millimetre, and tells you when it has arrived. the palette has a Drives & Axes category (the VFD of the case packer chapter moved there too) with a Linear Axis part. Three things make a servo axis, and it pays to keep them apart: the axis is the mechanics, a toothed-belt or spindle profile with a carriage; the servo motor is bolted to its end; the drive is the servo controller, a box in the cabinet. The part on the floor is the axis with its motor. The drive is the module in I/O Configuration, and the PLC talks to it over EtherNet/IP with Festo’s FHPP profile, the Festo Handling and Positioning Profile. This chapter builds the small panel that drives it and walks the handshake rung by rung. Level 10 (chapter 42) puts the axis to work. What FHPP is A Festo drive on EtherNet/IP exchanges eight bytes each way on the implicit connection, and FHPP says what the bytes mean. The PLC writes two control bytes , CCON and CPOS, a record number, a velocity and a position; the drive answers with two status bytes , SCON and SPOS, the record it ran, a fourth byte (the actual velocity in Direct mode, the record status byte in Record Select) and its actual position, in hundredths of a millimetre unless the drive is scaled otherwise. A real CMMT is scaled in Festo Automation Suite; the axis module’s Position unit on the bus (0.1, 0.01 or 0.001 mm, in the axis’s properties) is set to match it. Logix Connect gives every bit a name under the module, so the rungs read Axis1:O.Enable and Axis1:I.Motion_Complete rather than Axis1:O.Data[0].0 ; the bit map underneath is the profile’s. The part has no wired signals at all; it moves on the module’s tags, which is exactly how the real one works. Its properties are the axis you ordered: Axis size (Festo builds them in profile sizes, 45 to 185 mm wide, toothed belt or ball-screw spindle; the size sets the drawn width, the stroke range and the drive’s velocity and acceleration ceiling, and a setting past the ceiling is held at it), Stroke in millimetres, the maximum velocity that 100 % in a record means, the acceleration , the homing and jog speeds, and the records : a position and a velocity percentage each, 200@50, 1000@80, 1800@100 here. Read them in order: power, fault handling, homing, the record, the start, the handshake. Reading the drive: the control and status bits, and what a healthy one looks like Two things about FHPP trip up everybody the first time, and they are the same thing seen from both ends. On the way out, the bits named Stop and Halt are permissions , not commands: a 1 means allowed , a 0 means stop or hold . On the way back, the drive answers every permission with an acknowledge bit that mirrors it, so a healthy, idle drive shows a row of 1s where you might expect 0s. Learn the idle picture once and every fault afterwards is a bit that is not where it should be. The Power rung XIC(Run) [OTE(Axis1:O.Enable),OTE(Axis1:O.Stop),OTE(Axis1:O.Halt),OTE(Lamp_Run)]; HOW THIS RUNG WORKS In words. When Run is on, the rung turns Axis1:O.Enable on (and off again whenever the rung is false), turns Axis1:O.Stop on (and off again whenever the rung is false), turns Axis1:O.Halt on (and off again whenever the rung is false) and turns Lamp_Run on (and off again whenever the rung is false). Left to right: 1. XIC(Run) Examine If Closed asks: true when Run is on. 2. A branch of 4 parallel paths: each path is tested on its own and does its own work. Path 1 1. OTE(Axis1:O.Enable) Output Energize does: turns Axis1:O.Enable on (and off again whenever the rung is false). Path 2 1. OTE(Axis1:O.Stop) Output Energize does: turns Axis1:O.Stop on (and off again whenever the rung is false). Path 3 1. When Run is true all three drive bits go to 1 and the drive reads them as: Output FHPP bit 1 means 0 means Axis1:O.Enable CCON.0 ENABLE Power stage on: the motor is under closed-loop control and holds position Disabled: no torque, no commands taken; a running move coasts to a controlled stop and the task is dropped Axis1:O.Stop CCON.1 STOP Operation enabled , despite the name. The drive’s "OK to run" Controlled stop on the stop ramp; the task is cancelled; no Start is taken until the bit is 1 again Axis1:O.Halt CPOS.0 HALT Not halted : a move runs The move pauses on its ramp but the task is kept ; raise Halt and a Start resumes to the same target. The sandbox panel’s Hold button works this bit The drive sequences them itself, Enable → Stop → Halt, so writing all three in one rung is normal; when the last one is in it answers with Op_Enabled , and that is the bit the Home and Start rungs wait on. Stop throws a move away; Halt parks it. That is the whole difference, and it decides what you tie each bit to. Tying all three to Run, as above, means a Stop button or an E-stop cancels the move and takes the torque off: fine for a pick-and-place. On a machine that should hold position on a stop, keep Enable on and drop only Stop; the axis stands still under torque and the next Start begins a fresh move. A healthy drive, idle and homed This is the axis in the sandbox scene after Axis_On and a Home, standing at 0 with nothing to do. Every bit in both tables is in the state it should be; the two rows of 1s on the status side are the acknowledges. Input FHPP bit Healthy What it tells you Enabled SCON.0 ENABLED 1 The power stage is on: your Enable was accepted Op_Enabled SCON.1 OPEN 1 All three permissions are in; the drive will take Home, Start, Jog. Everything downstream waits on this Warning SCON.2 WARN 0 A command was ignored (a Start while moving, a Start with Halt low). Not a fault: the drive carries on, and Reset clears it Fault SCON.3 FAULT 0 Faulted: Op_Enabled drops, the axis stops, nothing runs until the rising edge of Reset Input FHPP bit Healthy idle What it tells you Load_Voltage SCON.4 VLOAD 1 The motor supply is present. Separate from the 24 V logic supply: on a real panel this is the bit that goes to 0 when the safety contactor drops the motor power while the drive stays awake FCT_Control SCON.5 FCT/MMI 0 The PLC has control. When a technician takes device control from the Festo Configuration Tool this goes to 1 and your Starts are ignored; Lock (CCON.5) refuses it OPM1_Ack , OPM2_Ack SCON.6, SCON.7 0, 0 The operating mode the drive is actually in: 0 0 is Record Select, 1 0 is Direct mode. Drops the instant a move or a homing starts, returns when the target is reached. Gate your in-position logic on it Teach_Ack SPOS.3 TEACH 0 1 after a Teach stored the position Moving SPOS.4 MOV 0 The axis is in motion; use it to keep a second Start out Drag_Error SPOS.5 DEV 0 Following error: the axis is not where the drive commanded, a mechanical problem or an overload Standstill SPOS.6 STILL 1 At rest with operation enabled; off while moving Referenced SPOS.7 REF 1 Homed. 0 after power-up (and after a homing starts) until the reference run completes; a Start with this 0 is the positioning- before-homing fault Record_No , Actual_Vel , Actual_Pos bytes 3, 4, 5- 8 last record, 0, position The record that ran; byte 4 is the speed in percent in Direct mode and the record status byte in Record Select (0 here: no record chaining); the position in the module’s unit, 0.01 mm unless set otherwise: 150000 is 1500 mm The LEDs on the motor The drive’s status is also on the machine, where a technician sees it without a laptop: four LEDs on the motor end of the axis. They are the four status bits that matter most, and the healthy idle picture is three lit and one dark. Dark with Axis_On on: look at the Power rung’s conditions, or ERR is lit REF blue Referenced (SPOS.7) The axis is homed; positioning is allowed. The log names the fault Read them as a pattern. EN REF MC : healthy and idle, ready for a Start. EN alone: powered but not homed, the state right after power-up. EN REF with MC dark: moving. REF MC with EN dark: Axis_On is off, or Stop or Halt has dropped: the drive remembers it is homed, it just will not move. ERR : Reset, then see which of the others comes back. Nothing lit: no power to the drive, or the module is not connected (Axis1 red in I/O Configuration). What does the rung do? Work it out from the rung before you read on. The answer is at the end of this chapter. HOW THIS RUNG WORKS In words. When Run is on, Axis1:I.Op_Enabled is on, Axis1:I.Referenced is off, Axis1:I.Moving is off and Axis1:I.Fault is off, the rung turns Axis1:O.Home on (and off again whenever the rung is false). Left to right: 1. XIC(Run) Examine If Closed asks: true when Run is on. 2. XIC(Axis1:I.Op_Enabled) Examine If Closed asks: true when Axis1:I.Op_Enabled is on. 3. XIO(Axis1:I.Referenced) Examine If Open asks: true when Axis1:I.Referenced is off. 4. XIO(Axis1:I.Moving) Examine If Open asks: true when Axis1:I.Moving is off. 5. XIO(Axis1:I.Fault) Examine If Open asks: true when Axis1:I.Fault is off. 6. OTE(Axis1:O.Home) Output Energize does: turns Axis1:O.Home on (and off again whenever the rung is false). The lesson programs home from a button so the fault can be shown on purpose; a cell that runs on its own homes itself like this. The instant the drive is in operation and the axis is not referenced, Home goes true; the drive takes the rising edge and runs its reference move; Referenced comes on and the XIO opens. Two details that make it right: XIO(Moving) opens as soon as homing starts, so Home is a short pulse rather than held for the whole run, which is fine because HOM is edge-triggered and dropping it does not abort the homing; and XIO(Fault) means a faulted drive is never asked to home, but since Referenced is still 0 it homes again by itself the moment Reset clears the fault. Where the homing goes is not in the program at all: the method, to a reference switch, to the end stop with a current limit, or switch then index, is configured in the drive. With an absolute multiturn encoder there is no homing run and Referenced is 1 from power-up. Field notes: the first program, and what went wrong This section is the log of one afternoon spent writing the Level 10 program and the guided track from scratch, kept because every item in it is a mistake the next person will make too. Each is a symptom, the cause, and the fix. Going through a program this way, one failure at a time, is what makes it bulletproof: a rung you have watched fail is a rung you understand. Every Go faults, and the fault lamp is on Where to read it: the axis itself says FAULT: not referenced, Home first under the carriage, and the Simulator Log tab (bottom of the window; on the phone, Output → Simulator Log) has the full line: Axis1: fault: positioning before homing (axis not referenced): pulse Home first . The simulated drive raises exactly three faults: a Start before the axis is referenced; a Start for a record that is not set ( record 3 is not set (records 1 to 2) ); a target past the stroke. Everything else the drive refuses is a warning , not a fault: a Start while moving (a double start), a Start with Halt low. A warning sets the Warning bit and a log line, the axis carries on, Reset clears it. A fault drops Op_Enabled and stops the axis until Reset. The cause, that afternoon: the Home rung had been typed with the controller in Run. It was a pending online edit, verified and visible and not running. See the Watch-for above; the card now says so, and Program → Run (a download) or the card’s Assemble button makes it the program. The carriage is stranded over a bin Clear Parts removed the bottle the gripper was holding; the set-down rung, which is what sent the carriage back to the pick point, never fired because there was nothing to set down. Any program whose return move is triggered by an event has this hole; a fault reset mid-cycle or a dropped bottle opens it too. Make the return depend on the state : empty-handed, standing still, not at the pick point → go home. OTL(Axis1:O.Start) Output Latch does: latches Axis1:O.Start on. Why it is built this way: One-shot : once per event, not once per scan. A latch : it stays on until an OTU clears it. Two questions this rung raised, worth answering here. What unlatches Record_No? Nothing, and nothing needs to: it is not a bit, it is a number the drive samples once , on the rising edge of Start. The value left in it afterwards means nothing until the next Start, and the next Start’s own MOV writes what that move wants. The latch in this rung is Start , and the Start_Ack / Fault rung drops it. Does the ONS fire only once, ever? Once per rising edge of the rung condition . The conditions go true when the carriage is stranded, one pulse, the move starts, Moving makes the rung false, the ONS re-arms; at the pick point GRT is false and nothing fires; the next time something strands the carriage the rung rises again and it fires again. Without the ONS the rung would stay true for the several scans before the drive reports Moving, re-latch Start each scan after Start_Ack dropped it, and the drive would log a double start. By hand, meanwhile: Toggle on Axis1:O.Jog_Neg (Tags tab, pick the tag, Toggle on the toolbar) jogs the carriage back at the jog speed and stops it at the stroke end; toggle it off there. Jog works for this because no rung writes it. Toggling Home does not: the auto-home rung is an OTE that writes Home false every scan, so the drive never sees the edge. A tag a rung writes is the rung’s, not yours. The in-position rung is true everywhere A LIM with its High Limit still 0: Low 149500, High 0. With High below Low, LIM tests outside the band, so the rung was true at every position except 0 to 1495 mm, nearly the opposite of the window wanted. Fill both limits before you trust a LIM, and read the rung’s power flow against the position display once: it should be true in exactly one place. The record rung asks for a different box every time A three-position selector gives the controller two inputs, Left and Right; the middle position is both of them off, which is why the middle branch is two XIOs. The RECORD rung is one rung with three branches, one per position, each a MOV into Record_No; built one branch at a time it is one of three, and the guide’s card used to name only the first missing box, so it seemed to want something different each time a branch changed. It now lists everything missing with a count. The handshake rung that stuck Covered under the guided track: a Start the drive refuses gets a fault, not a Start_Ack, so an unlatch rung that waits only for Start_Ack leaves Start high, and the first Go after Reset is no edge. The fault branch in [XIC(Axis1:I.Start_Ack),XIC(Axis1:I.Fault)]OTU(Axis1:O.Start) is the fix, and a latch needs a way out for every way in. Strict or inclusive LES(Axis1:I.Actual_Pos,200) against the reference’s LEQ : on a measured word the two differ by one count of one hundredth of a millimetre, and the guide accepts either. On a counter or a step word it does not, because GRT(Pick_Count,16) and GEQ(Pick_Count,16) are different programs, and that difference is exactly the kind of bug a compare hides. Watch for: the bit that is not where it should be Keep the healthy table in your head and read the status bytes against it. Op_Enabled 0 with Enabled 1: Stop or Halt is low, look at your Power rung’s conditions. Load_Voltage 0: the motor supply is off, the safety circuit or a contactor, not the program. FCT_Control 1: somebody has the configuration tool connected. Referenced 0 with Motion_Complete 1: not homed; the next Start will fault. Warning 1: a Start was ignored, usually a double start, look for a missing Moving or Motion_Complete contact. Fault 1: open the axis in the Device Monitor, the log names the fault, Reset clears it on the rising edge and nothing else does. Direct mode, jog and teach Records are the production way: the positions live in the drive and the PLC picks a number. FHPP also has Direct mode : set Axis1:O.OPM1 to 1, write the target into Setpoint_Pos (0.01 mm) and the speed into Setpoint_Vel (percent), and Start runs to it; Record_No then carries the control byte, where bit 0 makes the target relative to where the axis is. Jog_Pos and Jog_Neg move while held, at the jog speed, and stop at the ends of the stroke. Teach writes the actual position into the selected record, Teach_Ack answers, and the record list in the part’s properties changes: that is how positions are set up on a real machine, by jogging to the spot and teaching it. Try it: jog and teach Add two push buttons, Jog_P and Jog_N , and a Teach_PB ; add rungs XIC(Jog_P_Pressed)OTE(Axis1:O.Jog_Pos); , XIC(Jog_N_Pressed)OTE(Axis1:O.Jog_Neg); and XIC(Teach_PB_Pressed)OTE(Axis1:O.Teach); . Jog to 1500 mm with the selector in the middle, press Teach, and look at the axis properties: record 2 now reads 1500@80. Go runs there from now on. Guided: servo axis Watch For Each lesson checks its own routine. A rung that does the lesson’s job but was typed into the lesson before (the fault lamp rung in A2_Move, say, when the lesson is A3_Reset) is still found: the card says where it is and offers Move it. Take the move: a rung left in both places puts two coils on one tag. the handshake above is also a guided track, the run-up to Level 10: Guided → New Guided Project: Servo Axis . The scene is a small pick cell, the axis with its gripper standing over the end of a short belt, a hopper, the pick eye, a bin at 1500 mm, and a panel with the power selector, Hold, Home, Go, Reset, a record selector, Grip, the fault lamp, two in-position lamps and the position display. The guide panel takes it one routine at a time and checks each lesson while you run it, the way the bottle-line track does: the rungs you write are verified against the reference by their logic, and proven the first time they go true in Run. A Start the drive refuses, because the axis is not referenced, gets no acknowledge; it gets a fault. Start then sat high, and after Reset and Home the first Go was no rising edge: the drive saw Start already on and did nothing, and the cell looked dead until somebody pressed Go a second time. The fault branch in the unlatch rung is the fix, and it is in the sandbox program and Level 10’s reference as well now. A latch needs a way out for every way in. Two things the sim does when you add rungs from the guide: it restarts the machine, so the drive comes up clean and unreferenced (Home again), and it puts the selector back. Both are what a download does to a real cell. Watch for: a rung typed while online If you type a lesson’s rung with the controller in Run, it is an online edit : a pending (i) rung that is in the controller but not running until it is accepted and assembled, exactly as in Logix Designer. The card will tell you (’1 online edit in A4_Home not running yet’) and its button assembles it; or go to Program and back to Run, which is a download. The symptom, if you miss it, is a rung that verifies and does nothing: a Home that never fires, and every Go faulting with positioning before homing. Rungs the guide adds for you go straight in. The vacuum cup at work the gripper shows what its vacuum is doing. With Grip on, the vacuum builds in about a fifth of a second: the cup’s bellows squash and the ring turns blue; while there is nothing under it, suction rings run inward, which on a real cell is the hiss of a cup pulling air. A held part shows the cup’s seal on its top. When Grip drops the cup gives a short blow-off puff and the part is set down. With the vacuum fault injected the cup stays grey however long Grip is on: that is the picture of Grip 1, Gripped 0 . Machine faults on the servo axis Tools → Inject Machine Fault… lists the faults that belong to the parts on this floor. Each has a fault card: the symptom, what to watch in the I/O to confirm it, the repair, and what a program should do about it. Repair on an active fault removes its cause the way a technician would; whether the machine runs again is up to the program. The axis also carries the belts’ and the eyes’ faults when the cell has them. Fault Watch Repair The program should Servo axis: load voltage lost The safety contactor in front of the drive opens: the logic supply stays, the power stage loses its load voltage. A move in progress faults. Load_Voltage 0, Op_Enabled 0, with Enable 1. Close the safety contactor (Repair). Op_Enabled lost while Axis_On is on stops the cycle and lights the fault lamp; after Repair, Reset and Home again. Servo axis: following error The mechanics are blocked: every move faults a moment after it starts. Fault 1 a moment into every move; the log says following error. Free the mechanics (Repair), then Reset. Fault stops the cycle and lights the fault lamp; Reset pulses the drive’s Reset; the axis is homed again before the next pick. Servo axis: vacuum lost No vacuum at the cup: Grip does nothing and a held part drops. Grip 1, Part_Below 1, Gripped 0. Clear the vacuum line (Repair). Grip on and no Gripped within half a second: release, retry once, then alarm. XIC(Home_PB_Pressed)XIC(Axis1:I.Op_Enabled)XIO(Axis1:I.Moving)OTE(Axis1:O.Home); HOME: Home (CPOS.B2) starts the reference run, the only move the drive allows before the axis is referenced. The axis runs to the home switch at the homing speed, sets position 0 and raises Referenced (SPOS.B7) and Motion_Complete. [XIC(Rec_Sel_Left)MOV(1,Axis1:O.Record_No),XIO(Rec_Sel_Left)XIO(Rec_Sel_Right)MOV(2,Axis1:O.Record_No),XIC(Rec_Sel_Right)MOV(3,Axis1:O.Record_No)]; RECORD: the selector picks the record to run, 1, 2 or 3 (200 mm at 50 %, 1000 mm at 80 %, 1800 mm at 100 % of the maximum velocity). The record is read when Start rises. XIC(Go_PB_Pressed)XIC(Axis1:I.Referenced)XIO(Axis1:I.Moving)ONS(Go_ONS)OTL(Axis1:O.Start); START: on Go, if the axis is referenced and not moving, latch Start (CPOS.B1), through a one-shot on Go_ONS just before the latch, so holding Go gives one Start. The Moving check is what keeps a double start out: a Start while a move runs is ignored by the drive with Warning. Motion_Complete drops at once and returns when the axis is in position. [XIC(Axis1:I.Start_Ack),XIC(Axis1:I.Fault)]OTU(Axis1:O.Start); The handshake: the drive answers a Start with Start_Ack (SPOS.B1); drop Start then, so the next Go is a new rising edge. A refused Start (a fault) drops it too, so the first Go after Reset is a fresh edge.
ch57: The elevator running its reference program: the shaft, the cab and the hall calls. Every PLC simulator worth the name has an elevator, because an elevator is the smallest machine that has all the hard parts of a big one: requests that arrive while you are busy, a direction to choose and stick to, a door that must never be open while you move, people who stand in it, and a safety chain that has the final say over the program. The classic student exercise for it, the four-floor elevator with a shaft encoder and a main routine that is nothing but an index of subroutine calls, is the shape this chapter follows. Logix Connect has the machine for it, under File → New Project → Classic: elevator : a four-floor panoramic lift with hall calls, cab buttons, a shaft encoder, a door with its end switches and photo eye, and passengers who press the buttons by themselves. The scene comes with its tags made and an empty routine: this is one to write yourself. The program below is the reference ( File → Load Reference Solution: Elevator ), built in the order the exercise asks for it. The machine The Elevator part is under a new palette category, Classic scenes . Its properties are the building: the number of floors (two to six), the travel time floor to floor, the door travel time, whether passengers call by themselves and how often, and whether the safety switches (eye and overload) are wired. Its I/O is what an elevator controller sees: Signal Meaning Call_1 input Hall call button on floor 1 (1 while pressed) Call_2 input Hall call button on floor 2 (1 while pressed) Call_3 input Hall call button on floor 3 (1 while pressed) Call_4 input Hall call button on floor 4 (1 while pressed) Cab_1 input Cab button for floor 1 (1 while pressed) Cab_2 input Cab button for floor 2 (1 while pressed) Cab_3 input Cab button for floor 3 (1 while pressed) Cab_4 input Cab button for floor 4 (1 while pressed) At_1 input Floor switch: the cab is level with floor 1 At_2 input Floor switch: the cab is level with floor 2 At_3 input Floor switch: the cab is level with floor 3 At_4 input Floor switch: the cab is level with floor 4 Encoder analog in Shaft encoder on the hoist: the cab position in counts, 1000 per floor (floor 1 = 1000, floor 2 = 2000 …) Door_Open input Door fully open (end switch) Door_Closed input Door fully closed (end switch) Door_Eye input Door photo eye: blocked while someone is in the doorway Overload input Cab overload switch (too many passengers) Up output Hoist motor up Down output Hoist motor down (never with Up: the contactors are interlocked) Open output Door motor: open Close output Door motor: close Lamp_1 output Built-in lamp of the floor 1 hall switch and cab button: a call is registered Lamp_2 output Built-in lamp of the floor 2 hall switch and cab button: a call is registered Lamp_3 output Built-in lamp of the floor 3 hall switch and cab button: a call is registered Lamp_4 output Built-in lamp of the floor 4 hall switch and cab button: a call is registered Signal Meaning Ind_1 output Floor indicator 1: the lamp above every door and in the cab that says the cab is at floor 1 Ind_2 output Floor indicator 2: the lamp above every door and in the cab that says the cab is at floor 2 Ind_3 output Floor indicator 3: the lamp above every door and in the cab that says the cab is at floor 3 Ind_4 output Floor indicator 4: the lamp above every door and in the cab that says the cab is at floor 4 Buzzer output Alarm buzzer Four things about it are physical, not programmable. Up and Down together do nothing: the contactors are mechanically interlocked, and the log says so. Moving with the door open moves, but the log shouts and the part counts it as unsafe: on a real elevator the door contact is in the safety chain and the hoist cannot run; the part leaves that to your program so you can see what it is for. Levelling : when the hoist drops inside the door zone the drive creeps the car level, as a real one does, so a stop a few counts early still lines up with the sill. And the door eye : a passenger boarding or leaving stands in the doorway for a second and a half, and a Close commanded then does not close (the log notes it). Two ways to know where the car is. At_1 to At_4 are floor switches, made only while the car is level. Encoder is the shaft encoder on the hoist, an analog word that reads 1000 counts a floor: 1000 at floor 1, 4000 at floor 4, 2500 half way between 2 and 3. The classic exercise gives you only the encoder and has you find the floor values by trial; here you have both, and the reference uses each where it is best. Passengers: on their own every nine seconds or so ( Seconds between passengers ), or when you click a call plate, somebody appears on a floor and presses the call button once, a 0.3 s press. When the car stands at their floor with the door fully open they board, one at a time through the eye, and press a cab button for where they want to go; at that floor, door open, they leave. A passenger who has waited 45 s takes the stairs and is counted as lost. The cab holds four; a fifth makes Overload . The displays over every door and in the car show whichever Ind_N you turn on; the call plates and cab buttons light with Lamp_N . The elevator has three views like every scene, and it opens in the side view, the elevation above, because that is where the machine is easiest to read. The top view is a sheet of floor plans, one per floor, the way an architect draws a lift core: the lobby, the hoistway with its glass walls on four steel columns, the guide rails and the counterweight at the back, the landing doors, the floor indicator, the hall call station with its lamp, and the people waiting. The car is drawn on the floor it is at, fading as it leaves, with its doors, the eye across them, the car operating panel and its riders. The hall buttons and the car’s panel work in the plan as they do in the elevation. The program’s index The exercise starts with structure, not logic: a main routine that only lists the tasks, each a subroutine with a flag that says when it is scanned. The flags pass control round a loop: DoNext_Or_Wait (at a floor, door open, deciding) → Close_And_Go (a floor chosen) → Car_Moving (the hoist runs) → Stop_And_Open (arrived) → back to DoNext_Or_Wait . Two routines are scanned every time: catching requests, and the safety chain. Read the main routine like a table of contents: S:FS is the controller’s first-scan bit, 1 for the first scan after a download or Program → Run and 0 after. These are the tags the program adds to the scene’s aliases: Tag Type Description Served_Count DINT Shown on the toolbar: door cycles Trip_Count DINT Shown on the toolbar: trips DoNext_Or_Wait BOOL Flag: at a floor with the door open; Next_Or_Wait is scanned and decides where to go next Close_And_Go BOOL Flag: a floor was chosen; Close_And_Move closes the door and hands over to Track_Car Car_Moving BOOL Flag: the hoist runs; Track_Car watches for the floor to stop at Stop_And_Open BOOL Flag: at a wanted floor; Stop_And_Open_Door stops the hoist, settles and opens Going_Up BOOL Direction of travel: up, latched while anything is wanted above Going_Dn BOOL Direction of travel: down Req_Above BOOL A lit request lamp above the car Req_Below BOOL A lit request lamp below the car Floor DINT The floor the car is at or nearest, from the encoder (1000 counts per floor) Settle TIMER Two seconds between stopping and opening the door Min_Open TIMER The door stays open at least five seconds before the next request is processed Trip_ONS BOOL One-shot storage for the trip counter Fault BOOL Safety fault: the hoist with the door not closed, or an overload; cleared by Reset Exercise 1: initialise Everything latched must start somewhere known. The car begins at floor 1 with its door closed, so the first thing the program does is treat that as an arrival: Stop_And_Open is the one flag set, and the arrival routine settles, opens the door and hands over to the decision routine. Exercise 2: catch the requests The exercise’s trick, and the reason it is allowed to use latches: the lamp in the hall switch is the request flag. Press and it latches; the car opens at that floor and it unlatches. One output doubles as the passenger’s confirmation, the program’s memory of the floor, and, read against the car’s position, the direction to go. The routine first turns the encoder into a floor number and lights the indicator, then latches a lamp for any button pressed for a floor the car is not already at, then sums up what is wanted above and below. Exercise 3: to the top, and back The exercise first asks only for this: a call from the fourth floor takes the car up and stops it there. That is one pass round the loop, and it needs every routine to exist with just enough in it. Here they are in the order the loop runs them, already complete for all four floors. Next request, or wait Scanned while the car stands at a floor with its door open. It holds the door five seconds (the minimum open time the exercise asks for; requests arriving meanwhile wait, latched), picks a direction, and goes. Close the door and move Track the car Scanned while the car moves. The hoist outputs are latched, which is unusual and deliberate: this routine stops being scanned the instant the car arrives, and an OTE in a routine that is not scanned keeps its last state. With latches, the arrival routine unlatches the hoist explicitly, and a fault that unlatches it is re-energised here after Reset. Stop and open Exercise 4: the safety chain, the counts, the lamps Exercise 5: multi-floor The exercise’s last and hardest part is already in the routines above, and it is worth seeing where. Collective control means: keep going in the direction of travel while anything is wanted that way, stop at every wanted floor on the way, turn round only when nothing is left ahead, and rest when nothing is wanted at all. The direction is the latch pair in Next_Or_Wait; the stop on the way is Track_Car’s third rung, which only looks at lamps in the direction of travel; the turn-round is the unlatch rungs, which release a direction only when nothing is left that way; the rest is both flags off with the door open. Run it, click the call plates in awkward orders, and watch the displays. Guided: the elevator the scene opens with its guided track on ( File → New Project → Classic: elevator ; or Guided → Guide This Scene: the Elevator on a crossing whose guide was closed). Eight lessons, one routine each and in the order above rather than the index’s: Init (the first scan opens the door), Stop_And_Open_Door (the car stops, the door opens, the passenger steps in), Catch_Requests (a hall call lights its plate and makes a request), Next_Or_Wait (a direction is picked and Close_And_Go set), Close_And_Move (the door is proved closed before the hoist), Track_Car (the car travels, arrives and levels), Safety (the service switch trips the fault) and Ready . Each lesson adds its JSR to the index with the condition the reference has, XIC(Car_Moving)JSR(Track_Car) , not a bare JSR, because the index’s conditions are the state machine: an Init called every scan would open the door forever. The reference rungs sit under the fold with hints first, so write each from its comment and ask for the shape only when the comment is not enough; the run checks are the ones a commissioning engineer would make with a hand on the call plate. Watch for: the lesson order is not the scan order The track writes Stop_And_Open_Door second and Track_Car sixth, because a door that opens is something you can see on the first scan and a car that moves is not worth having until there is somewhere to send it. The index still runs them in the reference’s order. If a lesson’s run check never turns green, open the Simulator Log: the most common cause is the door check, Door_Closed, failing because the previous lesson’s rung was typed while the controller was in Run and is still a pending edit. Run it Run mode: the car settles two seconds, opens at floor 1 and waits. Watch the first passenger: the call plate on their floor lights (the lamp latched), the car closes its door after the minimum open time, the hoist lamp over the shaft comes on, the sheave turns and the encoder counts up, the displays follow the floor, the car stops level, settles, opens; the eye flickers as they board and press a cab button; the lamp for that floor lights. Let it run five minutes and look at the count under the shaft: served and, if the car is slow, lost. Try It Set Seconds between passengers to 4 and run: the collective control starts losing people, because a passenger on 1 going to 4 waits while the car serves everything between. Then the harder one: give each hall call a direction, two buttons per floor, and stop for a hall call only when the car is going the way that passenger wants. That is a full collective, and it is the program a real elevator runs. And the encoder exercise as set: delete the four floor switches from Track_Car’s stop rung and stop on LIM(1970,Encoder,2030) windows instead, then find the widest window that still stops the car inside the levelling zone. Machine faults on the elevator Tools → Inject Machine Fault… lists the faults that belong to the parts on this floor. Each has a fault card: the symptom, what to watch in the I/O to confirm it, the repair, and what a program should do about it. Repair on an active fault removes its cause the way a technician would; whether the machine runs again is up to the program. None of them is caught by the reference program as it stands: the door-close timeout, the no-motion timeout and the encoder cross-check are the exercises. Fault Watch Repair The program should Elevator: door-closed switch stuck open The doors shut but the door-closed switch never makes, so the car never proves its doors closed. Close 1, the doors shut, Door_Closed 0; the car never leaves. Adjust the switch (Repair). A door-close timeout: Close on for six seconds without Door_Closed reopens the door and alarms. Elevator: encoder dead The shaft encoder stops counting: the car moves, the count does not. Up or Down 1, the At_ floor switches changing, Encoder frozen. Replace the encoder (Repair). The floor from the encoder disagreeing with an At_ switch stops the car and alarms. Elevator: hoist overload tripped The hoist motor’s overload trips: Up and Down are commanded and nothing turns. Up (or Down) 1, Encoder not changing. Reset the overload (Repair). A no-motion timeout: Up or Down on and the encoder not moving for two seconds drops the hoist and alarms. Elevator: floor 2 call button stuck in The floor 2 hall button is jammed in. Call_2 1 with nobody there; the car keeps going back to floor 2. Free the button (Repair). A call input on for more than ten seconds is ignored and alarmed: no real passenger holds a button that long.  XIC(S:FS)JSR(Init); THE INDEX. Every task has its own routine and a flag that says when it is scanned; the main routine only lists them.
