ch62: The inspection line running its reference program. This chapter is about a line from a real plant. Cards with 64 wells come off a carousel feeder, get their wells filled from 64 bags of media, pass under a camera that checks every well against the product’s recipe, and either drop through a reject gate or go on to a tray of 130, which goes up one tower of a drying chamber and down the other. It started as a simulator Devon wrote of his own line, LineSim, with a calculator version and a PC version, and it is in Logix Connect as a classic scene, under File → New Project → Inspection line , with its guided track and its own faults. The model is LineSim’s, ported: the timing, the camera’s grey levels, the tracking, the dryer’s clock. What is new here is everything round it: the camera is the Vision Sensor that can talk to a real In-Sight, the recipe goes to it over TCP, and the machine is built to the model standard. The machine The cards start in the carousel feeder : 20 magazines of 200 blank cards round a turntable in front of the track, 4000 cards when it is full. The magazine at the feed station drops a card onto the feeder’s short track every pitch. When it is empty the turntable indexes the next full one round; for those few seconds a pitch or two go by with no card. When all 20 are empty the track runs on with nothing on it and the line shows MAGAZINES EMPTY until they are reloaded. The machine is a table , and its card track is an L: two straight tracks and a corner (Devon: “i just need the L shape”). Each track is a bed between black guide rails held by knurled knobs: white perforated plastic on the first two, and on the camera’s track strips of dark orange rubber either side of the card lane, for traction. Nothing moves the bed: the cards are pushed , and everything that pushes them is underneath. Under each track a Festo electric axis, as long as its stroke, carries a pneumatic lift cylinder and a finger. The finger lifts up through a slot in the bed behind the card at the drive’s pick place, the carriage runs forward one card width, pushing that card and the solid train ahead of it, then the finger drops below the bed and the carriage runs back while the cards stand (Devon: “the drives with fingers lift the finger from behind the card and push it forward”). M1’s drive is the smallest; M4’s the longest, since it pushes a row into the tray. Each drive has a job and waits on the next one. The feeder stands on the outside of the L at the start of the first track, and its own short Festo drive, M5 , pushes each card off the magazine station sideways onto the track. M1 pushes the cards along the first track to the corner, and the filler head, M3 , comes down and doses each one a pitch before the corner. Round the corner, M2 indexes them along the second track, past the laser marker, under the camera and over the reject gate, and on to the end sensor at the very end of the track, right before the tray. The cards stand nested, a card width apart, the whole length of the track: every drive pushes a solid train one card a stroke, its finger lifting behind the card at its pick place (M5 the feed place, M1 corner A, M2 corner B). The camera inspects each card as it stops in front of it; the gate, a card on, drops a failed one. When 13 stand on the end section, one at the end sensor and one at the 13th-card sensor, M4 takes them. With 13 at the end and a tray in position, the card picker M4 , a Festo axis under the track in line with M2’s, lifts its finger behind the 13th card and shoves the 13 along the track’s end into the tray row in line with it, in one stroke; the finger drops and M4 runs home. M2 holds while the 13 stand and refills as soon as the pick slot is clear, before M4 is home. every one of these drives is a PLC output, so the program runs the line (below). The table feeds the loading conveyors in line: the transfer carries each full tray straight onto the first conveyor, and the four run on in a line to the chamber. The bag enclosure stands behind the camera’s track, beside the conveyors, and the lines to the head run across to it. The camera and the UV laser marker stand on the back of the camera’s track, the enclosure side, and face the operator in front. The camera hangs from its mast over the cards. The marker is a big 3-axis head on an extrusion stand, with its scan nose over the track and the window on the nose’s underside; in the model it is the machine only, with no signals. The bag lines run up and over the marker’s head to the pump bank. At the filler , beside the first track on the outside of the L, a pitch before the corner, the head rides a vertical Festo electric axis (M3) down about three inches onto the card and doses every well the recipe fills, each from its own bag through its own pump and line. The bags hang in a glycol-cooled enclosure with clear doors, 8 by 4 feet, on a 2 ft platform; its lid lamps show where the recipe’s bags hang, and a well the recipe leaves empty gets an empty bag, so the enclosure shows the product’s layout, and its line runs clear. The 64 lines are clear tubes, so you see the media in each; a tube runs clear when its bag is empty. The enclosure has its own terminal, the Bag_HMI, with its own recipe sequence: load a recipe with the line stopped, hang the lit bags, BAGS HUNG, the lines prime, the chest cools, READY. Only then is Filler_Ready on. The camera is the Vision Sensor, an In-Sight on module Cam1 in I/O Configuration, hanging from the line’s camera arm over a backlight. Backlit, a filled well reads dark (about 70) and an empty one light (about 220); the threshold, 100, splits them, or the Otsu option finds it from the card. A card on, right after the camera, the reject gate is a trap door in the track: it opens under a failed card and the card drops into the red bin. Good cards go on to the pick position, and M4 pushes them into the tray a row of 13 at a time, ten rows a tray. A full tray goes out onto four level loading conveyors , which carry it and hold it until the chamber takes it straight into the bottom of the load tower , which steps every rail up once a step (30 s); at the top it crosses into the unload tower , which steps down, and leaves at the bottom. With 130 rails a tower that is 2 h 10 min of drying; past the expiry (4 h) a tray comes out EXPIRED. The tray loader and the loading conveyors The trays are open aluminium ladder trays, a pocket for every card, 13 across and 10 rows. At the far end of the table a lift holds a stack of empty trays and raises the top one to the transfer level, a tray pitch at a time. The tray transfer is a square platen plate with four pneumatic grippers at its corners, on a carriage under one beam that runs over the centre line from the lift to the nest, on a portal at each end; an energy chain rides beside the beam. The platen comes down on the top empty tray on the lift, the grippers close on its rim, and it carries the tray over and sets it down in the nest , its first row in line with the card track, just past the track’s end. From there two index cylinders , one at each end of the tray, take over: each is a slide along the tray’s travel with a pawl that lifts behind the tray’s trailing rail. With the pawls up and M4’s fingers locked down on the tray, the indexers step it one row toward CONV 1 after every row M4 pushes in, so the next empty row lines up with the track ( Tray_In_Pos is off while it moves). When the tenth row is in, the indexers run right through and push the full tray out onto the first loading conveyor (CONV 1, which has no lid), drop their pawls and run back behind the next empty tray the platen has meanwhile brought over. Devon: “The index cylinders push the tray ahead of the transfer, then get behind an empty tray the transfer brought over. The fingers lock down, then the indexers get behind the tray, lift, then index each slot until full, then push the tray to conveyor 1 and get behind the next empty tray.” M4’s fingers open when the tray is indexed and in fill position, and close and lift while it is indexing. The trays ride with their rows of 13 across the conveyors and the chamber. The loader is run by the PLC, by the Loader routine below, so every one of those moves is a rung you can read. There are four loading conveyors, level, end to end, carrying the trays toward the chamber and holding them there: an enclosed module each, black side walls on legs, twin flat belts on a stainless bed, a hinged polycarbonate lid, a proximity sensor that sees the tray and a yellow bumper it stops against. They are numbered from the filler: CONV 1 takes the full tray from the nest and CONV 4 enters the chamber. They accumulate: a tray runs forward while the conveyor in front of it is clear, so while the chamber is waiting to step the trays fill CONV 4, then 3, 2 and 1. The chamber takes the tray on CONV 4 straight into the bottom of the load tower and every tray moves up one: a small pneumatic door, 2 inches tall and as wide as the conveyor, lifts, the tray runs in onto the bottom rail, and the door shuts behind it. If all four hold a tray, the full tray stays in the fill position, the rows wait and the drives stop short one after another: the whole line holds until the chamber steps. If the lift runs out of empty trays, the rows wait too and the line shows TRAY STACK EMPTY ; REFILL STACK on the TRAY page loads it again. The number of empty trays on the lift is a setting on the line (20 to start). Try it: run the carousel dry On the FEEDER page press ONE MAGAZINE LEFT with the line running. The magazine at the track empties, the turntable goes looking for a full one and finds none: MAGAZINES EMPTY, and the Simulator Log says so. The track keeps running and the camera, the gate and the tray see nothing come. Press RELOAD MAGAZINES ; the cards come again from the next pitch. Then reload and watch an ordinary magazine change: count the pitches with no card while the turntable indexes. Try it: run the lift dry In the line’s properties set the empty trays on the lift to 3 and run at 90 cards a minute. Three trays fill; then the rows stop, the TRAY page shows WAITING FOR THE LIFT and the Simulator Log shows TRAY STACK EMPTY. Press REFILL STACK and the next tray comes up and the rows start again. Before that, watch the track: 13 fill the end section and M2 holds with the stream behind them, because M4 cannot move without a tray. A blocked tray loader stops the whole line. The recipe string: rows in, columns inspected A product is one line of text: 1,SMP- GLD01,64,255,255,255,255,255,255,255,255,000,000,000,000,000,000,000,000 . The name and the 64 are not used by the inspection. The next eight numbers are the card’s rows , one byte each, row 1 first; the last eight are the no-test mask , laid out the same way. The card is numbered by columns : well 1 is at the bottom right of the card, well 8 at the top right; column 2 is wells 9 to 16, and so on to well 64 at the top left. So the string is sent in rows and the camera inspects in columns: well = (column − 1) × 8 + row, and column 1 is the 128 bit of every row byte, column 8 the 1 bit. A column is not one byte: it is the same bit of all eight. Take a card whose rows read 254, 254, 254, 254, 254, 252, 252, 252. The 1 bit is off in every row, so column 8 is empty all the way up: wells 57 to 64. The 2 bit is off in rows 6 to 8 as well, so column 7 is empty at its top three wells: 54, 55, 56. Byte C1 C2 C3 C4 C5 C6 C7 C8 128 64 32 16 8 4 2 1 Row 1 254 1 1 1 1 1 1 1 0 Row 2 254 1 1 1 1 1 1 1 0 Row 3 254 1 1 1 1 1 1 1 0 Row 4 254 1 1 1 1 1 1 1 0 Row 5 254 1 1 1 1 1 1 1 0 Row 6 252 1 1 1 1 1 1 0 0 Row 7 252 1 1 1 1 1 1 0 0 Row 8 252 1 1 1 1 1 1 0 0 A 1 in the no-test mask means that well is not inspected at all, whatever it holds; it does not mean "expect it empty". The page carries a sample set of made-up products and the test strings (Wells-Empty, Well-01 to Well-64, Wells-Filled); a real table loads from a text file with LOAD TABLE… and stays in that browser, never in the scene or the page. The camera on Cam1, the string over TCP The camera has to know what each card should hold, so the PLC sends it the card’s string as the card arrives, over a TCP Client Socket ( Cam_Socket ), the way the plant’s DVT camera gets it. The socket’s message is {card} , which becomes the string of the card at the camera. Then the PLC triggers the camera through its module’s tags. In the simulator the socket hands the string straight to the camera, and the camera judges the card under its lens with LineSim’s inspection; it answers on the socket in the DVT format, 1,NAME,64,PASS, and the eight row bytes it measured. With a real In-Sight on Cam1 and the socket going through the bridge, the same rungs run the real camera, and the real camera decides. The program The reference program is the line’s own rungs moved onto the camera module’s tags, with the stack light added, a routine that runs the five drives and one that runs the tray loader: six routines, forty-one rungs. File → Load Reference Solution: Inspection line loads it; Guide This Scene walks it with you, a lesson a routine (rung 0 and the JSRs; the drives; the loader; the camera; the tracking; the lamps), each lesson checking your routine against the reference and watching the line do what the rungs say: the platen grips a tray and carries it over, the tray indexes a row, a full tray goes out onto CONV 1. MainRoutine Rung 0 seals Line_Run in from START until STOP; then a JSR for each part of the job. Drives Each drive is run like a cylinder with two reed switches. Its output on carries the comb one pitch and holds it at the end ( Mx_Ext ); the rung lets go there, and the drive runs home with its pins down ( Mx_Home ). Every drive rung is the same shape: the conditions to start from home, a branch that holds the output on, and XIO(Mx_Ext) to let go. What differs is what each one waits for, and that is the machine’s order. M5 waits for corner A to be clear. M1 waits for the head to be up, its card dosed and corner B clear. The head waits for M1 to stop pushing, and M2 for a card in corner B and the camera’s answer. M4 waits for a full row and the tray in position: Row_Full comes on with 13 standing on the end section (the end sensor and the 13th-card sensor both made, M2’s stroke done), and M4 pushes the 13 into the tray row at once; a tray must be in position before M4 makes a move. Fill_Pending remembers that M1 has brought a card under the head, and M3_Done clears it. Cam_Wait holds M2 from the moment a card reaches the camera until Results_Valid , so the fail bit is always in Fail_Mem before M2’s index pulse shifts it, at any speed. The camera’s 0.5 s therefore sets the line’s top rate: about 75 cards a minute with the drives at 90. RunOut_TMR lets M2 index with no card in corner B after 1.5 s, so the last cards of a lot reach the row. Loader The loader is the same shape again: an output for each move, a switch at each end of it, and the rungs in the machine’s order. FULL TRAY OUT : with the tray’s ten rows in ( Tray_Full ), the pawls still up behind it and CONV 1 clear, Idx_Out latches and the indexers run right through, and Tray_Req asks for the next tray at the same moment, so the platen brings it over behind the full one going out (Devon: the indexers push the tray “ahead of the transfer”); at Idx_AtOut the tray is on the conveyor and the out stroke unlatches. GRIP waits for the platen at the stack and a tray up on the lift ( Lift_Top ), then closes the grippers; BRING IT OVER seals TT_Go in on TT_Gripped until the platen is over the nest, where SET DOWN opens the grippers once the nest is empty ( Tray_Seated off), and the request clears with the tray in position. PAWLS UP lifts the pawls behind a seated tray and keeps them up through the out stroke; they drop while the platen is bringing a tray in and after each row step so the indexers can run back. INDEX : a one-shot on M4_Ext remembers a row placed ( Row_Placed ); with the pawls up and M4 home the indexers step a row ( Idx_Step to Idx_Ext ), and Row_Done holds the step until they are home again. LOCK closes M4’s fingers on the tray whenever it is moving or not in position. The whole routine runs on eleven inputs and six outputs, and every one of its times is a placeholder until it is measured. Camera_Handshake Triggering is enabled while the string link is up. The eye’s first scan on a card sends that card’s string and requests a trigger. A scan later (the string has gone) and with Trigger_Ready , the trigger latches; Trigger_Ack drops it. Half a second on, Results_Valid : with Job_Pass off the card failed, Fail_Mem latches, and the PLC acknowledges the result so the camera can present the next. Reject_Tracking The gate is a card past the camera, so the fail has to travel with the card from the camera to the gate. Every M2 stroke moves every card one place, so one stroke is one shift. The index pulse comes once a pitch from M2’s stroke, 0.85 of a pitch along it, after the result is in: BSL shifts Fail_Mem into bit 0 of Fail_Track and moves the older cards on, and the next rung clears Fail_Mem for the next card. The card standing at the gate is bit 0, so the gate eye with bit 0 set opens the trap door; the next card’s result, latching Fail_Mem meanwhile, cannot touch it. The camera itself is the Vision Sensor (module Cam1) PE_Gate input Photo-eye at the reject gate, one pitch past the camera (the card at the gate is bit 0 of the fail track) Index input Index pulse: 0.1 s once an M2 stroke, as a card leaves the camera (a gap in the stream shifts nothing) Bag_Low input A media bag the filler uses is below 20 %: short shots start Filler_Ready input The bag enclosure is READY (or RUN): its recipe loaded, the bags hung, the lines primed, the chest at temperature. Until then the filler dispenses nothing PE_CornerA input Photo-eye at corner A, where M5’s track meets M1’s: a card is in the corner PE_Filler input Photo-eye under the filler head on M1’s track: a card stands under the head still to be dosed (an empty card; it clears once the head has dosed it) PE_CornerB input Photo-eye at corner B, where M1’s track meets M2’s: a card is in the corner Row_Full input The end section of M2’s track holds 13 cards: one at the end sensor, one at the 13th-card (pick) sensor, nested between PE_Pick input The 13th-card sensor: a card stands in the pick slot, where M4’s finger lifts Tray_In_Pos input The tray in the nest is in position: an empty row lined up with the picker (off while it indexes a row and while trays swap) M5_Home input M5 at home: the carriage back, its finger down M5_Ext input M5 at the end of its stroke: the cards pushed on one card width M1_Home input M1 at home: the carriage back, its finger down Signal Kind What it is M1_Ext input M1 at the end of its stroke: the cards pushed on one card width M2_Home input M2 at home: the carriage back, its finger down M2_Ext input M2 at the end of its stroke: the cards pushed on one card width M3_Up input M3, the filler head’s vertical axis, up M3_Done input M3 down on the card and the dose complete M4_Home input M4, the card picker, at the pick position M4_Ext input M4 at the end of its stroke: the row is in the tray M5_Push output M5, the feeder track’s Festo drive: carry the cards one pitch toward corner A (hold on to the end; off runs it home) M1_Push output M1, the filler track’s drive: carry the cards one pitch, past the filler, toward corner B M3_Fill output M3, the filler head: down onto the card under it and dose; off, back up M2_Push output M2, the inspection track’s drive: carry the cards one pitch through the camera and the reject gate to the pick position M4_Place output M4, the card picker: push the row of 13 along the track into the tray row in position; off, back to the pick position TT_AtStack input The transfer platen at the stack end of its axis TT_AtNest input The transfer platen over the nest TT_Gripped input The platen’s four grippers closed on a tray Idx_Home input The tray indexers at home: their pawls back at the nest’s rear Idx_Up input The indexers’ pawls up behind the tray’s trailing rail Idx_Ext input The indexers at the end of a row stroke Idx_AtOut input The indexers at the end of the out stroke: the tray on CONV 1 Tray_Seated input A tray is seated in the nest (the nest sensor) Conv1_Clear input No tray on CONV 1 (the conveyor eye) Tray_Full input The tray in the nest holds its 10 rows Lift_Top input An empty tray up at the top of the lift, under the platen TT_Go output The transfer platen: run from the stack to the nest; off, back to the stack TT_Grip output Close the platen’s four grippers on the tray under it Idx_Lift output The tray indexers: pawls up behind the tray (one each end) Idx_Step output The indexers: stroke the tray one row forward and hold; off (pawls down) run back a row Idx_Out output The indexers: run the full tray right through onto CONV 1 Signal Kind What it is Pick_Lock output M4’s fingers: close and lift to lock the tray while it indexes; open with the tray in fill position Reject_Gate output Reject gate, two pitches past the camera: a trap door in the conveyor opens and the card on it drops into the reject bin below Alarm output Stack light, red Stack_Amber output Stack light, amber Stack_Green output Stack light, green Tag Type What it holds Send_OS BOOL One-shot storage: the send-and-trigger rung Trig_Req BOOL A card is at the camera and its string has gone: trigger once the camera is ready Fail_Mem BOOL The camera said FAIL for the card it just inspected (latched until the next index pulse) Fail_Track DINT The fail bits of the cards between the camera and the gate, shifted one place every index pulse (BSL, length 8) Fail_Ctl CONTROL The BSL control for Fail_Track Line_Run BOOL The line is running: START sets it, STOP drops it (the drives run from it) Fill_Pending BOOL M1 has brought a card under the filler head: it is to be dosed before M1 pushes again RunOut_TMR TIMER No card in corner B for 1.5 s: M2 indexes anyway, so the last cards of a lot run out to the row Cam_Wait BOOL A card has come to the camera and the camera has not answered yet: M2 holds it under the lens Wait_OS BOOL One-shot storage: the card-at-the-camera rung Tray_Req BOOL The nest needs a tray: set when the full one has gone out, cleared when the platen has set the new one down Row_Placed BOOL M4 has placed a row and the tray is to index Row_Done BOOL A row stroke is in: the pawls drop for the run back Row_OS BOOL One-shot storage: the row-placed rung The drying chamber on the terminal The console (START, STOP, RESET), the camera’s socket and the three terminals stand on the open floor beside the bag enclosure, under the conveyors. The Operator View (Window menu) shows the line too: its screen is the Line_HMI’s pages, or the bag enclosure’s (Screen: Bag enclosure), and its control panel presses the console’s own START, STOP and RESET, with a RUNNING lamp on Line_Run and an ALARM lamp for any line alarm. The line’s own terminal (Line_HMI) has a page for each station. The DRYER page draws LineSim’s drying-chamber panel: the rails of both towers with their shelf tabs, every fifth numbered, each tray a bar on its rail with its number, product and load time, the step and the dryer log (FTI first tray in, LTI last tray in, FTO first out, LTO last out). With 130 rails a tower the page shows 17 at a time; ▲ and ▼ move the window, and the strip beside each tower shows all of them. Try it: a recipe with empty wells On the Bag_HMI open RECIPES with the line stopped, pick a product whose last row is 0 (the sample SMP-RED01), LOAD RECIPE, then BAGS HUNG on the SEQUENCE page. Watch the lid lamps: row 8 stays dark, no bags hang there, their tubes stay clear. Run the line and look at a card on the Cam_HMI: wells 8, 16 … 64 read light and are boxed grey, right as they are. Try it: take an interlock out In the Drives routine delete XIO(PE_CornerA) from the M5 rung and run. M5 now pushes while a card is still standing in corner A. The card behind stops against it, and so does the comb: M5 never reaches M5_Ext , its rung never lets go, and the plan shows M5 in red, STOPPED SHORT: CORNER A IS NOT CLEAR, until M1 clears the corner. Nothing breaks and nothing passes through anything, but the line has lost its rhythm. Put it back. Then take XIC(M3_Up)XIO(Fill_Pending) out of the M1 rung: M1 now pushes with the head down in a card and stops short at the head. Try it: break the tracking The tracking can only break with the old one-bit control, where the index does not wait for the camera. In the line’s properties set Drive control to Machine and load the reference solution again (it is the old program then), then set the rate to 90 cards a minute, Test Mode to 30 % and the index pulse to 0.5 pitch. Run it: the shift now comes before the result is in, so a card’s fail lands on the card behind it. Escapes (a bad card on the tray) and good cards dropped at the gate both count up on the LINE page. In this port it starts from about 70 cards a minute. Put the index back to 0.85 and they stop. With the PLC drives, Cam_Wait in the M2 rung does what the 0.85 does here, at every speed. Try it: no string, no pass Clear the socket’s message (or unplug the string link by giving Cam_Socket a message without {{card}} ). The camera still triggers, but with no recipe it fails every card as NO STRING, and they all drop: good cards in the bin. That is why the camera setup rung enables triggering only while the link is up. Watch For The drive times are placeholders. A push takes half a card’s cycle (M2 0.35), the run back 0.3, the dose 0.35, scaled from the line rate; the picker takes 0.6 s in and 0.4 s back. With the PLC drives the rate setting is the drives’ speed, and the line makes what the handshakes allow. A drive that stops short is not a fault. It is waiting for the way to clear; the plan says which drive and why. If it never clears, look at the rung that should have waited. The loader’s times are placeholders. The platen’s 2.0 s over, 0.3 s to grip, 0.3 s for the pawls, 0.5 s a row step, 1.2 s out and 1.0 s back, the 3 s lift and the 20 trays on the lift are not measured on the real machine, nor the carousel’s 2.5 s index; change them when they are. A gap is not a fault. While the carousel indexes, pitches go by with no card. A program that counts index pulses as cards will be off by those gaps; count what the photo-eyes see. The bit order. Column 1 is the 128 bit of each row byte, column 8 the 1 bit. 254 is a row with column 8 empty, not column 1. A column is not a byte. The camera reads column by column, but the string holds rows: a column is the same bit of all eight bytes. The no-test mask skips a well. A 1 there means the well is not inspected; it does not mean the well should be empty. Send, then trigger. The trigger rung waits a scan after the send (XIO on the send bit), so the camera has the card’s string when it grabs the card. Clear the fail at the index. Without the OTU on the index pulse, one failed card keeps failing every card after it. Filler_Ready. Until the enclosure is READY the filler doses nothing; the cards go on dry and the camera fails them. Interlock the conveyor (or at least the alarm) on it. Its faults Faults → Inject has three for the line. Corrupted product strings : every eighth card’s string has its first byte off by one; the camera fails those cards as STRING != TABLE whatever the wells hold. The glycol supply stops : the chest warms, past 8 °C the Bag_HMI shows MEDIA WARM and Filler_Ready drops. The dryer stops stepping : the trays in it keep ageing, and those past the expiry come out EXPIRED when it steps again. The camera has its own alarms on the Vision Sensor: off line, a trigger while busy, a full results buffer. ch63: In the app File → New Project… → Air compressor room opens the room with its tags made and an empty program, and its guided track ( Guided: the air compressors ) on. File → Load Reference Solution: Air compressors loads the program of this chapter. Two 50 HP screw compressors discharge through their check valves into a header and a 400-gallon receiver with a pressure transmitter, a high-pressure switch, a relief valve and a timed drain. The plant draws air from the receiver, and the program keeps the pressure up with as little running as it can: a lead unit on a band from 100 to 115 psi, a lag unit on a lower band from 90 to 110 that comes in only when the lead cannot keep up, the lead swapped after every cycle so the run hours share out, HAND / OFF / AUTO on each unit, and a high-pressure trip at 125 psi that latches until Reset. The relief valve at 135 psi is there for a program that misses it. The compressor room running: the two packages on their pad, the header, the receiver with its gauge, and the console. ch64: In the app File → New Project… → Material silo: bulk filling opens the scene with its tags made and an empty program, and its guided track ( Guided: bulk filling ) on. File → Load Reference Solution: Material silo loads the program of this chapter. Level 22 is the same machine as a graded level. A bulk filling line after LogixPro’s silo. A welded cone-bottom tank on four legs holds white paint; under the cone a butterfly valve with its actuator and a dribble valve on a bypass, each proved shut by its switch; a telescopic fill lance on an air cylinder that goes down into the container and centres it; a radar level transmitter on the roof, a high-level switch through the shell, and a refill valve piped from a supply tote. Under the lance a weighing conveyor, with an infeed before it and an outfeed after, all on one VFD; a registration eye and an encoder. The FORMAT thumbwheel picks the container (1 pail, 2 drum, 3 bag-in-box, 4 jug); the feeder’s Part to Emit has to match. The modes: ONE fills one container per Start, CONT runs on, DEMAND waits for FILL. The material silo filling a pail: the tank on its legs, the lance down in the pail on the weighing conveyor, the console with FORMAT. ch65: In the app File → New Project… → Card Sort Cell opens the cell in Automatic, with its tags made and an empty routine. Guided → New Guided Project: Card Sort Cell… opens it with Card motion on PLC, the two modules and the tags, and walks through the program below a routine at a time. File → Load Reference Solution: Card Sort Cell loads the whole program into the cell that is open. The Card Sort Cell is the bench fixture for Level 11’s camera cards, modelled on a real one: a baseboard with a red fixture on it, holding a magazine of the eighteen Level 11 cards on a grip ramp, a nest under a ring light, and a PASS tray and a FAIL tray; a copy stand with an In-Sight camera ( Vision_1 , module Cam1 ) and a DataMan code reader ( Code_1 , module Reader1 ) over the nest; a push button, PASS and FAIL lamps, a TCP socket and an HMI. Vision_1 judges the card in the nest (cap, label, fill, and the lot code against the lot it was told), Code_1 reads its serial, and the cell keeps a tally against the answer key. The 3D view shows it at its real size on a bench. The Card Sort Cell: the magazine on its ramp, the nest under the light, the PASS and FAIL trays, and the camera and reader on the copy stand. How the cards move The cell’s Card motion setting decides who moves the cards. By hand : in Run mode, click the magazine to feed the next card and a tray to sort it. Automatic (the default in the New Project card): the cell feeds the next card when the nest is empty and sorts the card in the nest on the camera’s result, code 0 to PASS and anything else to FAIL. PLC : the cell gives the program three outputs, Feed , Sort_Pass and Sort_Fail (each acts on its rising edge), and a Pusher_Home input. A feed is the pusher: the block at the end of the ramp runs out to the magazine in half a second, carrying the bottom card into the nest, and goes home. A sort answers with a pulse, Sorted_Pass or Sorted_Fail , as the card leaves the nest. The program The reference program runs the cell with Card motion on PLC. One step register carries each card through the cycle: 10 feed, 20 lot, 30 inspect, 40 results, 50 sort, and back to 10. Each routine acts only in its own steps, so MainRoutine is just the index. In step 10, with the nest empty, a timer gives the last card 0.6 s to land in its tray; then Feed , with the pusher home, carries the bottom card into the nest. The card in: count it, forget the last card’s handshakes, and move on to step 20. The cycle ends when the magazine is empty, the nest clear and the pusher home. That last condition matters: while the pusher is out with the eighteenth card the magazine is already empty and the nest still clear, and without it the cycle would end with a card in transit. The lot over TCP The camera judges each card’s lot code against the lot it was told, so it has to be told before the picture. The magazine holds the three lots in order, six cards each, so LIM finds the lot from the card number. A new lot goes into the socket’s SendValue ( TCP_Lot ) and is sent as LOT n on a rising edge of TCP_Send , held 0.2 s by a timer. Then the card settles for 0.3 s and the step moves on to the picture. With the socket down the cycle waits here, which is what it should do. Two triggers, 250 ms apart Both readers look into the nest, and each has its own light. So the camera goes first and the DataMan 250 ms after it, once the camera’s light is off. Each trigger is the handshake from Level 8 (chapter 40): latch Trigger when the reader is ready, drop it on Trigger_Ack . A flag per reader ( Cam_Fired , DM_Fired ) makes it once per card. The results, and the cross-check Each reader’s result is taken while it is offered, then acknowledged. From the camera: its result code, and the card ID in byte 10 of Inspection_Results . From the DataMan: its result code, and the serial it read, copied into a STRING (the bytes into DATA with COP , the count into LEN ). The serial’s last character is the card ID too: SN-4801 is card 1, since '1' is 49 and 49 less 48 is 1. If the reader read nothing, or the two disagree on which card this is, the cross-check fails and the card can’t pass. PASS needs code 0 and the cross-check good. The lamps show the last card’s verdict. Sort, count, and the next card In step 50 the verdict picks the output, Sort_Pass or Sort_Fail , on its rising edge. The cell answers with Sorted_Pass or Sorted_Fail as the card leaves the nest: count it and go back to step 10 for the next card. A full magazine runs in a little over a minute at 4×, and the tally under the board should read 18 right. What to break on purpose Shuffle the magazine (the cell’s Magazine order ) and run again: the lots no longer come six at a time, and the wrong-lot results show it. Dirty the DataMan’s window ( Machine Faults → Code reader window dirty ): every read is a no read, and the cross-check sends every card to FAIL. Stop the socket (its Host set to an address nobody answers): the cycle waits in step 20 for the lot. With a real 5603 and DataMan, their modules set to Implicit I/O, the same rungs run the bench. Try it Run the cell in Automatic first and watch the tally build up, so you know what right looks like. Then start Guided → New Guided Project: Card Sort Cell… and write the five routines one at a time, running after each; the guide checks each one in Run mode.  JSR(CC_Feed); THE INDEX: the feed, the lot, the inspection, the results, the sort. Each routine acts on its own value of Step JSR(CC_Lot);  JSR(CC_Inspect);  JSR(CC_Results);  JSR(CC_Sort);  XIC(Push_1)XIO(Cycle_On)XIO(Mag_Empty)ONS(Start_ONS)[OTL(Cycle_On),CLR(Card_No),CLR(Lot_Sent),CLR(Pass_Count),CLR(Fail_Count),CLR(Mismatches),OTU(Has_Res),MOV(10,Step)]; START: Push_1 starts a cycle with cards in the magazine. The counts and the lot sent start over XIC(Cycle_On)EQU(Step,10)XIO(Card_In_Nest)XIO(Mag_Empty)TON(Feed_T,600,0); FEED WAIT: the nest is empty; give the last card 0.6 s to land in its tray (the pusher won't move while a card is still sliding) XIC(Feed_T.DN)XIC(Pusher_Home)XIO(Card_In_Nest)OTE(Feed); FEED: the pusher runs on the rising edge and carries the bottom card into the nest. Feed drops as the pusher leaves home EQU(Step,10)XIC(Card_In_Nest)[ADD(Card_No,1,Card_No),OTU(Cam_Fired),OTU(DM_Fired),OTU(Cam_Got),OTU(DM_Got),MOV(20,Step)]; CARD IN: count it, forget the last card's handshakes, on to the lot XIC(Cycle_On)EQU(Step,10)XIC(Mag_Empty)XIO(Card_In_Nest)XIC(Pusher_Home)[OTU(Cycle_On),MOV(0,Step)]; DONE: the magazine is empty, the last card sorted, and the pusher home (it is out while the last card rides into the nest) EQU(Step,20)[LIM(1,Card_No,6)MOV(101,Lot_Want),LIM(7,Card_No,12)MOV(102,Lot_Want),LIM(13,Card_No,18)MOV(103,Lot_Want)]; THE LOT this card belongs to: the magazine holds the three lots in order, six cards each EQU(Step,20)NEQ(Lot_Want,Lot_Sent)MOV(Lot_Want,TCP_Lot); A new lot: put it in the socket's SendValue EQU(Step,20)NEQ(Lot_Want,Lot_Sent)XIC(TCP_Connected)TON(Send_T,200,0); …and with the socket connected, send it: TCP_Send on for 0.2 s XIC(Send_T.TT)OTE(TCP_Send); SEND: the socket sends LOT n on the rising edge XIC(Send_T.DN)MOV(Lot_Want,Lot_Sent); Sent: the camera now judges the lot code against this lot EQU(Step,20)EQU(Lot_Sent,Lot_Want)TON(Settle_T,300,0); SETTLE: the lot is set; let the card settle in the nest for 0.3 s XIC(Settle_T.DN)MOV(30,Step); …then the picture [OTE(Cam1:O.Trigger_Enable),OTE(Cam1:O.Buffer_Results_Enable),OTE(Reader1:O.Trigger_Enable)]; THE TWO READERS: the camera and the DataMan may be triggered; the camera's results are buffered EQU(Step,30)XIO(Cam_Fired)XIC(Cam1:I.Trigger_Ready)[OTL(Cam1:O.Trigger),OTL(Cam_Fired)]; TRIGGER THE CAMERA once per card, when it is ready XIC(Cam1:O.Trigger)XIC(Cam1:I.Trigger_Ack)OTU(Cam1:O.Trigger); …Trigger_Ack: drop the trigger EQU(Step,30)XIC(Cam_Fired)TON(DM_Delay,250,0); THE DATAMAN 250 MS LATER: the camera's light is off by then XIC(DM_Delay.DN)XIO(DM_Fired)XIC(Reader1:I.Trigger_Ready)[OTL(Reader1:O.Trigger),OTL(DM_Fired)]; TRIGGER THE DATAMAN once per card XIC(Reader1:O.Trigger)XIC(Reader1:I.Trigger_Ack)OTU(Reader1:O.Trigger); …Trigger_Ack: drop it EQU(Step,30)XIC(DM_Fired)MOV(40,Step); Both triggered: wait for the results XIC(Cam1:I.Results_Valid)XIO(Cam1:O.Inspection_Results_Ack)[MOV(Cam1:I.Inspection_Result_Code,Cam_Code),MOV(Cam1:I.Inspection_Results[10],Cam_Card),OTL(Cam_Got),OTL(Cam1:O.Inspection_Results_Ack)]; THE CAMERA'S RESULT: the code, and the card ID from byte 10; then acknowledge XIO(Cam1:I.Results_Valid)OTU(Cam1:O.Inspection_Results_Ack); …drop the ack once Results_Valid has gone XIC(Reader1:I.Results_Available)XIO(Reader1:O.Results_Ack)[MOV(Reader1:I.Result_Code,DM_Result),COP(Reader1:I.Result_Data[0],Code_Text.DATA[0],16),MOV(Reader1:I.Result_Length,Code_Text.LEN),OTL(DM_Got),OTL(Reader1:O.Results_Ack)]; THE DATAMAN'S RESULT: the code, and the SN into a STRING (the bytes into DATA, the length into LEN); then acknowledge XIO(Reader1:I.Results_Available)OTU(Reader1:O.Results_Ack); …drop its ack EQU(Step,40)XIC(Cam_Got)XIC(DM_Got)[SUB(Code_Text.DATA[6],48,DM_Card),OTU(Cross_Fail),OTU(Verdict_Pass),OTL(Has_Res),MOV(50,Step)]; BOTH IN: the card ID in the SN is its last character (SN-4801: '1' is 49, less 48 is 1) EQU(Step,50)[XIO(DM_Result.0),NEQ(DM_Card,Cam_Card)]OTL(Cross_Fail); CROSS-CHECK: the reader read nothing, or the two disagree on which card this is EQU(Step,50)XIC(Cross_Fail)ONS(Cross_ONS)ADD(Mismatches,1,Mismatches); …counted EQU(Step,50)EQU(Cam_Code,0)XIO(Cross_Fail)OTL(Verdict_Pass); THE VERDICT: PASS only on a clean result with the reader agreeing XIC(Has_Res)XIC(Verdict_Pass)OTE(Lamp_Pass); THE LAMPS show the last card's verdict XIC(Has_Res)XIO(Verdict_Pass)OTE(Lamp_Fail);  EQU(Step,50)XIC(Verdict_Pass)OTE(Sort_Pass); SORT: the card to its tray on the rising edge EQU(Step,50)XIO(Verdict_Pass)OTE(Sort_Fail);  EQU(Step,50)XIC(Sorted_Pass)[ADD(Pass_Count,1,Pass_Count),MOV(10,Step)]; SORTED: count it, on to the next card EQU(Step,50)XIC(Sorted_Fail)[ADD(Fail_Count,1,Fail_Count),MOV(10,Step)];
ch66: The book ends here; the program does not. A few directions to take it. Build cells of your own Every part in Part III works in an empty sandbox the way it does on the template, and the program’s test suite builds a scrap cell from the parts list in an empty floor every release: a Raised Conveyor with a Bottle Feeder, a Broken-bottle Eye, a pivot gate over a Grinder, a Box Conveyor with a Box Feeder and Box Photoeye, a second gate over a Divert Conveyor, and six rungs — a run bit, the belts, a gate on its own photoeye, the box conveyor on LS, the shredder on an empty box. It runs. Start there. Real hardware Bridge & Tools runs the TcpBridge program on your PC that connects the page to the outside: a TCP socket a vision system or a test bench talks to (the TCP Client Socket part), and EtherNet/IP devices. Communications → Start Bridge, then the socket part’s settings. Help → Bridge & Tools covers it. The bench The Card Sort Cell (chapter 65) is a model of a real bench fixture, and Help → Bench Files has the printable parts and the camera cards, so the same program can be tried against a real camera on a real bench through the bridge. Studio 5000 Export L5X and import the file into Studio 5000: the tags, aliases and routines come across, and the program that ran the simulated line is the program you would download to a CompactLogix driving the real one — the I/O addresses are already in the right shape. Going the other way, Import L5X brings a real project’s routines in to run against a sandbox machine you lay out to match.

appC: The bit each station reads, in the frame its rung runs in (chapter 10). During the dwell, bit n of a head register is the bottle standing n + 1 stops past its sensor; after the shift ( Dwell.DN ), the bottle n stops past it. Station x Exist Large Broken Reject Frame Filler 440 7 6 5 — after the shift Capper 560 10 9 8 — after the shift Labeler 600 11 — 9 — after the shift Camera 640 12 — 10 — after the shift Scrap gate 720 13 12 11 0 during the dwell Divert gate 1000 20 19 18 7 during the dwell End-of-line check (LS11) 1240 26 25 24 13 during the dwell The four registers are DINT[2], 48 bits long, shifted by the four BSLs of step 4 on Dwell.DN . Reject takes Cam_Bad , the camera’s verdict, so its bits count from the camera.
appD: Every sensor and vision part, with what it detects, its range, its settings and its signals in each configuration, from the page’s own reference. Fill Level Sensor (liquid in the bottle) Settings: Fill line (px above the belt; a small bottle is 40 tall, a large 56; the liquid tops out at about 80 % of that); Sensor; Analog output (adds a Percent analog input: fill of the bottle under the sensor, 0-100 % of its label) Tag Controller I/O Type Description Device_Detect Input BOOL Liquid at or above the fill line in the bottle under the sensor Diffuse Sensor (photoelectric) Diffuse photoelectric sensor: its own light reflects off the part, so no reflector is needed. The shaded band on the lane shows the sensing range. LED: Red: detecting. Detectable: Solids: any part. Sensing range: 0 – 100 px, default 20 px (≈ 0.3 m). Factory I/O: 0 – 1.6 m. Settings: Sensing range (px; 60 px = 1 m); Sensitivity (%): the gain. 100 sees every part at full range; lower it and the range shrinks and dull targets (glass bottles, broken glass, dark cartons) drop out before bright ones (metal, cans, white and yellow cartons); Beam; Sees Tag Controller I/O Type Description Device_Detect Input BOOL Detecting: a solid part is within range Retroreflective Sensor and Reflector The sensor and its reflector face each other across the conveyor. Detect is 1 while the beam is interrupted. Use the beam height to ignore low parts: a lid (8 px) passes under a 12 px beam, a carton does not. LED: Green: aligned with the reflector. Yellow: beam not interrupted (goes out while a part blocks it). Detectable: Solids taller than the beam height. Sensing range: Across the lane (≈ 1 m here; the real device reaches 6 m). Settings: Beam height (px above the belt) Tag Controller I/O Type Description Device_Detect Input BOOL Light beam interrupted Light Array (8 beams) Eight parallel beams form a light curtain. Beam 1 is lowest. Digital gives one BOOL per beam, Numerical packs the beams into one INT (bit 0 = beam 1), Analog gives 10 V × interrupted beams ÷ 8 as hundredths of a volt. With the default 6 px spacing a small carton (22 px) breaks beams 1-4, a medium one 5, a large one 7, a crate all 8, a lid only beam 1. LED: Green: emitter and receiver synchronised. One red LED per interrupted beam. Detectable: Solids; measures how tall a part is. Sensing range: Across the lane; 8 beams spaced by the beam-spacing setting. Digital gives Detect. Analog gives Volts: 0 V with the part at the sensor, rising to 10 V (1000) at the edge of the range, and 1000 when nothing metal is in range. LED: Red: detecting. Detectable: Conductive parts only: metal blocks, metal stock, metal bases and lids, cans. Sensing range: 0 – 60 px, default 10 px (≈ 0.17 m). Factory I/O: 0 – 0.1 m. Digital gives Detect. Analog gives Volts exactly like the inductive sensor, without the material filter. LED: Green: detecting. Detectable: Any material: solids (and liquids on the real device). Sensing range: 0 – 60 px, default 12 px (≈ 0.2 m), same as the real sensor. LED: The head shows the colour it sees. Detectable: Coloured plastic parts: red, blue, green, yellow. Metal gives no bank. Sensing range: Directly beneath the head. Tag Controller I/O Type Description Device_Red Input BOOL Bank 1: red Device_Blue Input BOOL Bank 2: blue Device_Green Input BOOL Bank 3: green Device_Yellow Input BOOL Bank 4: yellow Vision Sensor Recognises the part under it. Digital : one BOOL per ticked part. Bits : the part code as five binary inputs Bit0-Bit4 (Factory I/O's "All Digital"). Numerical : one INT with the part code (the number next to each part in the list; 0 = none or not ticked). ID : the serial number of the part in view plus its code, usable like a barcode. Size : the older Small/Medium/Large/Metal outputs. Tick Triggered for a Trigger output with Busy and Complete, like a real smart camera: the result then holds until the next trigger. Set Inspection job to Bottle inspection and it checks a bottle's cap, label and fill instead: Pass is a bottle with all three, and on a camera module the result code is bit 0 no cap, bit 1 no label, bit 2 short fill, bit 3 no part in view, with the fill in % of the label in byte 9 of Inspection_Results. On a camera module, Buffer_Results_Enable queues results up to the buffer depth until the PLC acknowledges each one (Results_Buffer_Overrun when one is lost). A Process HMI set to show the sensor draws its camera screen. Card mode (bottle job): the bottle cards SN-4801 to SN-4804 decide each bottle. The hopper sends plain good bottles; when a result comes back, the bottle under the camera takes the card's verdict (no cap, no label, short fill; no card in view makes it a reject) and moves on. Each bottle waits at the camera until its result is presented, so there is time to swap the card. With the simulated camera, pick the card in Card under the lens or on the camera screen's CARDS page; with the camera module live on a real In-Sight, the real card decides: its result code, the fill in byte 9 and the card ID in byte 10 of Inspection_Results. LED: Green: a part in view. Amber: result valid for a selected part. The ring light flashes on a trigger. Detectable: Every part in the catalogue; tick the ones to detect. Sensing range: Directly beneath the camera. 0 = none) Device_Code Input INT Part code, as in Numerical mode Configuration: size Tag Controller I/O Type Description Device_Detect Input BOOL A part is in the field of view Device_Pass Input BOOL The part is one of the selected parts Device_Small Input BOOL Small part Device_Medium Input BOOL Medium part Device_Large Input BOOL Large part Device_Metal Input BOOL Metal part Configuration: camera tags only Tag Controller I/O Type Description RFID Reader Single-trigger command interface: set Command , pulse Execute ; when CommandID increments the command has finished and Status says how it went (0 = success). Command 0 only checks for a tag, 1 reads the serial into ReadData, 2 reads the word at MemoryIndex, 3 writes WriteData there, 4 clears the memory. Two tags in range give status 2. Write a route code into a part at one station and sort on it at the next. LED: Green: idle. Orange: executing a command. Red: the last command failed. Detectable: RFID tags. Every part carries one except raw stock, housing bases and housing lids. Each tag has a unique serial number and 16 words of memory. Sensing range: 0 – 60 px, default 16 px. Settings: Reading range (px); Command time (ms) Tag Controller I/O Type Description Device_Command Output INT Command to execute: 0 = is a tag available?, 1 = read serial number, 2 = read data, 3 = write data, 4 = clear all data Device_Execute Output BOOL Rising edge executes the command Device_MemoryIndex Output INT Tag memory index for read/write (0-15) Device_WriteData Output INT Data written by command 3 Device_CommandID Input INT Number of commands executed so far; changes when the current one has finished Device_Status Input INT 0 = success, 1 = no tag, 2 = too many tags, 3 = invalid index, 4 = invalid command Device_ReadData Input INT Result of command 1 (serial) or 2 (data) Device_TagPresent Input BOOL Exactly one tag is within range Code Reader (DataMan 260 series, EtherNet/IP) A fixed-mount code reader of the Cognex DataMan 260 series (the DM262 and kin) on EtherNet/IP. It has no wired signals: it works on its module's tags. Type the module's name into Reader module , or use Add DataMan Module in its properties. The handshake is the reader's own: set Trigger_Enable ; a 0 → 1 on Trigger with Trigger_Ready on takes an image (hold Trigger until Trigger_Ack ); after the decode time Results_Available comes on with Result_ID (the trigger it answers), Result_Code (bit 0 = read, bit 1 = matches the match string), Result_Length and the string in Result_Data ; set Results_Ack and drop it once Results_Available clears. Buffer_Results_Enable queues results until each is acknowledged; a result that finds the queue full is lost and Results_Buffer_Overrun says so. A trigger while it is busy is missed ( Missed_Acq , and bit 3 on the next result). SoftEvent 1 trains the match string from the next read, 4 clears it, 7 sets it from User_Data. Add Example Routine writes a routine with the whole handshake. Click the reader in Run mode for its screen. Implicit mode: the module talks to your reader through the bridge and the part shows what the real reader decoded. LED: On top: green ready (Trigger_Ready), green good read, red fault or no read. The window's illumination LEDs flash on each trigger; the field across the lane turns green on a read, orange on a no read. Detectable: The code on a part: the date coder's mark on a bottle, or a code label from the emitter (Code labels). Sensing range: Across the lane, the field of view along the belt (default 12 px, 0.2 m): a part is read when its centre is in it. appF: The terms used in this workstation and in Logix Designer, A to Z, as the page’s own glossary has them. A Accumulator (.ACC) The running value of a timer (milliseconds elapsed) or a counter (counts so far). It is a DINT, so it shows up for compare and math instructions, not for XIC. Adapter The EtherNet/IP device that is owned and answers the scanner: a camera, a drive, a rack of remote I/O. Add-On Instruction (AOI) An instruction you define yourself: parameters, local tags and a ladder routine, packaged under one name and used like TON or MOV. Every call needs its own backing tag. See the Add-On Instructions section. Alias tag A second name for another tag or an I/O point. Start_PB aliased to Local:1:I.Data.0 is that input, under a readable name. Cross Reference treats the alias and its target as the same thing. Analog I/O A channel that carries a number instead of on/off: a level, a weight, a speed reference. Here it is an INT on the 1769-IF4 and 1769-OF4 cards. Array A tag with a Dim: Name[0] to Name[Dim-1], all of one data type. Used by the file, shift, FIFO and sequencer instructions. Assemble (edits) The last step of an online edit: the accepted edits become the program and the original rungs are removed. Assembly (CIP) A block of bytes an EtherNet/IP device exposes as one object, class 4. The input assembly is what the device produces, the output assembly is what it consumes. The EDS file gives the instance numbers and sizes. B Backing tag The tag of an Add-On Instruction's own data type that goes with one call. It holds that call's parameters and local tags, so two calls with two backing tags run independently. Backplane The bus the controller and its local cards sit on. Local:3:O.Data.0 means slot 3 on the backplane. Base tag The real tag or I/O address behind an alias. BOOL One bit: 0 or 1. What XIC, XIO and OTE work on. Branch A parallel path in a rung, written [ leg , leg ]. Power gets through if any leg is true. Bridge The small server (TcpBridge, built into LogixConnect.exe) that gives the page real TCP and UDP sockets. Everything that talks to hardware goes through it. Bumpless transfer Switching a PID loop between manual and automatic without a jump in the output. C Carousel feeder A turntable carrying magazines of parts round to a feed station, so one machine can run from many magazines: when the one at the station is empty the turntable indexes the next full one round. On the inspection line, 20 magazines of 200 cards feed the transport track. CIP Common Industrial Protocol: the object model (classes, instances, attributes, services) that EtherNet/IP carries. Class 1 connection A cyclic I/O connection: after a Forward Open, both ends send their data over UDP 2222 every RPI. Also called implicit messaging. CompactLogix The Allen-Bradley controller family this workstation is modelled on (1769-L33ER). Consumed tag A controller tag whose value is read from another controller at a fixed interval (RPI). Continuous task The task that runs over and over as fast as it can. Here MainTask scans every 20 ms. CONTROL The structure the file instructions use to keep their place: .LEN, .POS and the status bits .EN .DN .ER .EM .UL. Control variable (CV) The output a control loop moves: a valve position, a heater power, a speed reference. Controller Organizer The tree on the left: controller tags, tasks, programs and routines, Add-On Instructions, data types, I/O configuration. Controller tags Tags every program can use. All I/O and alias tags are controller tags. Program tags belong to one program. Counter CTU and CTD count rung transitions into .ACC and set .DN when .ACC reaches .PRE. RES clears it. Cross Reference A list of every instruction that reads or writes a tag, across all routines, with the ones that write it marked Destructive. Ctrl+E. D Data context Which call of an Add-On Instruction you are looking at when its logic is open: the definition, or one backing tag's live values. Data type What a tag holds: BOOL, SINT, INT, DINT, REAL, STRING, a structure such as TIMER, a user-defined type or an Add-On Instruction's type. Deadband A range around the setpoint inside which the error is treated as zero, so the output does not chase noise. Destructive reference A place where an instruction writes a tag (OTE, MOV destination, a timer instruction on its timer). Cross Reference marks these with Y. Destructive reference An instruction that writes the tag (OTE, MOV destination, TON on its timer) rather than only reading it. Two destructive references to one bit is the classic double-coil bug. DINT A 32-bit signed integer. The default number type in Logix. Done bit (.DN) Set by a timer when .ACC reaches .PRE, by a counter when the count is reached, by a message when it completes. E EDS file Electronic Data Sheet: the text file a vendor ships that describes an EtherNet/IP device. The identity, the assemblies, the connections and their sizes come from it. Enable bit (.EN) True while the instruction's rung-in condition is true (timers, messages, file instructions). EnableIn / EnableOut The two built-in parameters of every Add-On Instruction: the rung-in condition it was called with, and the rung-out condition it passes on. EtherNet/IP CIP carried over standard Ethernet: explicit messages on TCP 44818 and cyclic I/O on UDP 2222. Event task A task that runs when something happens: an EVENT instruction, a trigger tag going true or changing, or a timeout with no trigger. Exclusive owner The one scanner allowed to write a device's outputs. A second one is refused with an ownership conflict. Explicit messaging Request and reply, one at a time, on TCP: read this attribute, write that tag. The MSG instruction does this. Expression A formula written out, as in CPT, CMP, FAL, FSC and Structured Text: Level > 50 AND NOT Fault, or Src[C.POS] * 2 + 1. F Fault handler A program under Controller Fault Handler that runs when a major fault happens. Here it runs once and the fault is cleared. Fault, major An error that stops the controller: mode shows Faulted and logic stops until Clear Faults, unless a fault handler program clears it. Integer divide by zero is one. Fault, minor An error that is logged while the scan carries on, such as arithmetic overflow. FBD_TIMER, FBD_COUNTER, FBD_ONESHOT The structures the Structured Text timers, counter and one-shots work on (TONR, TOFR, RTOR, CTUD, OSRI, OSFI). You set their inputs, such as .TimerEnable and .PRE, then call the instruction. FIFO First in, first out: FFL loads a value into an array, FFU unloads the oldest one. File instruction An instruction that works through an array one element at a time using a CONTROL tag: FAL, FSC, AVE, SRT, STD, COP, FLL. Force An override on an I/O point from the programming software, on top of the device (inputs) or the logic (outputs). Forces act only while enabled. Forward Open The CIP request that opens a connection. The scanner asks for sizes and an RPI, the device answers with the connection IDs, then cyclic data starts. FreqCommand / OutputFreq A drive's speed reference and its actual output frequency, in hundredths of a hertz: 6000 is 60.00 Hz. G GSV / SSV Get / Set System Value: read or write controller data such as the wall clock, task scan times or a module's EntryStatus. I I/O Configuration The part of the organizer listing the local cards and the Ethernet modules the controller owns. I/O Monitor The live list of every input and output point with its value, the device wired to it and the rungs that use it. Implicit messaging Cyclic I/O data with no request: both ends just send at the RPI. See Class 1 connection. In-Sight Cognex's vision system family. Over EtherNet/IP it exposes trigger and status bits and an inspection results area. Index pulse A short input once a pitch, at a fixed point of the card's travel, used to clock a shift register (BSL) so each card's result moves with it. On the inspection line it comes 0.85 of a pitch past the camera, after the result is in. Indirect addressing Choosing an array element with a tag instead of a number: Recipe[Step]. The element is picked each time the instruction runs. A subscript outside the array is a major fault. Inhibit Configured but switched off: an inhibited task or module stays in the project and does not run. Input / Output / InOut (parameter) How an Add-On Instruction parameter is passed. Input: the value is copied in. Output: the value is copied out. InOut: the logic works on the caller's tag directly. Instruction One element of a rung: a contact, a coil or a box such as TON, MOV or an Add-On Instruction. INT A 16-bit signed integer. Interlock A condition in series that must be true before an output may come on. J JSR / SBR / RET Jump To Subroutine, and the Subroutine and Return instructions that receive and hand back its parameters. L L5X The XML file Studio 5000 uses to export and import a project or a piece of one. File → Import L5X and Export L5X read and write it. Ladder Diagram (LD) The relay-style language of rungs between two power rails. The only language here. Latch / Unlatch OTL sets a bit and it stays set until OTU clears it, whatever the rungs do in between. LIFO Last in, first out: LFL loads a value into an array, LFU unloads the newest one. Listen-only A connection that receives a device's inputs without owning its outputs. In-Sight cameras do not offer one. Local tag A tag that belongs to an Add-On Instruction and exists once per backing tag: its timers, counters and working values. M Main routine The routine a program runs each scan. Other routines run only when a JSR calls them. MCR zone The rungs between two MCR instructions. While the first MCR rung is false, every rung in the zone is scanned as false, so ordinary outputs drop. It is not a substitute for a hard-wired safety relay. Module A device in the I/O configuration: a local card, or an EtherNet/IP device created from an EDS file. MSG The Message instruction: one explicit request to a device or another controller, with .EN .DN .ER status bits. N Neutral text The text form of a rung, for example XIC(Start)OTE(Motor); . Press Enter on a rung to edit it this way. No-test mask The last eight bytes of a recipe string, laid out like the row bytes: a well whose bit is 1 is not inspected, whatever it holds. O One-shot ONS, OSR, OSF: true for exactly one scan when the rung goes true (or false), so something happens once per event. Online Connected to the controller, so you see live values. Here the workstation is always online with its own controller unless you go offline. Online edit Changing logic while the controller runs. The change is pending (i), then accepted (I), then tested, then assembled. See the Online edits section. Operand A value or tag an instruction works on: the bit of an XIC, the source and destination of a MOV. OTE Output Energize: the coil. The bit follows the rung, every scan. Overlap A task triggered again before its previous run had started or finished. Counted in GSV(Task,name,OverlapCount). Ownership conflict The error a device returns when a second scanner asks for a connection it has already given to another. P Pen One tag plotted on a trend. A trend holds up to 8, each with its own colour. Pending edit An online edit that is still only in the editor: the i rung. The controller has not been given it yet. Periodic task A task that runs at a fixed period in milliseconds, for logic that must run at a known rate. PID Proportional, Integral, Derivative: the standard closed-loop control instruction. It compares the process variable with the setpoint and moves the control variable to close the gap. PLC Programmable Logic Controller: the industrial computer that reads inputs, runs the logic and writes outputs, over and over. Power flow Whether the rung is true up to a given point. The green highlighting on contacts and wires. Pre-emption A higher-priority task interrupting a lower one part-way through. Here it happens between rungs; the interrupted task then carries on from where it stopped. Preset (.PRE) The target of a timer (milliseconds) or counter (counts). Priority (task) 1 is highest, 15 lowest. Periodic and event tasks all outrank the continuous task. Process variable (PV) The measured value a control loop is controlling: a level, a temperature, a speed. Produced / consumed tag A tag one controller broadcasts and another receives cyclically. Not supported here. Produced tag A controller tag that is sent to another controller at a fixed interval (RPI). Program A group of routines with its own tags, scheduled in a task. Program mode Controller mode where inputs update but no logic runs and outputs are off. Program tags (local tags) Tags that belong to one program, listed under Parameters and Local Tags. Only that program's routines can use them, and inside that program they win over a controller tag of the same name. Q Quick Watch Your own list of tags with live values that you can change, shown in a floating window (Alt+3) and in the Watch tab of the output window. Saved with the project. R REAL A 32-bit floating-point number. Recipe string (card) The product's line in the product table: 1,NAME,64, then eight row bytes (a byte a row of the 8 × 8 card, the 128 bit being column 1), then eight no-test bytes. Sent in rows; the camera inspects in columns: well = (column − 1) × 8 + row. Remote controller Another controller this one shares produced and consumed tags with: simulated inside the project, or a real one reached through the bridge. Remote I/O Inputs and outputs on a block out on the network instead of in the controller chassis. Their tags are named after the module, such as RIO1:I.Pt00. Requested Packet Interval (RPI) How often, in milliseconds, each end of a cyclic connection sends its data. Retentive Keeps its value when the rung goes false. RTO is a retentive timer; only RES clears it. Rodless cylinder A pneumatic cylinder whose piston drives a carriage running along the outside of the tube instead of a rod, so a long stroke takes no more room than the tube. On the inspection line it pushes the empty tray from the lift into the fill position. Routine A list of rungs. Each program has a main routine and may have more. Run mode Controller mode where logic scans and outputs are driven. Rung One line of ladder: conditions on the left, outputs on the right. Rung comment Free text above a rung saying what it does. Ctrl+D. S Sandbox The free-form project where you place your own devices and wire them to I/O. Scan One pass: read inputs, run the tasks, write outputs. 20 ms here. Scanner The EtherNet/IP device that opens connections and owns the adapters: normally the PLC, here the workstation. Scope Where a tag lives and who can see it: the controller (everyone) or one program (only its routines). The Scope box in the tag editor switches between them. Seal-in A branch around a start contact using the output's own bit, so a momentary start keeps the output on until a stop breaks the rung. Sequencer SQO steps through an array of words and copies each to an output through a mask. Setpoint (SP) The value a control loop is trying to hold. SINT An 8-bit signed integer. Slot A position on the backplane. In a route, slot 0 is the CompactLogix controller. STRING Text of up to 82 characters with a .LEN and the characters in .DATA. Structure A tag made of members: TIMER, COUNTER, CONTROL, MESSAGE, a user-defined type or an Add-On Instruction tag. Structured Text (ST) A text language for routines: assignments with :=, IF, CASE, FOR, WHILE and REPEAT. Good for math, loops and decisions that are clumsy in ladder. See the Structured Text section. T Tag A named piece of controller memory. Logix addresses everything by tag name. Task What schedules programs: continuous, periodic or event. Each has a priority; a higher-priority task interrupts a lower one. TCP Client Socket A sandbox device that opens a plain TCP connection through the bridge to send and receive text, for equipment that speaks ASCII. Test (edits) Running the accepted edits in place of the original rungs without committing to them. Untest goes back. Test mode Controller mode where logic scans but outputs stay off. Timer TON, TOF, RTO: time a condition in milliseconds into .ACC and set .DN at .PRE. .TT is true while timing. Timing bit (.TT) True while a timer is counting: enabled and not done yet. Transfer platen A square plate on a carriage under a beam, with grippers at its corners, that picks a tray up (from the top of a tray lift, say), carries it along the beam and sets it down in a nest. On the inspection line it brings each empty tray over behind the full one going out; TT_Go runs it, TT_Grip closes the grippers, TT_AtStack, TT_AtNest and TT_Gripped say where it is and what it holds. Trap-door reject gate A section of the conveyor that drops open under a failed card so it falls into the bin below, instead of a pusher sweeping it off. Tray indexer (pawl indexer) A cylinder each end of a tray that lifts a pawl behind the tray's trailing rail and strokes it one row forward, then drops the pawl and runs back a row for the next stroke. Run right through, the pawls push the full tray out onto the conveyor. On the inspection line: Idx_Lift (pawls up), Idx_Step (a row), Idx_Out (the tray out); Idx_Home, Idx_Up, Idx_Ext, Idx_AtOut say where it is. Tray lift (tray destacker) A lift that holds a stack of empty trays and raises the top one to a transfer level, a tray pitch at a time, so a transfer can take it into the machine. Trend A chart of tag values against controller time. Each plotted tag is a pen. See the Trends section. Trigger The signal that makes a camera acquire an image. Over EtherNet/IP: set Trigger Enable, pulse Trigger, wait for the acknowledge and Results Valid. U UCMM Unconnected Message Manager: explicit messages sent without opening a connection first. UID / UIE User Interrupt Disable and Enable. Rungs between them cannot be interrupted by another task. User-Defined Data Type (UDT) A structure you define: named members of any type. A tag of that type gets Tag.Member for each. V Variable frequency drive (VFD) A drive that runs an AC motor at a commanded frequency. The built-in one uses the PowerFlex 525 tags: Start, Stop, FreqCommand out; Ready, Active, Faulted, OutputFreq in. Verify Check every rung for errors without running anything. The results are in the Errors window. W Watchdog The limit on how long a task may run. Here a loop that never ends is stopped with a major fault (type 6) instead of freezing the controller. X XIC Examine If Closed: a contact that is true when the bit is 1. XIO Examine If Open: a contact that is true when the bit is 0. Z Zone markers (i I r R d D) The letters in the rung margin during an online edit. Lower case is pending, upper case is in the controller: i/I the new rung, r/R the original it replaces, d/D a rung being deleted.

BSL/BSR, FFL/FFU, SQO, FLL and COP take the first element you want to use, e.g. Track[0] ; a bare array name means element 0. A BOOL array is one bit per element; BSL/BSR on a DINT array use all 32 bits of each element. Subroutines. JSR(Routine,2,In1,In2,Ret1) passes two inputs and takes one return: the routine starts with SBR(P1,P2) and ends with RET(Result) ; rungs after RET do not run. Jumps. JMP(Skip) continues at the rung holding LBL(Skip) , forward or back (a backward jump repeats rungs in the same scan, up to 1000 times). System values. GSV(WallClockTime,,LocalDateTime,Date[0]) fills 7 DINTs (year, month, day, hour, minute, second, microsecond); GSV(Task,MainTask,LastScanTime,Scan) and MaxScanTime are in microseconds; GSV(Module,Cam1,EntryStatus,St) gives 16#4000 while the connection runs, 16#3000 connecting, 16#1000 faulted, 0 simulated; FaultCode , Program … LastScanTime/DisableFlag , Controller … TimeSinceLastReset . SSV sets the clock, the task Watchdog/Priority/Rate and a program's DisableFlag.
